1removedimport LF.SFLCompat
2removed
3removed-- # Basics: Functional Programming in Lean
4removed
5removed-- Note to developers (Jonathan Chan @ionathanch):
6removed-- [BCP: Old comment -- might be out of date?] There should be some
7removed-- instruction on interaction with the IDE, namely:
8removed--
9removed-- - how to read the proof state
10removed--
11removed-- - clicking immediately after a tactic will show you what it changed
12removed--
13removed-- - clicking after each `h` in `rw [h₁, h₂, ...]` will show you what was
14removed-- rewritten
15removed--
16removed-- - hovering over a tactic will provide documentation on how to use it
17removed--
18removed-- - hovering over a definition will give its type
19removed--
20removed-- - hovering over a Unicode character will tell you how to type it
21removed--
22removed-- - Ctrl-clicking on a definition will take you to the definition location
23removed
24removed-- The *functional style* of programming is founded on simple, everyday
25removed-- mathematical intuitions: If a program has no side effects, such as reading
26removed-- or writing files or network packets, then (ignoring efficiency) all we need
27removed-- to understand about it is how it maps inputs to outputs. That is, we can
28removed-- think of it as just a concrete means for computing a mathematical function.
29removed-- This direct connection between programs and simple mathematical objects
30removed-- supports both formal correctness proofs and sound informal reasoning about
31removed-- program behavior. This is one sense of the word "functional" in "functional
32removed-- programming."
33removed
34removed-- The other sense in which functional programming is "functional" is that it
35removed-- emphasizes the use of functions as *first-class* values -- i.e., values
36removed-- that can be passed as arguments to other functions, returned as results,
37removed-- included in data structures, etc. The recognition that functions can be
38removed-- treated as data gives rise to a host of useful and powerful programming
39removed-- idioms.
40removed
41removed-- Other common features of functional languages include *algebraic data
42removed-- types* and *pattern matching*, which make it easy to construct and
43removed-- manipulate rich data structures, and *polymorphic types* supporting
44removed-- abstraction and code reuse. Lean offers all of these features.
45removed
46removed-- The first half of this chapter introduces some key elements of Lean's
47removed-- functional programming language. The second half introduces some basic
48removed-- *tactics* that can be used to prove properties of programs.
49removed
50removed-- ## Data and Functions
51removed
52removed-- Lean's set of built-in features is extremely small. For example, instead of
53removed-- providing the usual palette of atomic *datatypes* -- types whose values are
54removed-- data, such as booleans, integers, and strings -- as primitives, Lean's
55removed-- extensive standard library *defines* them, along with many common data
56removed-- structures besides, like lists and hash tables. It does so with a single
57removed-- powerful and general mechanism: the *inductive definition*. A type
58removed-- introduced this way is called an *inductive type*; the word "inductive"
59removed-- hints at the use of mathematical induction to prove statements about its
60removed-- values.
61removed
62removed-- To demonstrate how inductive definitions work, and illustrate their
63removed-- expressive power, we will recapitulate most of the datatype definitions we
64removed-- need in this course, rather than immediately referring to those in the
65removed-- standard library. We take care to harmonize the definitions we present with
66removed-- the actual definitions in the standard library, which we gradually
67removed-- introduce throughout the course. By the time you are finished, you will
68removed-- have a good grasp of how the Lean standard library is organized and how to
69removed-- efficiently navigate it.
70removed
71removed-- ### Days of the Week (Enumerated Types)
72removed
73removed-- To see how inductive datatype definitions work, let's start with a very
74removed-- simple example. The following declaration tells Lean that we are defining a
75removed-- set of data values, i.e. a *type*.
76removed
77removedinductive Day : Type where
78removed | monday
79removed | tuesday
80removed | wednesday
81removed | thursday
82removed | friday
83removed | saturday
84removed | sunday
85removed
86removed-- The new type is called `Day`, and its members are `monday`, `tuesday`, etc.
87removed-- These members are also called the *constructors* of the `Day` type, since
88removed-- they can be use to construct elements of that type. We often call this sort
89removed-- of inductive type an *enumerated type* since all values that have the type
90removed-- are enumerated in its definition.
91removed
92removed-- Having defined `Day`, we can write Lean functions that operate on days.
93removed
94removeddef nextWorkingDay (d : Day) : Day :=
95removed match d with
96removed | Day.monday => Day.tuesday
97removed | Day.tuesday => Day.wednesday
98removed | Day.wednesday => Day.thursday
99removed | Day.thursday => Day.friday
100removed | Day.friday => Day.monday
101removed | Day.saturday => Day.monday
102removed | Day.sunday => Day.monday
103removed
104removed-- Note that the argument and return types of this function are explicitly
105removed-- declared on the first line. Like most functional programming languages,
106removed-- Lean can often figure out these types for itself when they are not given
107removed-- explicitly -- i.e., it can do *type inference* -- but we'll generally
108removed-- include them to make reading easier.
109removed
110removed-- The `match` keyword is Lean's keyword for *pattern matching*: the
111removed-- functional programming way of examining and making decisions on data. When
112removed-- evaluating `match d with...`, Lean will examine the structure of `d` to see
113removed-- which case to execute; if `d` is `Day.monday`, for example, it will
114removed-- evaluate the first case of the `match` statement; if `d` is `Day.friday` it
115removed-- will evaluate the fifth case. (There is much more to say about pattern
116removed-- matching -- we'll introduce more of its features as the need arises.)
117removed
118removed-- You may notice that we qualified all the constructors before using them,
119removed-- writing `Day.monday` instead of just `monday`, for example. Lean places all
120removed-- constructors into a "namespace" associated with their type, and requires
121removed-- uses of those constructors to be prefixed with their namespace. There are a
122removed-- few circumstances in which this requirement can be relaxed, which we shall
123removed-- see in a little bit. For now we proceed by fully qualifying all constructor
124removed-- names.
125removed
126removed-- If you ever need to know the type of **any** pattern, object, or function,
127removed-- you can hover over it with your mouse in any editor that supports Lean,
128removed-- like VS Code or the web version we provide.
129removed
130removed-- Having defined a function, we should check that it works on some examples.
131removed-- There are a few different ways to do this in Lean. One is to use the
132removed-- `#eval` command to evaluate a compound expression involving
133removed-- `nextWorkingDay`. (Lean's responses are shown in comments.)
134removed
135removed#eval nextWorkingDay Day.friday
136removed
137removed#eval nextWorkingDay (nextWorkingDay Day.saturday)
138removed
139removed-- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1):
140removed-- Where are we showing responses in comments? I don't see them. MWH: I
141removed-- think we landed at three possibilities:
142removed--
143removed-- 1. Don't include them
144removed--
145removed-- 2. Include responses in comments
146removed--
147removed-- 3. Use `#guard_msgs(...)` to include the responses and also check that
148removed-- they are correct. I vote that we do the last of these. It's useful for
149removed-- quietening the build, for helping readers be sure that things are
150removed-- working as expected, and for keeping things up to date.
151removed--
152removed-- Also: Further down in the text it says you can hover over the
153removed-- definitions to see their output. This is not happening in the web
154removed-- interface; it just shows the type of `#eval` and the types of the
155removed-- arguments, not the "message" it produces.
156removed
157removed-- We can also record what we *expect* the result of calling a function to be
158removed-- in the form of a Lean `example`:
159removed
160removedexample : nextWorkingDay (nextWorkingDay Day.saturday) = Day.tuesday := by
161removed rfl
162removed
163removed-- This declaration asserts that the second working day after `saturday` is
164removed-- `tuesday`. Having made the assertion, we can also ask Lean to *verify* it.
165removed-- The `by rfl` can be read as "The assertion we've just made can be proved by
166removed-- observing that both sides of the equality evaluate to the same term."
167removed
168removed-- `rfl` stands for "reflexivity," which is the principle that any value is
169removed-- equal to itself. After evaluation, both sides of the equality are the same
170removed-- value, so the assertion is true by reflexivity. If we had made a different
171removed-- assertion, such as
172removed-- `example : nextWorkingDay (nextWorkingDay Day.saturday) =
173removed-- Day.monday`, then
174removed-- Lean would not be able to verify it and would instead signal an error. Try
175removed-- it out!
176removed
177removed-- ### Aside: Using the VS Code Lean Extension
178removed
179removed-- If you have a computer handy, this would be an excellent moment to fire up
180removed-- VS Code with the Lean extension or the Lean web interface and try it for
181removed-- yourself. Load this file, `Basics.lean`, from the book's Lean sources, find
182removed-- the above example, and observe the result in the Lean InfoView panel.
183removed
184removed-- In VS Code, development of Lean code is supported by the [Lean
185removed-- Extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=leanprover.lean4),
186removed-- which provides an interactive "InfoView" panel that displays the results of
187removed-- commands like `#eval`, as well as the current goal state when working on
188removed-- proofs. You can hover over expressions in the source code to see their
189removed-- types, and you can click on the results in the InfoView to navigate to
190removed-- their definitions. This makes it easier to understand how your code is
191removed-- being interpreted by Lean and to debug any issues that arise.
192removed
193removed-- The InfoView always follows your cursor, and Lean typechecks the file as
194removed-- you edit it, so you can see the results of your changes immediately. You
195removed-- can also use the InfoView to explore the definitions of functions and types
196removed-- that you're using, which can be very helpful for understanding how they
197removed-- work.
198removed
199removed-- If you haven't already, either install the Lean Extension in VS Code and
200removed-- open the `Basics.lean` file or open `Basics.lean` on the interactive Lean
201removed-- web client to see the InfoView in action. Try hovering over the
202removed-- `nextWorkingDay` function and the `Day` type to see their definitions, and
203removed-- experiment with adding your own `#eval` commands to test other inputs.
204removed
205removed-- Note to developers (mwhicks1):
206removed-- What is the "interactive web client"? Is it just the Verso-rendered
207removed-- book? That's not interactive in the sense that you can see `#eval`
208removed-- output or change code. Let's link the thing we mean.
209removed
210removed-- For `#eval` and other commands, we show Lean's responses in comments; if
211removed-- you hover over the `#eval` commands above, you will see the popup that
212removed-- contains the output should match what's in the comment below. Experiment
213removed-- with adding your own `#eval` commands explore how other functions work.
214removed
215removed-- ### Booleans
216removed
217removed-- Following the pattern of the days of the week above, we can define the
218removed-- standard type `Bool` of booleans by enumerating its members `true` and
219removed-- `false`.
220removed
221removed-- We define our own `MyBool` to teach the concept of building booleans from
222removed-- scratch. Our definition is equivalent to Lean's built-in `Bool`, which we
223removed-- switch to later.
224removed
225removedinductive MyBool : Type where
226removed | true
227removed | false
228removed
229removed-- The next command opens the namespace associated with the `MyBool` type, so
230removed-- subsequent definitions will be part of the `MyBool` namespace. In Lean,
231removed-- functions on a type are typically defined in that type's namespace, which
232removed-- avoids name clashes with functions of the same name elsewhere (e.g.,
233removed-- functions on the built-in `Bool` type). We give a full treatment of
234removed-- namespaces below.
235removed
236removednamespace MyBool
237removed
238removed-- Functions over booleans can be defined in the same way as functions over
239removed-- days of the week.
240removed
241removeddef not (b : MyBool) : MyBool :=
242removed match b with
243removed | MyBool.true => MyBool.false
244removed | MyBool.false => MyBool.true
245removed
246removeddef and (b1 : MyBool) (b2 : MyBool) : MyBool :=
247removed match b1 with
248removed | MyBool.true => b2
249removed | MyBool.false => MyBool.false
250removed
251removeddef or (b1 : MyBool) (b2 : MyBool) : MyBool :=
252removed match b1 with
253removed | MyBool.true => MyBool.true
254removed | MyBool.false => b2
255removed
256removed-- The last two definitions illustrate Lean's syntax for multi-argument
257removed-- functions. The corresponding multi-argument *application* syntax is
258removed-- illustrated by the following tests, which effectively constitute a complete
259removed-- specification -- a truth table -- for the `or` function:
260removed
261removedexample : or MyBool.true MyBool.false = MyBool.true := by rfl
262removedexample : or MyBool.false MyBool.false = MyBool.false := by rfl
263removedexample : or MyBool.false MyBool.true = MyBool.true := by rfl
264removedexample : or MyBool.true MyBool.true = MyBool.true := by rfl
265removed
266removed-- We can define new symbolic notations for existing definitions. Don't worry
267removed-- for now about how the notation is defined.
268removed
269removedlocal prefix:40 (priority := high) "!" => not
270removedlocal infixl:35 (priority := high) " && " => and
271removedlocal infixl:30 (priority := high) " || " => or
272removed
273removedexample : (MyBool.false || MyBool.false || MyBool.true) = MyBool.true := by rfl
274removed
275removedexample : (!MyBool.false) = MyBool.true := by rfl
276removed
277removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): nand ⭐
278removed
279removed-- The `sorry` keyword is a placeholder for an incomplete proof or definition.
280removed-- We use it in exercises to indicate the parts that we're leaving for you --
281removed-- i.e., your job is to replace `sorry` with real definitions and proofs.
282removed
283removed-- Remove `sorry` below and complete the definition of the following function.
284removed-- The function should return `MyBool.true` if either or both of its inputs
285removed-- are `MyBool.false`. Make sure that the `example` assertions below can be
286removed-- verified by Lean.
287removed
288removeddef nand (b1 : MyBool) (b2 : MyBool) : MyBool
289removed := sorry
290removed
291removedexample : nand MyBool.true MyBool.false = MyBool.true := sorry
292removedexample : nand MyBool.false MyBool.false = MyBool.true := sorry
293removedexample : nand MyBool.false MyBool.true = MyBool.true := sorry
294removedexample : nand MyBool.true MyBool.true = MyBool.false := sorry
295removed
296removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): and3 ⭐
297removed
298removed-- Do the same for the `and3` function below. This function should return
299removed-- `true` when all of its inputs are `true`, and `false` otherwise.
300removed
301removeddef and3 (b1 : MyBool) (b2 : MyBool) (b3 : MyBool) : MyBool
302removed := sorry
303removed
304removedexample : and3 MyBool.true MyBool.true MyBool.true = MyBool.true := sorry
305removedexample : and3 MyBool.false MyBool.true MyBool.true = MyBool.false := sorry
306removedexample : and3 MyBool.true MyBool.false MyBool.true = MyBool.false := sorry
307removedexample : and3 MyBool.true MyBool.true MyBool.false = MyBool.false := sorry
308removed
309removed-- ### Basic Proofs
310removed
311removed-- Now that we've defined some basic functions on booleans, let's see how to
312removed-- *prove* some simple properties of those functions. Here is a simple rule
313removed-- about `&&`:
314removed
315removed-- - `(MyBool.true && b) = b`
316removed
317removed-- This is an example of a *proposition*, a logical *claim* that we can try to
318removed-- prove. It says that `MyBool.true && b` is equal to `b` for every `MyBool`
319removed-- `b`.
320removed
321removed-- How might we write this proposition in Lean?
322removed
323removed-- - `theorem true_and : ∀ (b : MyBool), (MyBool.true && b) = b`
324removed
325removed-- The keyword `theorem` indicates that we are stating (and eventually
326removed-- proving) a proposition; the text after the first `:` is the proposition we
327removed-- want to prove. You'll notice that this proposition looks a lot like the one
328removed-- we wrote above, but with some additional symbols in front. The `∀` symbol,
329removed-- pronounced "forall" and written `\all` or `\forall`, is called a *universal
330removed-- quantifier* because it *quantifies* the variable `b` that appears in the
331removed-- proposition. Quantifying a variable with a `∀` means that the proposition
332removed-- applies to all possible values of its type; here, we annotate `b` with the
333removed-- type `MyBool` to signify that the proposition holds for all `b`s of type
334removed-- `MyBool`.
335removed
336removed-- Now that we've stated the theorem we'd like to prove, let's set about
337removed-- proving it.
338removed
339removedtheorem true_and : ∀ (b : MyBool), (MyBool.true && b) = b := by
340removed intro b
341removed rfl
342removed
343removed-- What does this mean?
344removed
345removed-- First we have the `by` keyword, which signals to Lean that we are beginning
346removed-- a sequence of *tactics*. The `intro b` and `rfl` that you see after the
347removed-- `by` are examples of tactics.
348removed
349removed-- Tactics manipulate the *proof state*, as you can can see the in the Lean
350removed-- InfoView panel. The proof state is divided into the *context*, before the
351removed-- ⊢, and the *goal*, after the ⊢. The context records what we know at each
352removed-- point in the proof; the goal is what we are trying to prove at each point.
353removed
354removed-- A tactic manipulates both the goal and the context to get the goal into a
355removed-- shape that is closer to the one we want. A tactic can also *close* (solve)
356removed-- the current goal, finishing its proof.
357removed
358removed-- Let's walk through the example above with this terminology in mind.
359removed
360removed-- Note to developers (mwhicks1):
361removed-- The theorem below has wonderful explaining what's going on, but it is
362removed-- not typeset. Are we planning to fix that problem? I re-flowed the text
363removed-- so it reads better on the WWW in case not.
364removed
365removedtheorem true_and_explained : ∀ (b : MyBool), (MyBool.true && b) = b := by
366removed /- Move your cursor (click) here to see the initial proof state in
367removed the InfoView. The context (before the ⊢) is empty.
368removed The goal is `∀ (b : MyBool), (MyBool.true && b) = b`. -/
369removed intro b
370removed /- Now click here to see the new proof state that results from the
371removed tactic. Notice how `intro b` has changed the _context_: it now
372removed contains `b : MyBool`.
373removed
374removed The `intro` tactic is used to name variables quantified by a `∀`.
375removed Since we are trying to prove a property of all `MyBools`, we
376removed proceed by introducing an unknown `MyBool` `b` and prove
377removed the property holds for `b`, regardless of what it is. Informally,
378removed this move can be read, "We want to prove <some property> for all
379removed `MyBool`s `b`. So suppose `b` is some arbitrary `MyBool`...
380removed <and then go on to prove the property for this particular `b`>..."
381removed Since `b` was chosen arbitrarily, we've now proved the property
382removed for all `b`.
383removed
384removed A proof of a theorem beginning with a ∀ will typically start with
385removed an `intro`.
386removed
387removed As in the `example`s above, we can use the `rfl` tactic,
388removed which closes goals about equality where both sides are equal to
389removed one another according to the principle of reflexivity. Now,
390removed inspecting our goal will show that it is `(MyBool.true && b) = b`,
391removed which may not appear to be equal to itself. However, the tactic
392removed _evaluates_ both sides of the equality before comparing them. In
393removed this case, if we look at the definition of `and`, we can see that,
394removed when its first argument is `MyBool.true`, the result is its second
395removed argument. So the two terms `MyBool.true && b` and `b` are in fact
396removed equal because one evaluates to the other.
397removed -/
398removed rfl
399removed /- The proof is now done! The Lean InfoView tells us there are "No goals". -/
400removed
401removed-- It's also important to point out that, as with languages like Python and
402removed-- Haskell, Lean is *whitespace-sensitive*. That is, the indentation in proofs
403removed-- is important and changing it can change the meaning of the proof, usually
404removed-- causing the proof to break. If we had instead written the following:
405removed
406removedsf_expect_failure
407removed theorem true_and_wrong : ∀ (b : MyBool), (MyBool.true && b) = b := by
408removed intro b
409removed rfl
410removed
411removed-- Lean would complain, since the `rfl` is not at the same level of
412removed-- indentation as the `intro b`, so it does not recognize these two tactics as
413removed-- being sequential in the way they should be. In general, sequential tactics
414removed-- applied to the same goal must be on subsequent lines at the same level of
415removed-- indentation or separated on the same line by a `;` like so:
416removed
417removedtheorem true_and' : ∀ (b : MyBool), (MyBool.true && b) = b := by
418removed intro b; rfl
419removed
420removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): false_or_exercise ⭐
421removed
422removed-- Here's a simple proof for you to try. Remove `sorry` and fill in the proof.
423removed
424removedtheorem false_or : ∀ (b : MyBool), (MyBool.false || b) = b := by
425removed sorry
426removed
427removed-- While in this book we often use `sorry` as a placeholder for you to replace
428removed-- with an actual proof, in general, `sorry` tells Lean that we want to skip
429removed-- trying to prove a theorem and just accept it as a given. This can be useful
430removed-- for developing longer proofs.
431removed
432removed-- Be careful, though: every time you say `sorry` you are leaving a door open
433removed-- for total nonsense to enter Lean's safe, formally checked world!
434removed
435removed-- Note to developers (Harrison Goldstein @hgoldstein95):
436removed-- In the terse .lean output this ends up looking like an exercise.
437removed
438removedsf_experiment
439removed theorem really_bad : MyBool.true = MyBool.false := by sorry
440removed
441removed-- The facts we've seen so far about booleans are quite simple, so the tactics
442removed-- we need to prove them are also quite simple. Over the course of this book
443removed-- we are going to introduce new tactics and proof techniques gradually,
444removed-- enriching the propositions we can prove along the way.
445removed
446removed-- Now that we've seen how to define our own booleans and prove some basic
447removed-- properties about them, let's switch to Lean's built-in `Bool` type, which
448removed-- has the same structure but comes with a lot of useful functions and lemmas.
449removed
450removedend MyBool
451removed
452removed-- ### Types
453removed
454removed-- Every expression in Lean has a type describing what sort of value it
455removed-- computes. The `#check` command asks Lean to print the type of an
456removed-- expression.
457removed
458removed#check Bool.true
459removed
460removed-- If the expression after `#check` is followed by a colon and a type, Lean
461removed-- will verify that the type of the expression matches the given type and
462removed-- signal an error if not.
463removed
464removed#check (Bool.true : Bool)
465removed#check (Bool.not Bool.true : Bool)
466removed
467removed-- Functions like `Bool.not` are themselves ordinary values, just like
468removed-- `Bool.true` and `Bool.false`. Their types are called *function types*, and
469removed-- they are written with arrows.
470removed
471removed#check Bool.not
472removed
473removed-- The type of `Bool.not`, written `Bool → Bool` and pronounced "`Bool` arrow
474removed-- `Bool`," can be read, "Given an input of type `Bool`, this function
475removed-- produces an output of type `Bool`." Similarly, the type of `Bool.and`,
476removed-- written `Bool → Bool → Bool`, can be read, "Given two inputs, each of type
477removed-- `Bool`, this function produces an output of type `Bool`."
478removed
479removed-- ### Aside: Unicode in Lean
480removed
481removed-- Note that → is a unicode symbol, not a simple ASCII character. The Lean
482removed-- Extension for VS Code provides convenient shortcuts for entering such
483removed-- symbols. Simply type `\` (backslash) followed by the name of the symbol,
484removed-- and the extension will automatically replace it with the actual symbol. For
485removed-- example, typing `\->` or `\to` will produce →, and `\lambda` will produce
486removed-- λ. To find out what backslash sequence produces a unicode symbol that you
487removed-- can see on the screen, just hover over it. To see all of the Unicode
488removed-- shortcodes, open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows/Linux or
489removed-- Cmd+Shift+P on macOS), type "Lean 4: Show Unicode Input Abbreviations", and
490removed-- press Enter.
491removed
492removed-- ### New Types from Old
493removed
494removed-- Note to developers (Harrison Goldstein @hgoldstein95):
495removed-- I feel like this section has too much content in terse, but I don't
496removed-- want to unilaterally make that call. TODO
497removed
498removed-- The enumerated types we have seen so far are so-named because their
499removed-- definitions explicitly enumerate a finite set of elements, their
500removed-- constructors. Here is a more interesting inductive type definition,
501removed-- `Color`, where one of the constructors takes an argument:
502removed
503removedinductive RGB : Type where
504removed | red
505removed | green
506removed | blue
507removed
508removedinductive Color : Type where
509removed | black
510removed | white
511removed | primary (p : RGB)
512removed
513removed-- An `inductive` definition does two things:
514removed
515removed-- - It introduces a set of new *constructors*. E.g., `RGB.red`,
516removed-- `Color.primary`, `Bool.true`, `Bool.false`, `Day.monday`, etc. are
517removed-- constructors.
518removed
519removed-- - It groups them into a new named type, like `Bool`, `RGB`, or `Color`.
520removed
521removed-- *Constructor expressions* are formed by applying a constructor to zero or
522removed-- more other constructors or constructor expressions, obeying the declared
523removed-- number and types of the constructor arguments. E.g., these are valid
524removed-- constructor expressions...
525removed
526removed-- - `RGB.red`
527removed-- - `Bool.true`
528removed-- - `Color.primary` `RGB.red`
529removed
530removed-- ...but these are not:
531removed
532removed-- - `RGB.red Color.primary`
533removed-- - `Bool.true RGB.red`
534removed-- - `Color.primary (Color.primary RGB.red)`
535removed
536removed-- We can define functions on colors using pattern matching, just as we did
537removed-- for `Day` and `Bool`.
538removed
539removeddef monochrome (c : Color) : Bool :=
540removed match c with
541removed | Color.black => Bool.true
542removed | Color.white => Bool.true
543removed | Color.primary p => Bool.false
544removed
545removed-- Since the `primary` constructor takes an argument, a pattern that matches
546removed-- `.primary` should include either a variable, a constant of appropriate
547removed-- type, or `_`. Lean's convention is to use a `_` (called a *wildcard*) when
548removed-- the argument to a constructor doesn't matter. In the definition of
549removed-- `monochrome`, we don't use the argument to `Color.primary`, so a more
550removed-- idiomatic definition would be:
551removed
552removeddef monochrome' (c : Color) : Bool :=
553removed match c with
554removed | Color.black => Bool.true
555removed | Color.white => Bool.true
556removed | Color.primary _ => Bool.false
557removed
558removed-- We can use a constant argument to `Color.primary` to match a specific
559removed-- primary color:
560removed
561removeddef isRed (c : Color) : Bool :=
562removed match c with
563removed | Color.black => Bool.false
564removed | Color.white => Bool.false
565removed | Color.primary RGB.red => Bool.true
566removed | Color.primary _ => Bool.false
567removed
568removed-- The pattern `Color.primary RGB.red` will match only when `c` is
569removed-- `Color.primary` with the argument `RGB.red`. The pattern `Color.primary _`
570removed-- matches every `Color.primary` color, but because patterns are checked in
571removed-- order, the `Color.primary _` case will never be reached if the color is
572removed-- `RGB.red`.
573removed
574removed-- An alternative way to write the same function would be to explicitly nest
575removed-- match statements:
576removed
577removeddef isRed' (c : Color) : Bool :=
578removed match c with
579removed | Color.black => Bool.false
580removed | Color.white => Bool.false
581removed | Color.primary r =>
582removed match r with
583removed | RGB.red => Bool.true
584removed | _ => Bool.false
585removed
586removed-- This `isRed'` function produces the same result as `isRed` but illustrates
587removed-- the *use* of a pattern matching variable: the `Color.primary r` pattern
588removed-- stores the `RGB` argument into variable `r`, and then pattern matches on
589removed-- that argument to produce the final result.
590removed
591removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): is_weekend ⭐
592removed
593removed-- Define a function that takes a `Day` and returns true if the day is a
594removed-- weekend, and false otherwise.
595removed
596removed-- Then, fill in right-hand sides of the `example` blocks below. If you've
597removed-- done both correctly, the blocks will produce no errors and contain no
598removed-- `sorry`.
599removed
600removed-- Hint: You could write this function by pattern matching on each possible
601removed-- day of the week, or you could try to come up with a shorter solution...
602removed
603removeddef is_weekend (d : Day) : Bool
604removed := sorry
605removed
606removedexample : is_weekend Day.sunday = true := sorry
607removedexample : is_weekend Day.friday = false := sorry
608removed
609removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): is_inversion ⭐
610removed
611removed-- Define a function that takes two colors and returns `true` if the second
612removed-- color is an *inversion* of the first, and false otherwise.
613removed
614removed-- Inversion is defined by cases: Black is an inversion of white, and vice
615removed-- versa. Red is an inversion of blue, and vice versa. Green is not an
616removed-- inversion of anything.
617removed
618removed-- As before, write the right-hand sides of the `example` blocks to ensure
619removed-- they pass with no `sorry`.
620removed
621removeddef is_inversion (c1 c2 : Color) : Bool
622removed := sorry
623removed
624removedexample : is_inversion Color.black Color.white = true := sorry
625removedexample : is_inversion Color.white Color.black = Bool.true := sorry
626removedexample : is_inversion (Color.primary RGB.red) (Color.primary RGB.blue) = Bool.true :=
627removed sorry
628removedexample : is_inversion (Color.primary RGB.green) (Color.primary RGB.red) = Bool.false :=
629removed sorry
630removed
631removed-- ### Namespaces
632removed
633removed-- We have been using Lean's system of *namespaces* for managing potentially
634removed-- conflicting names. Now we have seen enough that we can look more closely at
635removed-- how it works.
636removed
637removed-- When we enclose a collection of declarations in `namespace X ... end X`,
638removed-- references from outside this collection to names declared within it are
639removed-- referred to with prefix `X.`, like `X.foo` instead of just `foo`. In large
640removed-- Lean developments, namespaces are used to organize definitions and theorems
641removed-- the same way modules are used in other programming languages.
642removed
643removeddef myFoo : Bool := true
644removednamespace Playground
645removeddef myFoo : RGB := RGB.blue
646removedend Playground
647removed
648removed#check myFoo -- Bool
649removed#check Playground.myFoo -- RGB
650removed
651removed-- Namespaces can be opened and closed as often as you like to add new
652removed-- definitions and access old ones. When inside a `namespace`, definitions
653removed-- from the that namespace can be referenced without prefixes.
654removed
655removednamespace Playground
656removed-- this refers to the `myFoo` we defined in the `Playground` namespace previously
657removeddef myBar : RGB := myFoo
658removedend Playground
659removed
660removed#check Playground.myBar -- RGB
661removed
662removed-- When a type is created, a `namespace` with the same name as that type is
663removed-- implicitly created as well; definitions on that type are available inside
664removed-- that `namespace` without a prefix. In the example below, we can use the
665removed-- `blue` constructor without qualification because we are inside the `RGB`
666removed-- `namespace`, which is the same as `blue`'s type.
667removed
668removednamespace RGB
669removeddef myBlue : RGB := blue
670removedend RGB
671removed
672removed-- Top-level definitions can also be prefixed by a namespace, which opens the
673removed-- namespace temporarily for the body of the definition.
674removed
675removed-- Note to developers (Claude, NOW):
676removed-- Rendering bug in **student** and **terse** (solutions is fine): the
677removed-- leading `--- …` triple-dash comment lines in this block and the next
678removed-- one each render **twice** in a row (e.g. two consecutive
679removed-- `--- this works, because …` lines). The solutions build shows each
680removed-- once, so this is a Verso rendering quirk with `---`-style comments in
681removed-- the elided builds, not a source duplication.
682removed
683removed--- this works, because the definition is qualified by `RGB.`
684removeddef RGB.myOtherBlue : RGB := myBlue
685removed
686removed#check RGB.myBlue -- RGB
687removed#check RGB.myOtherBlue -- RGB
688removed
689removed-- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1):
690removed-- see my comment later in the file about guard msgs
691removed--
692removed-- `--- this doesn't work; the identifier is unknown
693removed-- /-- error: Unknown identifier `myBlue` -/
694removed-- #guard_msgs(error) in
695removed-- #check myBlue -- unknown identifier`
696removed
697removed-- Similarly, we could rewrite the definition of `nextWorkingDay` from above
698removed-- inside the `Day` namespace like so:
699removed
700removeddef Day.nextWorkingDay' (d : Day) : Day :=
701removed match d with
702removed | monday => tuesday
703removed | tuesday => wednesday
704removed | wednesday => thursday
705removed | thursday => friday
706removed | friday => monday
707removed | saturday => monday
708removed | sunday => monday
709removed
710removed-- We can also use `open` to bring the definitions of a namespace into the
711removed-- current scope; after that, we can refer to any of the namespace's
712removed-- definitions without a prefix.
713removed
714removednamespace MyNamespace
715removeddef myDef : Bool := Bool.true
716removedend MyNamespace
717removed
718removedopen MyNamespace
719removed
720removed#check myDef -- Bool
721removed
722removed-- If we only want to bring *some*, rather than all, of the definitions of a
723removed-- namespace into the current scope, we can use the `open (...)` form:
724removed
725removednamespace MyOtherNamespace
726removeddef myHiddenDef : Bool := Bool.true
727removeddef myVisibleDef : Bool := Bool.false
728removedend MyOtherNamespace
729removed
730removedopen MyOtherNamespace (myVisibleDef)
731removed
732removed-- `myVisibleDef` is now usable without qualification:
733removed#check myVisibleDef -- Bool
734removed
735removed-- But `myHiddenDef`, which we did not `open`, still needs its full name;
736removed-- using it unqualified is an error:
737removed
738removedsf_expect_failure
739removed #check myHiddenDef
740removed
741removed-- In fact, this is what exactly what Lean does with the standard `Bool` type
742removed-- by default. Since it is such an important part of many proofs and programs,
743removed-- Lean implicitly `open`s many of `Bool`s functions and constructors.
744removed-- Accordingly, we can use constructors like `true` and `false` and functions
745removed-- like `not` without qualifying them with `Bool.`.
746removed
747removed#check Bool.true -- Bool
748removed#check true -- Bool
749removed
750removed-- Finally, Lean can often automatically figure out which namespace a
751removed-- qualified name lives in, saving us the need to explicitly specify it every
752removed-- time we use the name. Instead of the fully qualified style (e.g.,
753removed-- `Day.monday`), we can opt for an implicitly qualified style, writing just
754removed-- `.monday`.
755removed
756removed-- When we do this, Lean tries to resolve the `.monday` name by seeing what
757removed-- its expected type is and inferring which namespace it must be from based on
758removed-- that type. If there is only one such namespace (i.e., if it is unambiguous
759removed-- which constructor we're referring to), then it will automatically resolve
760removed-- to the expected value.
761removed
762removed-- So, for example, we can also write `nextWorkingDay` as follows, using the
763removed-- shorter style for both the value being matched upon and the value being
764removed-- returned:
765removed
766removeddef nextWorkingDay' (d : Day) : Day :=
767removed match d with
768removed | .monday => .tuesday
769removed | .tuesday => .wednesday
770removed | .wednesday => .thursday
771removed | .thursday => .friday
772removed | .friday => .monday
773removed | .saturday => .monday
774removed | .sunday => .monday
775removed
776removed-- In the function above, both the type of `d` and the return type of the
777removed-- function are declared to be `Day`s. When we use the `.monday` style in the
778removed-- function body, Lean can figure out that we must mean `Day.monday`. However,
779removed-- in the example below, Lean can't figure out which version of `.true` we
780removed-- mean, since it could either be `Bool.true` or `MyBool.true`. In this case,
781removed-- it will raise an error:
782removed
783removedsf_expect_failure
784removed #check .true
785removed
786removed-- Here, though, because `not` is a function that takes a `Bool` argument,
787removed-- Lean knows that `.true` must here be a `Bool`:
788removed
789removed#check (Bool.not .true)
790removed
791removed-- ### Exercise (0 stars): custom_namespace_checks
792removed
793removed-- Predict the output of each of the statements below. Do you think their
794removed-- results would change depending on which namespace the statements appear in?
795removed-- How?
796removed
797removed-- #check .black -- Write your prediction here.
798removed-- #check Color.black -- Write your prediction here.
799removed-- #check RGB -- Write your prediction here.
800removed-- #check Playground.myFoo -- Write your prediction here.
801removed
802removed-- Once you have written your predictions, copy the lines from the comment
803removed-- into an active section of the book to evaluate them.
804removed
805removed-- Note to developers (mwhicks1):
806removed-- This namespace section is great, but it interrupts the pedagogical flow
807removed-- of the presentation of inductive types. We were prevoiusly looking at
808removed-- constructors With one argument, then there was this big digression, and
809removed-- now we are back to two. Are we able to move the namespace stuff to the
810removed-- end of this section (Data and Functions)? Then we can start it by
811removed-- saying we are finishing with it but readers can skip it if they prefer
812removed-- to "follow their nose" regarding namespaces, and come back when they
813removed-- want to know more.
814removed
815removed-- ### Constructors with Multiple Parameters (Tuple Types)
816removed
817removednamespace Playground
818removed
819removed-- A single constructor of an inductive type can have multiple parameters, not
820removed-- just zero or one. This feature is one way to define *tuple types* in Lean,
821removed-- which are like record/struct types but their fields are accessed by their
822removed-- *position* in patterns rather than by a specific (field) *name*.
823removed
824removed-- As an example, consider representing the four bits in a nibble (half a
825removed-- byte). We first define a datatype `Bit` that resembles `Bool` (using the
826removed-- constructors `b1` and `b0` for the two possible bit values) and then define
827removed-- the datatype `Nibble`, which is a tuple of four bits.
828removed
829removedinductive Bit : Type where
830removed | b1
831removed | b0
832removed
833removedinductive Nibble : Type where
834removed | bits (x0 x1 x2 x3 : Bit)
835removed
836removed#check (.bits .b1 .b0 .b1 .b0 : Nibble)
837removed
838removed-- Note: The `bits` constructor illustrates a feature of multi-parameter
839removed-- declarations, both for constructors and for functions: Instead of writing
840removed-- `(x0 : Bit) (x1 : Bit) ...` we write `(x0 x1 ... : Bit)` since all of the
841removed-- variables have the same type. We could have done the same with the function
842removed-- definition `or` above, writing `or (b1 b2 : MyBool)` rather than
843removed-- `or (b1 : MyBool) (b2 : MyBool)`.
844removed
845removed-- The `bits` constructor acts as a wrapper for its contents. Unwrapping is
846removed-- done by pattern matching, as in the `allZero` function below, which tests a
847removed-- Nibble to see if all its bits are `b0`.
848removed
849removeddef allZero (nb : Nibble) : Bool :=
850removed match nb with
851removed | .bits .b0 .b0 .b0 .b0 => true
852removed | .bits _ _ _ _ => false
853removed
854removedexample : allZero (.bits .b1 .b0 .b1 .b0) = false := by rfl
855removedexample : allZero (.bits .b0 .b0 .b0 .b0) = true := by rfl
856removed
857removedend Playground
858removed
859removed-- #### Aside: Structures
860removed
861removed-- When defining an inductive type with just case, we can instead use a
862removed-- `structure`:
863removed
864removedstructure NibbleStruct : Type where
865removed x0 : Playground.Bit
866removed x1 : Playground.Bit
867removed x2 : Playground.Bit
868removed x3 : Playground.Bit
869removed
870removed-- Rather than construct this as `.bits .b0 .b0 .b0 .b0` we construct it as:
871removed
872removed-- #check NibbleStruct.mk .b0 .b0 .b0 .b0
873removed
874removed-- The `.mk` constructor is created for us.
875removed
876removed-- ### Natural Numbers
877removed
878removed-- We put this portion of the chapter in a namespace so that our own
879removed-- definition of numbers does not interfere with the one from the standard
880removed-- library. In the remainder of the book, we'll use the standard library's.
881removed
882removednamespace NatPlayground
883removed
884removed-- All the types we have defined so far -- both enumerated types such as
885removed-- `Day`, `Bool`, and `Bit` and tuple types such as `Nibble` built from them
886removed-- -- are finite. The natural numbers, on the other hand, are an infinite set,
887removed-- so we'll need to use a slightly richer form of inductive type declaration
888removed-- to represent them: *recursive* inductive types.
889removed
890removed-- While the need for recursion is unequivocal, there are many
891removed-- recursively-defined representations of numbers to choose from. You are
892removed-- certainly familiar with decimal notation (base 10), using the digits 0
893removed-- through 9, for example, to form the number 123. You have likely also
894removed-- encountered hexadecimal notation (base 16), in which the same number is
895removed-- represented as 7B, or octal (base 8), where it is 173, or binary (base 2),
896removed-- where it is 1111011. Using an enumerated type to represent digits, we could
897removed-- use any of these as our representation of natural numbers.
898removed
899removed-- There are circumstances in which each of these choices is useful. The
900removed-- binary representation is valuable in computer hardware because the digits
901removed-- can be represented with just two distinct voltage levels, resulting in
902removed-- simple circuitry.
903removed
904removed-- Here we choose an even simpler *unary* (base 1) representation, for the
905removed-- sake of streamlining proofs. As a Lean datatype, it uses two constructors.
906removed-- The `zero` constructor represents the number zero. The `succ` constructor
907removed-- can be applied to the representation of the natural number `n`, yielding
908removed-- the representation of `n+1`, where `succ` stands for "successor." The
909removed-- number `n` is then represented by `n` applications of `succ` to `zero`.
910removed
911removed-- Here is the complete datatype definition:
912removed
913removedinductive Nat : Type where
914removed | zero
915removed | succ (n : Nat)
916removed
917removed-- Naturally, Lean has its own definition of natural numbers, with some
918removed-- slightly fancy features for reasoning and notation. As we are just
919removed-- beginning to reason about natural numbers, we use our own definition here
920removed-- and introduce the Lean one in a later chapter.
921removed
922removed-- We'll define some shorthands for numbers, putting them in the `Nat`
923removed-- namespace so we don't need to use `.` notation everywhere.
924removed
925removednamespace Nat
926removed
927removeddef one : Nat := succ zero
928removeddef two : Nat := succ one
929removeddef three : Nat := succ two
930removeddef four : Nat := succ three
931removed
932removed-- We can also write functions on `Nat`.
933removed
934removeddef pred (n : Nat) : Nat :=
935removed match n with
936removed | zero => zero
937removed | succ n' => n'
938removed
939removeddef minustwo (n : Nat) : Nat :=
940removed match n with
941removed | zero => zero
942removed | succ (zero) => zero
943removed | succ (succ n') => n'
944removed
945removed#eval minustwo four
946removed
947removed-- Look the types of `succ`, `pred`, and `minustwo`:
948removed
949removed#check succ -- Nat → Nat
950removed#check pred -- Nat → Nat
951removed#check minustwo -- Nat → Nat
952removed
953removed-- These are all things that can be applied to a number to yield a number.
954removed-- However, there is a fundamental difference between `Nat.succ` and the other
955removed-- two: functions like `Nat.pred` and `Nat.minustwo` are defined by giving
956removed-- *computation rules* -- e.g., the definition of `Nat.pred` says that
957removed-- `Nat.pred (succ (succ zero))` can be simplified to `succ zero` -- while the
958removed-- definition of `Nat.succ` has no such behavior attached. Although it is like
959removed-- a function in the sense that it can be applied to an argument, it does not
960removed-- *do* anything at all! It is just the way we write down numbers.
961removed
962removed-- We can also define *recursive functions*: functions that call themselves
963removed-- repeatedly down to a base case. Recursion is the essence of repeated
964removed-- computation in functional programming; in this course, we will make
965removed-- extensive use of recursive functions.
966removed
967removed-- We first define a simple recursive function, `even`, then a slightly more
968removed-- sophisticated recursive function `add`.
969removed
970removeddef even (n : Nat) : Bool :=
971removed match n with
972removed | zero => true
973removed | succ (zero) => false
974removed | succ (succ n') => even n'
975removed
976removedexample : even one = false := by rfl
977removedexample : even four = true := by rfl
978removed
979removed-- We could define `odd` by a similar recursive declaration, but here is a
980removed-- simpler way:
981removed
982removeddef odd (n : Nat) : Bool :=
983removed not (even n)
984removed
985removedexample : odd one = true := by rfl
986removedexample : odd four = false := by rfl
987removed
988removed-- This function takes multiple parameters, recursing on the second:
989removed
990removeddef add (n : Nat) (m : Nat) : Nat :=
991removed match m with
992removed | zero => n
993removed | succ m' => succ (add n m')
994removed
995removed#eval add one two -- succ (succ (succ zero)) -- aka, three!
996removed
997removed-- We can also define infix notation for our `add` functions.
998removed
999removed-- Don't worry too much about how this is defined; we will return to it in
1000removed-- more detail later.
1001removed
1002removedscoped infixl:65 " + " => add
1003removed
1004removed#eval one + two -- succ (succ (succ zero)) -- aka, three again.
1005removed
1006removed-- ## Proof by Rewriting
1007removed
1008removed-- ### Proving properties about functions in Lean
1009removed
1010removed-- Being recursive on a `Nat` and returning `Nat` as well, `add` is the first
1011removed-- example of a more sophisticated class of functions. In this chapter and
1012removed-- beyond, we will *prove* properties about recursive functions like `add`
1013removed-- over inductive datatypes like `Nat`, using *simplification rules* about
1014removed-- their behavior.
1015removed
1016removed-- Here is a simplification rule about `add`:
1017removed
1018removed-- - `n + zero = n`
1019removed
1020removed-- In Lean, this rule looks like this:
1021removed
1022removedtheorem add_zero : ∀ n : Nat, n + zero = n := by
1023removed intro n
1024removed rfl
1025removed
1026removed#check add_zero
1027removed
1028removed-- Using our simplification rule `add_zero`, we can carry out a simple proof
1029removed-- about natural numbers!
1030removed
1031removedtheorem add_zero_zero : ∀ n : Nat, n + zero + zero = n := by
1032removed intro n
1033removed rewrite [add_zero]
1034removed rewrite [add_zero]
1035removed rfl
1036removed
1037removed-- We'll walk through this proof in the next section.
1038removed
1039removed-- ### Proof state and tactics
1040removed
1041removed-- The `rewrite` tactic in the proof of `add_zero_zero` is used to transform
1042removed-- the goal of the proof according to an equality. The `add_zero` in brackets
1043removed-- is an *argument* to the `rewrite` tactic.
1044removed
1045removed-- Let's walk through the theorem again in detail.
1046removed
1047removedtheorem add_zero_zero_explained : ∀ n : Nat, n + zero + zero = n := by
1048removed intro n
1049removed /- After introducing `n`, our goal is `n + zero + zero = n`.
1050removed What can we do to simplify this expression? If you hover your cursor over the
1051removed `add_zero` in the rewrite below, you can see its type: `n + zero = n`. So,
1052removed we can use that rewrite rule to transform an appearnce of `n + zero` in the goal to `n`. -/
1053removed rewrite [add_zero]
1054removed /- Now click here to see the new proof state that results from the tactic.
1055removed Notice how `n + zero + zero` changes to `n + zero` in the goal. -/
1056removed rewrite [add_zero]
1057removed /- Again the goal changes, from `n + zero` to `n`. Now the proof state
1058removed is an equality with both sides equal, so it can be closed by the
1059removed tactic `rfl`. -/
1060removed rfl
1061removed /- The proof is now done! The Lean InfoView tells us there are "No goals". -/
1062removed
1063removed-- Give this proof a try (it's similar):
1064removed
1065removedtheorem add_zero_zero_zero : ∀ n : Nat, n + zero + zero + zero = n := by
1066removed sorry
1067removed
1068removed-- ### The `rewrite` tactic
1069removed
1070removed-- As we saw above, the tactic that tells Lean to rewrite (part of) a goal or
1071removed-- hypothesis based on a rule is called `rewrite`. Given the rule `add_zero`,
1072removed-- which states that `n + zero` is equal to `n` for any `n`, we can replace
1073removed-- any `n + zero` in our proof with `n` via `rewrite [add_zero]`.
1074removed
1075removed-- The `rewrite` tactic takes its argument(s) in square brackets.
1076removed
1077removed-- ### The `rfl` tactic
1078removed
1079removed-- The `rfl` tactic closes a goal of the shape `a = a`, for any `a`. It checks
1080removed-- that both sides of the equality are *definitionally equal* -- that is, that
1081removed-- they reduce to the same term. (So, in particular, a term is always
1082removed-- definitionally equal to itself.)
1083removed
1084removed-- ### A New `add` Rule
1085removed
1086removed-- Here is another fundamental rule about addition:
1087removed
1088removed-- `n + (succ m) = succ (n + m)`.
1089removed
1090removed-- This is the rule we need to push `succ` around.
1091removed
1092removed-- Here it is in Lean:
1093removed
1094removedtheorem add_succ : ∀ n m : Nat, n + (succ m) = succ (n + m) := by
1095removed intro n m
1096removed rfl
1097removed
1098removed-- Now, let's use `add_succ` in a proof:
1099removed
1100removedtheorem add_one (n : Nat) : n + (succ zero) = succ n + zero := by
1101removed rewrite [add_succ]
1102removed rewrite [add_zero]
1103removed rewrite [add_zero]
1104removed rfl
1105removed
1106removed-- Again, we recommend stepping through these proofs in VS Code -- that is,
1107removed-- moving past each tactic with your cursor to see how it changes the proof
1108removed-- state and hovering over each argument to `rewrite` to see its type.
1109removed
1110removed-- ### Irreducibility, Rewriting, and Proof Engineering
1111removed
1112removed-- Lean, like any other programming language, has conventions and best
1113removed-- practices for writing good software. In object-oriented programming, for
1114removed-- example, it is considered good practice not to access the fields of an
1115removed-- object directly, but instead to use getter and setter methods. This helps
1116removed-- to encapsulate the object's definition, so that, if its fields or
1117removed-- implementation ever change, the interface it exposes to the outside world
1118removed-- remains the same. In simple examples such conventions may seem trivial or
1119removed-- even silly; in complex codebases, it is the only way to maintain crucial
1120removed-- invariants that prevent a system from becoming unmaintainable.
1121removed
1122removed-- The same principle applies to definitions and proofs in Lean. In idiomatic
1123removed-- Lean, it is considered poor style to "peek" through definitions by using
1124removed-- `rfl` to implicitly simplify expressions that aren't syntactically
1125removed-- identical. If you take a look at the proofs of `add_zero` and `add_succ`
1126removed-- above, you will notice this is exactly what we did when we used the `rfl`
1127removed-- tactic.
1128removed
1129removed-- However, the foundational theorems `add_zero` and `add_succ` provide a
1130removed-- characterization of the behavior of `add` that makes using `rfl` to
1131removed-- simplify expressions unnecessary; instead, we can rewrite by these theorems
1132removed-- anywhere we want to describe how `add` evaluates.
1133removed
1134removed-- In this text, to enforce idiomatic style, we mark definitions with
1135removed-- `attribute [irreducible]` to prevent this peeking, also called
1136removed-- **definitional equality abuse** (**defeq abuse**, for short). We place this
1137removed-- attribute after the proofs of `add_zero` and `add_succ`, and can then
1138removed-- rewrite by these theorems anywhere we want to describe how `add` evaluates.
1139removed-- In real-world Lean developments, the style of writing proofs using
1140removed-- simplification rules is both standard and expected. Definitions in those
1141removed-- developments may not use `attribute [irreducible]`, but they *will* have
1142removed-- definitions that are not meant to be reduced.
1143removed
1144removed-- We use `attribute [irreducible]` here to enforce the style of using
1145removed-- simplification rules now so that it is natural to you moving forward. We
1146removed-- will relax this discipline in later chapters.
1147removed
1148removedattribute [irreducible] add
1149removed
1150removed-- These characterizing theorems also follow a particular pattern. Let's look
1151removed-- again at the definition of `add`, without the `+` notation for maximum
1152removed-- clarity:
1153removed
1154removednamespace AddPlayground
1155removed
1156removeddef add (n : Nat) (m : Nat) : Nat :=
1157removed match m with
1158removed | zero => n
1159removed | succ m' => succ (add n m')
1160removed
1161removedtheorem add_zero : ∀ (n : Nat), add n zero = n := by
1162removed intro n
1163removed rfl
1164removed
1165removedtheorem add_succ : ∀ (n m : Nat), add n (succ m) = succ (add n m) := by
1166removed intro n m
1167removed rfl
1168removed
1169removedend AddPlayground
1170removed
1171removed-- Each of `add_zero` and `add_succ` correspond to one branch of the `match`
1172removed-- statement defining `add` and describe how the evaluation of `add` proceeds
1173removed-- in that case. The `add_zero` theorem describes how `add n zero` evaluates,
1174removed-- while `add_succ` describes (symbolically) how `add n (succ m)` evaluates.
1175removed-- Because these theorems describe how to simplify more complex expressions
1176removed-- involving `add`, we call them *simplification lemmas* for `add`.
1177removed
1178removed-- These are instances of a general pattern: each definition operating over
1179removed-- enumerated types like `Nat`, `Bool`, `Day`, or `Color` needs a
1180removed-- simplification lemma for each branch of control flow through the function.
1181removed
1182removed-- So, for example, we need two simplification lemmas for the definition of
1183removed-- `pred`:
1184removed
1185removedtheorem pred_zero : pred zero = zero := by rfl
1186removedtheorem pred_succ n : pred (succ n) = n := by rfl
1187removed
1188removed-- Now that we have defined and proved `pred`'s simplification lemmas, we can
1189removed-- mark it `irreducible`, to enforce rewriting by these lemmas.
1190removed
1191removedattribute [irreducible] pred
1192removed
1193removed-- Similarly, for each of the three branches of the definition of `even`, we
1194removed-- need one simplification lemma:
1195removed
1196removedtheorem even_zero : even zero = true := rfl
1197removedtheorem even_one : even (succ zero) = false := rfl
1198removedtheorem even_succ_succ n : even (succ (succ n)) = even n := rfl
1199removed
1200removedattribute [irreducible] even odd
1201removed
1202removed-- In the remainder of this textbook, we will pair definitions with their
1203removed-- simplification lemmas. After proving these lemmas, instead of using `rfl`
1204removed-- to peek through the definitions, we will prefer rewriting by the lemmas.
1205removed
1206removed-- Eventually, we will introduce a way to automatically apply these
1207removed-- simplfication lemmas, but for now these tactics are forbidden by our
1208removed-- autograder. Real-world Lean uses automation extensively, and you will learn
1209removed-- to do so by the end of this book and in the following volumes. For the
1210removed-- moment it is important that you work through these early concepts by hand,
1211removed-- without automation. By the time the more powerful tools are introduced, you
1212removed-- will have the foundation to use them with precision and skill.
1213removed
1214removed-- ### Working with Numerals
1215removed
1216removed-- We know from our definitions above that `one` is just `succ zero`, `two` is
1217removed-- `succ one`, and so on. We can write rules for these equalities too:
1218removed
1219removedtheorem one_eq_succ_zero : one = succ zero := by rfl
1220removedtheorem two_eq_succ_one : two = succ one := by rfl
1221removedtheorem three_eq_succ_two : three = succ two := by rfl
1222removedtheorem four_eq_succ_three : four = succ three := by rfl
1223removed
1224removed-- We can rewrite with these rules to expand numerals into their definitions,
1225removed-- which allows us to use our `add` rules. Here's an example of how to start a
1226removed-- proof this way.
1227removed
1228removed-- Finish the proof using the `add` rules:
1229removed
1230removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
1231removed-- Should this be marked / formatted as an exercise or at least a
1232removed-- WORKINCLASS? RAB: Let's decide once we choose how to present the laws.
1233removed-- My intuition is yes.
1234removed
1235removedtheorem one_plus_one_eq_two : (one + one : Nat) = two := by
1236removed rewrite [one_eq_succ_zero]
1237removed sorry
1238removed
1239removed-- Try the same for `two + two = four`.
1240removed
1241removedtheorem two_plus_two_eq_four : two + two = four := by
1242removed sorry
1243removed
1244removed-- Now that we know how addition is defined, we can use it to define
1245removed-- multiplication:
1246removed
1247removeddef mul (n m : Nat) : Nat :=
1248removed match m with
1249removed | zero => zero
1250removed | succ m' => (mul n m') + n
1251removed
1252removedscoped infixl:70 " * " => mul
1253removed
1254removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): mul_simpl_rules ⭐
1255removed
1256removed-- Multiplication, like any function we will prove properties about, also has
1257removed-- simplification rules.
1258removed
1259removed-- Remove `sorry` and prove the simplification rules for `mul` below. You will
1260removed-- likely find the proofs of the simplification rules for `add` to be helpful
1261removed-- as a model.
1262removed
1263removed-- Note to developers:
1264removed-- @rogerburtonpatel: it would be nice if we could get the theorem
1265removed-- *statements* inside a `solution!` block as well.
1266removed
1267removedtheorem mul_zero : ∀ n : Nat, n * zero = zero := by
1268removed sorry
1269removed
1270removedtheorem mul_succ : ∀ n m : Nat, n * (succ m) = (n * m) + n := by
1271removed sorry
1272removed
1273removedattribute [irreducible] mul
1274removed
1275removed-- Prove these thoerems using rewriting with the simplification rules for
1276removed-- addition and multiplication.
1277removed
1278removed-- (We have given you the first line.) Notice how `rewrite` can take any
1279removed-- number of arguments. You can use this rewrite with all of the
1280removed-- simplification rules at once, for example.
1281removed
1282removed-- After each rewrite, check the proof state by placing the cursor immediately
1283removed-- after a rule to see how the goal is changing. This happens naturally as you
1284removed-- write the proof, which makes it convenient to use `rewrite` blocks with
1285removed-- multiple rules.
1286removed
1287removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): test_mul_add ⭐⭐
1288removed
1289removedtheorem zero_add_one : (zero + one : Nat) = one := by
1290removed rewrite [one_eq_succ_zero]
1291removed sorry
1292removed
1293removedtheorem one_add_one : (one + one : Nat) = two := by
1294removed rewrite [one_eq_succ_zero]
1295removed sorry
1296removed
1297removed
1298removedtheorem zero_mul_two : (zero * two : Nat) = zero := by
1299removed rewrite [two_eq_succ_one, one_eq_succ_zero]
1300removed sorry
1301removed
1302removedtheorem one_mul_two : (one * two : Nat) = two := by
1303removed rewrite [two_eq_succ_one, one_eq_succ_zero]
1304removed sorry
1305removed
1306removedtheorem two_mul_two : (two * two : Nat) = four := by
1307removed rewrite [two_eq_succ_one, one_eq_succ_zero]
1308removed sorry
1309removed
1310removed-- When we say that Lean relies on almost nothing that's truly built-in, we
1311removed-- really mean it: even testing equality is not a primitive operation, but an
1312removed-- ordinary function that we could re-implement ourselves as users.
1313removed
1314removed-- Here is a function `beq` that tests natural numbers for equality, yielding
1315removed-- a boolean.
1316removed
1317removeddef beq (n m : Nat) : Bool :=
1318removed match n with
1319removed | zero => match m with
1320removed | zero => true
1321removed | succ _ => false
1322removed | succ n' => match m with
1323removed | zero => false
1324removed | succ m' => beq n' m'
1325removed
1326removed-- We could also write this by pattern matching on both `n` and `m` at the
1327removed-- same time:
1328removed
1329removeddef beq' (n m : Nat) : Bool :=
1330removed match n, m with
1331removed | zero, zero => true
1332removed | zero, succ _ => false
1333removed | succ _, zero => false
1334removed | succ n', succ m' => beq n' m'
1335removed
1336removed-- The definitions of `beq` and `beq'` are equivalent.
1337removed
1338removed-- Similarly, the `ble` function tests whether its first argument is less than
1339removed-- or equal to its second argument, yielding a boolean.
1340removed
1341removeddef ble (n m : Nat) : Bool :=
1342removed match n with
1343removed | zero => true
1344removed | succ n' =>
1345removed match m with
1346removed | zero => false
1347removed | succ m' => ble n' m'
1348removed
1349removedtheorem zero_ble (n : Nat) : ble zero n = true := by rfl
1350removedtheorem succ_ble_zero (n : Nat) : ble (succ n) zero = false := by rfl
1351removedtheorem succ_ble_succ (n m : Nat) : ble (succ n) (succ m) = ble n m := by rfl
1352removed
1353removedexample : ble two two = true := by rfl
1354removedexample : ble two four = true := by rfl
1355removedexample : ble four two = false := by rfl
1356removed
1357removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): blt ⭐
1358removed
1359removed-- Define a less-than function in terms of `ble`.
1360removed
1361removeddef blt (n m : Nat) : Bool
1362removed := sorry
1363removed
1364removedexample : blt two two = false := sorry
1365removedexample : blt two four = true := sorry
1366removedexample : blt four two = false := sorry
1367removed
1368removedattribute [irreducible] blt ble
1369removed
1370removed-- We'll be using `beq` a lot, so let's give it an infix notation.
1371removed
1372removedscoped infixl:30 " == " => beq
1373removed
1374removed-- We now have two symbols that both look like equality: `=` and `==`. We'll
1375removed-- have much more to say about their differences and similarities later. For
1376removed-- now, notice that `x = y` is a logical *claim* -- a "proposition" -- that we
1377removed-- can try to prove, while `x == y` is a boolean *expression* whose value
1378removed-- (either `true` or `false`) Lean can compute.
1379removed
1380removed-- We can also now define the simplification lemmas for `beq` with our new
1381removed-- notation, one for each of the four cases of control flow through the
1382removed-- function.
1383removed
1384removedtheorem zero_zero_beq_true : (zero == zero) = true := by rfl
1385removedtheorem zero_succ_beq_false (n : Nat) : (zero == (succ n)) = false := by rfl
1386removedtheorem succ_zero_beq_false (n : Nat) : ((succ n) == zero) = false := by rfl
1387removedtheorem succ_succ_beq (n m : Nat) : ((succ n) == (succ m)) = (n == m) := by rfl
1388removed
1389removedattribute [irreducible] beq
1390removed
1391removed-- ## General Proofs about Natural Numbers
1392removed
1393removed-- We now begin to make claims about *general* natural numbers.
1394removed
1395removed-- We begin by making a universal claim about all numbers `n` and `m` that are
1396removed-- equal to each other (`n = m`). The arrow symbol is pronounced "implies."
1397removed-- Enter it with `\to` or `\->` or `\r`.
1398removed
1399removed-- The `intro` tactic moves the universally quantified variables and the
1400removed-- hypothesis into the context, giving them names. The goal is now to prove
1401removed-- `n + n = m + m` under the assumption `h : n = m`.
1402removed
1403removed-- The tactic that tells Lean to perform replacement is one we have seen
1404removed-- before: `rewrite`. It can take a hypothesis from the context as an
1405removed-- argument, just like it can take a previously proved theorem. In this case,
1406removed-- we want to rewrite with the hypothesis `h`, which says that `n` and `m` are
1407removed-- equal, so that we can replace `n` with `m` in the goal.
1408removed
1409removed-- After the rewrite, the goal is `m + m = m + m`, which can be closed by
1410removed-- `rfl`.
1411removed
1412removedtheorem add_id_example : ∀ n m : Nat,
1413removed n = m → n + n = m + m := by
1414removed intro n m
1415removed intro h
1416removed rewrite [h]
1417removed rfl
1418removed
1419removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): add_id_exercise ⭐
1420removed
1421removed-- Remove `sorry` and fill in the proof.
1422removed
1423removedtheorem add_id_exercise : ∀ n m o : Nat,
1424removed n = m → m = o → n + m = m + o := by
1425removed sorry
1426removed
1427removed-- The `#check` command can also be used to examine the statements of
1428removed-- previously declared lemmas and theorems.
1429removed
1430removed#check mul_zero -- ∀ (n : Nat), n * 0 = 0
1431removed#check mul_succ -- ∀ (n m : Nat), n * Nat.succ m = n + n * m
1432removed
1433removed-- ### Type Annotations
1434removed
1435removed-- Note that you may see a slight discrepancy in the output: `#check` might
1436removed-- show `NatPlayground.Nat.mul_zero (n : Nat) : n * zero = zero`.
1437removed-- Qualification, like `mul_zero` to `NatPlayground.Nat.mul_zero`, can happen
1438removed-- automatically when printing a type in Lean.
1439removed
1440removed-- Another simple but important-to-note automatic display feature is
1441removed-- *indexing*: `mul_zero : ∀ (n : Nat), n * zero = zero` may display as
1442removed-- `mul_zero (n : Nat) : n * zero = zero`.
1443removed
1444removed-- Note how the `(n : Nat)` has moved *before* the colon and has lost the ∀.
1445removed-- The two definitions are equivalent for our purposes right now, but the
1446removed-- second is preferred in idiomatic Lean developments.
1447removed
1448removed-- Note to developers:
1449removed-- Per Github discussion: Lean's convention is to prefer the declaration
1450removed-- header style (`mul_zero (n : Nat) : n * zero = zero`) over universal
1451removed-- quantification style (`mul_zero : ∀ (n : Nat), n * zero = zero`). We
1452removed-- probably still want to teach the universal quantification style at
1453removed-- first, but should switch over to declaration header style quickly since
1454removed-- that is the idiomatic Lean way to do things.
1455removed--
1456removed-- BCP: Needs to be explained better. And the "indexing" part doesn't

1460removed-- ## Proof by Case Analysis
1461removed
1462removed-- Of course, not everything can be proved by simple calculation and
1463removed-- rewriting: In general, the presence of unknown, hypothetical values
1464removed-- (arbitrary numbers, booleans, etc.) can block a proof.
1465removed
1466removed-- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1):
1467removed-- At the moment our convention for unfinished proofs is to end with sorry
1468removed-- and guard the "proof uses sorry" warning. However after going through
1469removed-- MRC's comments here I realized we don't need to do this: we can leave
1470removed-- the proof unfinished and guard the error about goals being unsolved.
1471removed-- IMO this is preferable because it illustrates more directly what is
1472removed-- going on.
1473removed--
1474removed-- However, before we can do this, I think we may require a minor change
1475removed-- to how Verso files get compiled to Lean. If we just naïvely strip out
1476removed-- #guard msgs, the generated .lean files will now have errors since those
1477removed-- commands were guarding actual errors rather than just warnings. So we
1478removed-- would need a way to have .lean files with errors in them permitted by
1479removed-- the make command, or we would need to leave in #guard msgs that are
1480removed-- guarding actual errors.
1481removed--
1482removed-- BCP: This is a tricky balancing act!! Let's talk about it.
1483removed--
1484removed-- `/--
1485removed-- error: unsolved goals
1486removed-- n : Nat
1487removed-- ⊢ (succ n == zero) = false
1488removed-- -/
1489removed-- #guard_msgs(error) in
1490removed-- example : ∀ n : Nat,
1491removed-- (succ n == zero) = false := by
1492removed-- intro n
1493removed-- /-
1494removed-- We can't rewrite by any lemmas here because `n` is unknown!
1495removed-- -/`
1496removed
1497removedexample : ∀ n : Nat,
1498removed (succ n == zero) = false := by
1499removed intro n
1500removed /-
1501removed We can't rewrite by any lemmas here because `n` is unknown!
1502removed -/
1503removed sorry
1504removed
1505removed-- The tactic that tells Lean to consider separate cases is called `cases`.
1506removed
1507removedtheorem add_one_neb_zero : ∀ n : Nat,
1508removed (succ n == zero) = false := by
1509removed intro n
1510removed cases n
1511removed case zero =>
1512removed rewrite [succ_zero_beq_false]
1513removed rfl
1514removed case succ n' =>
1515removed rewrite [succ_zero_beq_false]
1516removed rfl
1517removed
1518removed-- The `cases` tactic generates *two* subgoals, which we must prove,
1519removed-- separately, in order to get Lean to accept the theorem.
1520removed
1521removed-- The generated subgoals are tagged by the names of the constructors.
1522removed-- `case zero =>` and `case succ n' =>` select which subgoal to work on next
1523removed-- and introduce variable names.
1524removed
1525removed-- Note also that when we enter a `case`, we increase the level of indentation
1526removed-- at which we are working by two spaces.
1527removed
1528removed-- The `cases` tactic can be used with any inductively defined datatype. For
1529removed-- example, we use it next to prove that boolean negation is involutive (that
1530removed-- is, that negation is its own inverse).
1531removed
1532removedtheorem not_involutive : ∀ b : Bool, (!!b) = b := by
1533removed intro b
1534removed cases b
1535removed case false =>
1536removed rewrite [Bool.not_false, Bool.not_true]
1537removed rfl
1538removed case true =>
1539removed rewrite [Bool.not_true, Bool.not_false]
1540removed rfl
1541removed
1542removed-- You may also notice that in the above proof we have used some rewrite rules
1543removed-- that we didn't previously prove in this file! These proofs come from Lean's
1544removed-- standard library, in particular from the section about booleans. Having
1545removed-- access to these already-proved theorems about booleans instead of needing
1546removed-- them to prove them ourselves is a big advantage of using Lean's built-in
1547removed-- `Bool` type instead of defining our own.
1548removed
1549removed-- In a few chapters we will discuss how to search through the standard
1550removed-- library for theorems like these. For now, note that if you hover over the
1551removed-- name of these theorems in VSCode, the Lean 4 extension will show you their
1552removed-- type, i.e., what the theorem proves.
1553removed
1554removed-- We can also have nested case analysis:
1555removed
1556removedtheorem and_commutative : ∀ b c : Bool,
1557removed (b && c) = (c && b) := by
1558removed intro b c
1559removed cases b
1560removed case true =>
1561removed cases c
1562removed case true =>
1563removed rewrite [Bool.and_self]
1564removed rfl
1565removed case false =>
1566removed rewrite [Bool.and_false, Bool.and_true]
1567removed rfl
1568removed case false =>
1569removed cases c
1570removed case true =>
1571removed rewrite [Bool.and_true, Bool.and_false]
1572removed rfl
1573removed case false =>
1574removed rewrite [Bool.and_self]
1575removed rfl
1576removed
1577removedtheorem and3_exchange : ∀ b c d : Bool,
1578removed ((b && c) && d) = ((b && d) && c) := by
1579removed intro b c d
1580removed cases b
1581removed case false =>
1582removed cases c
1583removed case true =>
1584removed cases d
1585removed case false =>
1586removed rewrite [Bool.and_true, Bool.and_self]
1587removed rfl
1588removed case true =>
1589removed rewrite [Bool.and_true]
1590removed rfl
1591removed case false =>
1592removed cases d
1593removed case false =>
1594removed rewrite [Bool.and_self]
1595removed rfl
1596removed case true =>
1597removed rewrite [Bool.and_self, Bool.and_true]
1598removed rfl
1599removed case true =>
1600removed cases c
1601removed case true =>
1602removed cases d
1603removed case false =>
1604removed rewrite [Bool.and_self, Bool.and_false, Bool.and_true]
1605removed rfl
1606removed case true =>
1607removed rewrite [Bool.and_self]
1608removed rfl
1609removed case false =>
1610removed cases d
1611removed case false =>
1612removed rewrite [Bool.and_false]
1613removed rfl
1614removed case true =>
1615removed rewrite [Bool.and_false, Bool.and_true, Bool.and_self]
1616removed rfl
1617removed
1618removed-- As you can see, proofs by cases can become very verbose. We will introduce
1619removed-- some tactics for writing shorter proofs by case analysis in `Tactics.lean`.
1620removed
1621removed-- ### New Tactics: `rewrite ... at` and `exact`
1622removed
1623removed-- Some new tactics will be useful for the exercises ahead.
1624removed
1625removed-- The `rewrite ... at` tactic can be used to rewrite in a hypothesis instead
1626removed-- of the goal. For example, if `h : P` is in the context and we have a rule
1627removed-- `P = Q`, then `rewrite [P = Q] at h` changes the hypothesis to `h : Q`.
1628removed
1629removed-- The `exact` tactic closes a goal by providing the exact proof of the goal.
1630removed-- For example, if `h : P` is in the context and the goal is `P`, then
1631removed-- `exact h` closes the goal. You can also transform `h` slightly, but we will
1632removed-- explain how when we get to an example where we need to.
1633removed
1634removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): or_false_true ⭐⭐
1635removed
1636removed-- Prove the following claim.
1637removed
1638removed-- Tip: the rewrite rule to simplify `(b || false)` is called `Bool.or_false`.
1639removed
1640removedtheorem or_false_true : ∀ b : Bool,
1641removed (b || false) = true → b = true := by
1642removed sorry
1643removed
1644removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): zero_nbeq_add_1 ⭐
1645removed
1646removedtheorem zero_neb_add_one : ∀ n : Nat,
1647removed (zero == succ n) = false := by
1648removed sorry
1649removed
