1657removed-- ### More on Notation (Optional)
1658removed
1659removed-- Lean has a very flexible notation system. Operators like `+` and `*` are
1660removed-- defined with specified precedence and associativity. For example, `+` has
1661removed-- precedence 65 and is left-associative, while `*` has precedence 70 and is
1662removed-- also left-associative. This means that `1+2*3*4` is parsed as
1663removed-- `1+((2*3)*4)`.
1664removed
1665removed-- You can define custom notation using the `notation`, `infixl`, `infixr`,
1666removed-- `prefix`, and `postfix` commands.
1667removed
1668removed-- Lean handles notation scoping through namespaces and *type classes*. The
1669removed-- numeric literal `3` can be interpreted as `Nat`, `Int`, `Float`, etc.,
1670removed-- depending on the expected type, thanks to Lean's `OfNat` type class. We
1671removed-- will explain type classes in more detail in the `Typeclasses` chapter,
1672removed-- found in `Typeclasses.lean`.
1673removed
1674removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
1675removed-- In SF-classic, there was some special typesetting magic for chapter
1676removed-- titles that turned them into HTML links...
1677removed
1678removed-- ### Structural Recursion (Optional)
1679removed
1680removed-- Here is a copy of the definition of `even`:
1681removed
1682removeddef even' (n : Nat) : Bool :=
1683removed match n with
1684removed | zero => true
1685removed | succ (zero) => false
1686removed | succ (succ n') => even n'
1687removed
1688removed-- When Lean checks this definition, it verifies that the recursion
1689removed-- terminates. Specifically, it checks that one of the parameters is
1690removed-- *structurally decreasing* -- that each recursive call made in the body of
1691removed-- the definition is made on an argument that is smaller than the original
1692removed-- input. In `even` example above, the argument to the recursive call to
1693removed-- `even` is the variable `n'`. Because of our pattern match, we know that `n`
1694removed-- is equal to `succ (succ n')`, and therefore that `n'` is smaller than `n`.
1695removed-- This makes `n'` an acceptable argument to `even` for Lean's termination
1696removed-- checker, and so this recursive definition is accepted.
1697removed
1698removed-- This requirement is a fundamental feature of Lean's design: In particular,
1699removed-- it guarantees that every function that can be defined in Lean will
1700removed-- terminate on all inputs. However, because Lean's termination analysis is
1701removed-- not always able to figure things out automatically, it is sometimes
1702removed-- necessary to provide hints or write functions in slightly different ways.
1703removed
1704removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): decreasing ⭐⭐
1705removed
1706removed-- To get a concrete sense of how termination checking works in Lean, find a
1707removed-- way to write a sensible recursive definition (of a simple function on
1708removed-- numbers, say) that does actually terminate on all inputs, but that Lean
1709removed-- will reject because it cannot automatically prove termination.
1710removed
1711removed-- ### Binary Numerals
1712removed
1713removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): binary ⭐⭐⭐
1714removed
1715removed-- We can generalize our unary representation of natural numbers to the more
1716removed-- efficient binary representation by treating a binary number as a sequence
1717removed-- of constructors `b0` and `b1` (representing 0s and 1s), terminated by a
1718removed-- `z`.
1719removed
1720removed-- For example:
1721removed
1722removed-- decimal binary unary
1723removed-- 0 z zero
1724removed-- 1 b1 z succ zero
1725removed-- 2 b0 (b1 z) succ (succ zero)
1726removed-- 3 b1 (b1 z) succ (succ (succ zero))
1727removed-- 4 b0 (b0 (b1 z)) succ (succ (succ (succ zero)))
1728removed-- 5 b1 (b0 (b1 z)) succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero))))
1729removed-- 6 b0 (b1 (b1 z)) succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero)))))
1730removed-- 7 b1 (b1 (b1 z)) succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero))))))
1731removed-- 8 b0 (b0 (b0 (b1 z))) succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero)))))))
1732removed
1733removed-- Note that the low-order bit is on the left and the high-order bit is on the
1734removed-- right -- the opposite of the way binary numbers are usually written. This
1735removed-- choice makes them easier to manipulate.
1736removed
1737removed-- (Comprehension check: What unary numeral does `b0 z` represent?)
1738removed
1739removedinductive Bin : Type where
1740removed | z
1741removed | b0 (n : Bin)
1742removed | b1 (n : Bin)
1743removed
1744removedattribute [pp_nodot] Bin.b1 Bin.b0
1745removed
1746removeddef incr (m : Bin) : Bin
1747removed := sorry
1748removed
1749removeddef binToNat (m : Bin) : Nat
1750removed := sorry
1751removed
1752removedexample : incr (.b1 .z) = .b0 (.b1 .z) := sorry
1753removedexample : incr (.b0 (.b1 .z)) = .b1 (.b1 .z) := sorry
1754removedexample : incr (.b1 (.b1 .z)) = .b0 (.b0 (.b1 .z)) := sorry
1755removed
1756removedtheorem incr_z : incr .z = .b1 .z := sorry
1757removedtheorem incr_b0 m : incr (.b0 m) = .b1 m := sorry
1758removedtheorem incr_b1 m : incr (.b1 m) = .b0 (incr m) := sorry
1759removed
1760removedtheorem binToNat_z : binToNat .z = zero := sorry
1761removedtheorem binToNat_b0 m : binToNat (.b0 m) = binToNat m * two := sorry
1762removedtheorem binToNat_b1 m : binToNat (.b1 m) = binToNat m * two + one := sorry
1763removed
1764removed-- You may find your previous proofs of `zero_add_one`, `one_add_one`,
1765removed-- `zero_mul_two`, `one_mul_two`, and `two_mul_two` useful here.
1766removed
1767removedexample : binToNat (.b0 (.b1 .z)) = two := sorry
1768removedexample : binToNat (incr (.b1 .z)) = add one (binToNat (.b1 .z)) := sorry
1769removedexample : binToNat (incr (incr (.b1 .z))) = add two (binToNat (.b1 .z)) := sorry
1770removedexample : binToNat (.b0 (.b0 (.b1 .z))) = four := sorry
1771removed
1772removedattribute [irreducible] incr binToNat
1773removed
1774removedend Nat
1775removed

1816removed-- ### Course Late Policies, Formalized
1817removed
1818removed-- Note to developers:
1819removed-- This exercise needs to be changed. Per GitHub discussion: the way this
1820removed-- exercise is currently structured is at odds with our definition of Nats
1821removed-- (use of large digits that would be tedious to work with by rewriting).
1822removed-- The definitions of grades and letters also do not lend themselves well
1823removed-- to our discipline of defining and using rewrite rules for all our
1824removed-- functions, as they would require a frustrating number of such rules. We
1825removed-- should come up with a new exercise here of similar size and difficulty,
1826removed-- but that works better with the new presentation style of this material.
1827removed-- HG: Also, we should make sure that this reads OK in full/terse TODO
1828removed
1829removed-- Suppose that a course has a grading policy based on late days, where a
1830removed-- student's final letter grade is lowered if they submit too many homework
1831removed-- assignments late.
1832removed
1833removednamespace LateDays
1834removedopen scoped NatPlayground.Nat
1835removed
1836removed-- Numeric literals (`9`, `17`, `21`) for our unary `Nat`.
1837removed@[reducible] def ofNat : _root_.Nat → Nat
1838removed | .zero => .zero
1839removed | .succ n => .succ (ofNat n)
1840removed
1841removedinstance (n : _root_.Nat) : OfNat Nat n := ⟨ofNat n⟩
1842removed
1843removed-- First, we introduce a datatype for modeling the "letter" component of a
1844removed-- grade.
1845removed
1846removedinductive Letter : Type where
1847removed | A | B | C | D | F
1848removed
1849removed-- Then we define the modifiers -- a `natural` `A` is just a "plain" grade of
1850removed-- `A`.
1851removed
1852removedinductive Modifier : Type where
1853removed | plus | natural | minus
1854removed
1855removed-- A full `Grade`, then, is just a `Letter` and a `Modifier`. In Lean, a
1856removed-- combination of several values is called a *structure*. The `structure`
1857removed-- keyword is used to define a new structure type.
1858removed
1859removedstructure Grade where
1860removed letter : Letter
1861removed modifier : Modifier
1862removed
1863removed-- We will want to be able to say when one grade is "better" than another. In
1864removed-- other words, we need a way to compare two grades. As with natural numbers,
1865removed-- we could define `bool`-valued functions `grade_eqb`, `grade_ltb`, etc., and
1866removed-- that would work fine. However, we can also define a slightly more
1867removed-- informative type for comparing two values, as shown below. This datatype
1868removed-- has three constructors that can be used to indicate whether two values are
1869removed-- "equal", "less than", or "greater than" one another.
1870removed
1871removedinductive Comparison : Type where
1872removed | eq -- "equal"
1873removed | lt -- "less than"
1874removed | gt -- "greater than"
1875removed
1876removed-- Since we're in a namespace, we can open the relevant types to avoid having
1877removed-- to write `Letter.A`, etc.
1878removed
1879removedopen Letter Modifier Comparison
1880removed
1881removed-- Using pattern matching, it is not difficult to define the comparison
1882removed-- operation for two letters `l1` and `l2` (see below). This definition uses a
1883removed-- feature of `match` patterns: we can match against *two* values
1884removed-- simultaneously by separating them and the corresponding patterns with comma
1885removed-- `,`. This is simply a convenient abbreviation for nested pattern matching.
1886removed
1887removeddef letterComparison (l1 l2 : Letter) : Comparison :=
1888removed match l1, l2 with
1889removed | A, A => eq
1890removed | A, _ => gt
1891removed | B, A => lt
1892removed | B, B => eq
1893removed | B, _ => gt
1894removed | C, A => lt
1895removed | C, B => lt
1896removed | C, C => eq
1897removed | C, _ => gt
1898removed | D, F => gt
1899removed | D, D => eq
1900removed | D, _ => lt
1901removed | F, F => eq
1902removed | F, _ => lt
1903removed
1904removedexample : letterComparison B A = lt := by rfl
1905removedexample : letterComparison D D = eq := by rfl
1906removedexample : letterComparison B F = gt := by rfl
1907removed
1908removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): letter_comparison ⭐
1909removed
1910removedtheorem letterComparison_Eq : ∀ l : Letter,
1911removed letterComparison l l = eq := by
1912removed sorry
1913removed
1914removeddef modifierComparison (m1 m2 : Modifier) : Comparison :=
1915removed match m1, m2 with
1916removed | plus, plus => eq
1917removed | plus, _ => gt
1918removed | natural, plus => lt
1919removed | natural, natural => eq
1920removed | natural, _ => gt
1921removed | minus, minus => eq
1922removed | minus, _ => lt
1923removed
1924removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): grade_comparison ⭐⭐
1925removed
1926removed-- Here, we will need to access the fields of the `Grade` structure. The field
1927removed-- names are `letter` and `modifier`, so for a grade `g`, we can write
1928removed-- `g.letter` and `g.modifier` to access these fields.
1929removed
1930removeddef gradeComparison (g1 g2 : Grade) : Comparison
1931removed := sorry
1932removed
1933removedexample : gradeComparison ⟨A, minus⟩ ⟨B, plus⟩ = gt := sorry
1934removedexample : gradeComparison ⟨A, minus⟩ ⟨A, plus⟩ = lt := sorry
1935removedexample : gradeComparison ⟨F, plus⟩ ⟨F, plus⟩ = eq := sorry
1936removedexample : gradeComparison ⟨B, minus⟩ ⟨C, plus⟩ = gt := sorry
1937removed
1938removeddef lowerLetter (l : Letter) : Letter :=
1939removed match l with
1940removed | A => B
1941removed | B => C
1942removed | C => D
1943removed | D => F
1944removed | F => F -- Can't go lower than F!
1945removed
1946removed-- This theorem is not provable because of the edge case of `F`!
1947removed
1948removed-- theorem lowerLetter_lowers_bad : ∀ (l : Letter),
1949removed-- letterComparison (lowerLetter l) l = lt := by ...
1950removed
1951removedtheorem lowerLetter_F_is_F : lowerLetter F = F := by rfl
1952removed
1953removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): lower_letter_lowers ⭐⭐
1954removed
1955removedtheorem lowerLetter_lowers : ∀ l : Letter,
1956removed letterComparison F l = lt →
1957removed letterComparison (lowerLetter l) l = lt := by
1958removed sorry
1959removed
1960removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): lower_grade ⭐⭐
1961removed
1962removed-- In addition to the dot notation for accessing structure fields, we can also
1963removed-- use pattern matching to access these fields. For example, if `g` is a
1964removed-- grade, then we can write `match g with ⟨l, m⟩ => ...` to access the letter
1965removed-- and modifier components of `g` as `l` and `m`, respectively. Note: The
1966removed-- angle brackets `⟨` and `⟩` are typed as `\<` and `\>`.
1967removed
1968removeddef lowerGrade (g : Grade) : Grade
1969removed := sorry
1970removed

2002removed if Nat.ble lateDays 9 then g
2003removed else if Nat.ble lateDays 17 then lowerGrade g

2005removed else lowerGrade (lowerGrade (lowerGrade g))

2013removed else lowerGrade (lowerGrade (lowerGrade g))) := by

47removed/--
48removed This function is similar to `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`: Given `e` of the
49removed form `forall ..xs, A`, this combinator will create a new metavariable for
50removed each `x` in `xs` until it reaches an `x` whose type is defeq to `t`,
51removed and instantiate `A` with these, while also reducing `A` if needed.
52removed It uses `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`.
53removed
54removed This function returns a triple `(mvs, bis, out)` where
55removed - `mvs` is an array containing the new metavariables.
56removed - `bis` is an array containing the binder infos for the `mvs`.
57removed - `out` is `e` but instantiated with the `mvs`.
58removed
59removed Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Lean/Meta/Basic.lean#L41].
60removed-/
61removeddef forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq
62removed (e t : Expr) (kind : MetavarKind := MetavarKind.natural) :
63removed MetaM (Array Expr × Array BinderInfo × Expr) := do
64removed let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing e (some 1) kind
65removed unless ms.size == 1 do
66removed if ms.size == 0 then throwError m!"Failed: {← ppExpr e} is not the type of a function."
67removed else throwError m!"Failed"
68removed let mut mvs := ms
69removed let mut bis := bs
70removed let mut out : Expr := tp
71removed while !(← isDefEq (← inferType mvs.toList.getLast!) t) do
72removed let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing out (some 1) kind
73removed unless ms.size == 1 do
74removed throwError m!"Failed to find {← ppExpr t} as the type of a parameter of {← ppExpr e}."
75removed mvs := mvs ++ ms
76removed bis := bis ++ bs
77removed out := tp
78removed return (mvs, bis, out)
79removed
80removed/-- Get the user-facing name for the given metavariable. -/
81removeddef _root_.Lean.MVarId.getUserName (mvarId : MVarId) : MetaM Name := do
82removed let decl ← mvarId.getDecl
83removed return decl.userName
84removed
85removed/-- Given equations `eqs` in the local context of `mvarId`,
86removed unify them using [Lean.Meta.unifyEq?],
87removed but if unification fails, leave the equation in the context.
88removed This means we should never get a "Dependent elimination failed" error.
89removed While marked partial, this _should_ always terminate,
90removed decreasing on the sum of the sizes of the terms of each equation.
91removed
92removed Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyEqs]. -/
93removedpartial def unifyEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (mvarId : MVarId) (subst : FVarSubst) (caseName? : Option Name) : MetaM (MVarId × FVarSubst) := withIncRecDepth do
94removed match eqs with
95removed | [] => return (mvarId, subst)
96removed | eq :: eqs =>
97removed let some { mvarId, subst, numNewEqs } ← Option.join <$> (observing? $ unifyEq? mvarId eq subst MVarId.acyclic caseName?)
98removed | unifyEqs eqs mvarId subst caseName?
99removed let (newEqs, mvarId) ← mvarId.introN numNewEqs
100removed let eqs := eqs.map (Expr.fvarId! ∘ subst.get)
101removed unifyEqs (newEqs.toList ++ eqs) mvarId subst caseName?
102removed
103removed/-- Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyCasesEqs]. -/
104removeddef unifyCasesEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
105removed subgoals.filterMapM fun s => do
106removed let eqs := eqs.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
107removed let (mvarId, subst) ← unifyEqs eqs s.mvarId s.subst s.ctorName
108removed if (← mvarId.isAssignedOrDelayedAssigned) then return none
109removed else return some { s with
110removed mvarId := mvarId,
111removed subst := subst,
112removed fields := s.fields.map (subst.apply ·)
113removed }
114removed
115removed/-- Try to clear the given fvars from the local context of each subgoal,
116removed using the subgoals' substitution mappings to find the fvars.
117removed
118removed As with [MVarId.tryClearMany], the fvars must be in the order they appear in the context. -/
119removeddef casesClearMany (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) (fvarIds : Array FVarId) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
120removed subgoals.mapM fun s => do
121removed let fvarIds := fvarIds.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
122removed let mvarId ← s.mvarId.tryClearMany fvarIds
123removed return { s with mvarId }
124removed
125removedend Lean.Meta

131removed-- [https://github.com/leanprover-community/batteries/blob/main/Batteries/Tactic/Lemma.lean]
132removed/-- Synonym for `theorem`. -/
133removedmacro "lemma " thm:declId sig:declSig val:declVal : command => `(theorem $thm $sig $val)
134removed
135removed/--
136removed `apply t at i` uses forward reasoning with `t` at the hypothesis `i`.
137removed Explicitly, if `t : α₁ → ⋯ → αᵢ → ⋯ → αₙ` and `i` has type `αᵢ`, then this tactic adds
138removed metavariables/goals for any terms of `αⱼ` for `j = 1, …, i-1`,
139removed then replaces the type of `i` with `αᵢ₊₁ → ⋯ → αₙ` by applying those metavariables and the
140removed original `i`.
141removed
142removed Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Tactic/ApplyAt.lean].
143removed-/
144removedelab "apply " t:term " at " i:ident : tactic => withSynthesize <| withMainContext do
145removed let f ← elabTermForApply t
146removed let some ldecl := (← getLCtx).findFromUserName? i.getId
147removed | throwErrorAt i m!"Identifier {i} not found"
148removed let (mvs, bis, _) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq (← inferType f) ldecl.type
149removed for (m, b) in mvs.zip bis do
150removed if b.isInstImplicit && !(← m.mvarId!.isAssigned) then
151removed try m.mvarId!.inferInstance
152removed catch _ => continue
153removed let (_, mainGoal) ← (← getMainGoal).note ldecl.userName
154removed (← mkAppOptM' f (mvs.pop.push ldecl.toExpr |>.map some))
155removed let mainGoal ← mainGoal.tryClear ldecl.fvarId
156removed replaceMainGoal <| [mainGoal] ++ mvs.pop.toList.map (·.mvarId!)
157removed
158removedstructure InversionConfig where
159removed clear : Bool := false
160removed
161removeddeclare_config_elab elabInversionConfig InversionConfig
162removed
163removedopen Cases in
164removeddef inversionCore (h : FVarId) (config : InversionConfig) : TacticM (List CasesSubgoal) := withMainContext do
165removed let goal ← getMainGoal
166removed goal.withContext do
167removed let some ctx ← mkCasesContext? h
168removed | throwTacticEx `inversion goal "Target {Expr.fvar h} does not belong to an inductive type"
169removed -- If the target's type isn't a predicate with indices, behave like `cases`
170removed if ← hasIndepIndices ctx then
171removed let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn goal h default ctx
172removed let subgoals ← if config.clear
173removed then casesClearMany subgoals #[h]
174removed else pure subgoals
175removed return subgoals.toList
176removed -- Otherwise, use custom [unifyEqs] to not fail on unifying HEqs
177removed else
178removed let gis@⟨newGoal, _, newTarget, numEqs⟩ ← generalizeIndices goal h
179removed let (newEqs, newGoal) ← newGoal.introN numEqs
180removed let some targetEq := newEqs.back?
181removed | throwTacticEx `inversion newGoal "Failed to generalize target"
182removed let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn newGoal newTarget default ctx
183removed let subgoals ← elimAuxIndices gis subgoals
184removed let subgoals ← unifyCasesEqs newEqs.toList subgoals
185removed let subgoals ← if config.clear
186removed then casesClearMany subgoals #[h, targetEq]
187removed else pure subgoals
188removed return subgoals.toList
189removed
190removed/-- Given an inversion alternative and a list of goals,
191removed solve the tagged goal with the provided tactics,
192removed throwing an error if the goal cannot be found or solved. -/
193removeddef evalInvAlt (goals : List CasesSubgoal) (alt : TSyntax `invAlt) : TacticM (List MVarId) :=
194removed match alt with
195removed | `(invAlt| | $tag:ident $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
196removed if let some goal := goals.find? (matchTag tag.getId $ ·.ctorName.getD default) then
197removed return [← trySolveGoal vars tactics goal.mvarId]
198removed else throwError m!"Invalid alternative name `{tag.getId}`: {← errorMsg}"
199removed | `(invAlt| | _ $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
200removed if !goals.isEmpty then
201removed goals.mapM (trySolveGoal vars tactics ·.mvarId)
202removed else throwErrorAt alt m!"Invalid wildcard alternative: {← errorMsg}"
203removed | _ => throwErrorAt alt "Could not parse inversion alternative"
204removedwhere
205removed matchTag tag name : Bool :=
206removed tag == name || tag.isPrefixOf name || tag.isSuffixOf name
207removed trySolveGoal vars tactics goal : TacticM MVarId := do
208removed let goals ← renameInaccessibles goal vars >>= evalTacticAt tactics
209removed unless goals.isEmpty do
210removed reportUnsolvedGoals goals
211removed return goal
212removed errorMsg : TacticM MessageData := do
213removed let goalMsgs := goals.filterMap (.ofName <$> ·.ctorName)
214removed return if goals.isEmpty
215removed then m!"There are no unhandled alternatives"
216removed else m!"Expected {.orList goalMsgs}"
217removed
218removed@[tactic Lean.Parser.inversion, inherit_doc Lean.Parser.inversion]
219removedpublic meta def evalInversion : Tactic
220removed | `(tactic| inversion $config $h:ident $[with $[$alts?:invAlts]*]?) => do
221removed let config ← elabInversionConfig config
222removed let mut goals ← inversionCore (← getFVarId h) config
223removed if let some alts := alts? then
224removed let expandedAlts ← Array.flatten <$> alts.mapM expandInvAlts
225removed for alt in expandedAlts do
226removed let solvedGoals ← evalInvAlt goals alt
227removed goals := goals.filter (!solvedGoals.contains ·.mvarId)
228removed unless goals.isEmpty do
229removed reportUnsolvedGoals $ goals.map (·.mvarId)
230removed replaceMainGoal $ goals.map (·.mvarId)
231removed | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion tactic"
232removedwhere expandInvAlts
233removed | `(invAlts| $[| $args:caseArg]* => $tactics:tacticSeq) =>
234removed args.mapM (`(invAlt| | $(·) => $tactics))
235removed | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion alternatives"
236removed

1removedimport LF.Logic
2removedimport LF.CustomTactics
3removed
4removedimport LF.SFLCompat
5removed
6removed-- # IndProp: Inductively Defined Propositions
7removed
8removed-- Note to developers:
9removed-- `HIDE: BCP 25: After teaching the chapter this semester, I feel
10removed-- that (a) the Ev example, while arguably suboptimal, actually works
11removed-- acceptably well. (I just wish that the n in ``ev_succ_succ` n H` was not
12removed-- two smaller than the n that is being shown to be even -- that's
13removed-- always awkward. Wonder if there is some clever way around that...)
14removed--
15removed-- However, (b) the chapter is very long, and quite a few of the
16removed-- exercises are hard, especially if you do as I did this year and
17removed-- require the advanced exercises for everybody (on the assumption
18removed-- that they could get plenty of help from LLMs, etc.). I think it
19removed-- really needs to be at least significantly trimmed, if not split up.`
20removed--
21removed-- `HIDE: MRC 3/22: I offer a few remarks. I'm putting them here, above
22removed-- the BCP'21 comment, not to say that they are in any way more
23removed-- important; rather, just to preserve some chronological legibility.
24removed--
25removed-- - This chapter is an outlier in length. It now has the maximum line
26removed-- length (in the FULL version) of any chapter in LF, at about 2300
27removed-- LoC. That's a z-score of about 1.75 for the "blue arrow" chapters
28removed-- in the dependency diagram.
29removed--
30removed-- - This chapter has 39 exercises, of which 25 (!) are optional.
31removed--
32removed-- - The running example of evenness is known to be uncompelling
33removed-- because it is representable without inductively-defined
34removed-- propositions. There do exist compelling examples:
35removed--
36removed-- + Functions like `factorial` whose "natural" definitions are not
37removed-- structurally recursive. [Coq'Art 8.4] [BCP 25: FWIW, I don't
38removed-- find the "natural" definition of factorial suitable for present
39removed-- purposes: the reasons it is better and more natural than a
40removed-- simple fixpoint seem rather subtle.]
41removed--
42removed-- + Partial functions.
43removed--
44removed-- + Relations (that are not strictly functions).
45removed--
46removed-- I have a couple of personal opinions based on those observations:
47removed--
48removed-- - I favor BCP'21's "path 1" of de-emphasizing (to the extent
49removed-- perhaps of eliminating) evenness.
50removed--
51removed-- - I favor re-factoring this chapter into two files, with a main
52removed-- (blue) path that covers the essentials without cluttering
53removed-- optional exercises throughout the file.`

82removed--
83removed-- CH: In my Lyon course it became obvious to pretty much everyone that
84removed-- the inductive definition of evenness that this chapter uses
85removed-- intensiviely is so silly and artificial that it makes understanding
86removed-- very hard for most students. There's zero need to define evenness
87removed-- inductively, when `∃ k, n = 2*k` does the job fine, so inductive
88removed-- propositions seem to students not something useful, but just
89removed-- self-inflicted pain. All the inductive propositions, up to subsequences
90removed-- and the matching on Regular Expressions at the end, have this useless
91removed-- self-inflicted pain flavour. So I returned to this the following
92removed-- morning and showed to the students how to define reflexive-transitive
93removed-- closure as an inductive relation, and afterwards the were able to
94removed-- follow much better. The code I quickly hacked up for this is at:
95removed-- https://prosecco.gforge.inria.fr/personal/hritcu/teaching/lyon2019/Multi.v
96removed--
97removed-- BCP: Yes, this chapter needs a revamp! For the moment I am going to
98removed-- just add a couple of sentences to the opening sequence below, to warn
99removed-- students about this potential confusion. Moving forward, I wonder
100removed-- whether something like ordered binary trees would be a simple enough
101removed-- running example.
102removed--
103removed-- BCP 20: I remain puzzled by what is the really right example for this
104removed-- chapter. Ordered trees (and sorted lists) don't feel quite right
105removed-- because students might think we should define them with Fixpoint, not
106removed-- inductive. APT 21: Ordered trees are also surprisingly complex to
107removed-- describe (see VFA/SearchTree.v). Maybe Permutations would be be a good
108removed-- choice? The only problem is convincing students that the standard Lean
109removed-- inductive definition is actually correct (see VFA/Perm.v)!
110removed--
111removed-- We should also think about how to make the material flow better between
112removed-- this chapter and ProofObjects. When lecturing about this one I ended up
113removed-- introducing a lot of the concepts from that one.

149removed-- IMPORTBLOCK import LF.Logic IMPORTBLOCK import LF.CustomTactics
150removed
151removed-- ## Inductively Defined Propositions
152removed
153removed-- In the Logic chapter, we looked at several ways of writing propositions,
154removed-- including conjunction, disjunction, and existential quantification.
155removed
156removed-- In this chapter, we bring yet another new tool into the mix: *inductively
157removed-- defined propositions*.
158removed
159removed-- To begin, some examples...
160removed
161removed-- ### Example: The Collatz Conjecture
162removed
163removed-- The *Collatz Conjecture* is a famous open problem in number theory.
164removed
165removed-- Its statement is quite simple. First, we define a function `csf` on
166removed-- numbers, as follows (where `csf` stands for "Collatz step function"):
167removed
168removeddef div2 (n : Nat) : Nat :=
169removed match n with
170removed | 0 => 0
171removed | 1 => 0
172removed | n' + 2 => div2 n' + 1
173removed
174removeddef csf (n : Nat) : Nat :=
175removed if n.even then div2 n
176removed else (3 * n) + 1
177removed
178removed-- Note to developers:
179removed-- HIDE: CH: This is now called `csf` and not just `f` for a good reason.
180removed-- If one adds single letter global identifiers that badly interferes with
181removed-- inadvertently reusing the same names in pattern matching patterns,
182removed-- leading to confusing error messages from Lean.
183removed
184removed-- Next, we look at what happens when we repeatedly apply `csf` to some given
185removed-- starting number. For example, `csf 12` is `6`, and `csf 6` is `3`, so by
186removed-- repeatedly applying `csf` we get the sequence
187removed-- `12, 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1`.
188removed
189removed-- Similarly, if we start with `19`, we get the longer sequence
190removed-- `19,
191removed-- 58, 29, 88, 44, 22, 11, 34, 17, 52, 26, 13, 40, 20, 10, 5, 16, 8,
192removed-- 4, 2, 1`.
193removed
194removed-- Both of these sequences eventually reach `1`. The question posed by Collatz
195removed-- was: Is the sequence starting from *any* positive natural number guaranteed
196removed-- to reach `1` eventually?
197removed
198removed-- To formalize this question in Lean, we might try to define a recursive
199removed-- *function* that calculates the total number of steps that it takes for such
200removed-- a sequence to reach `1`. You can write this definition in a standard
201removed-- programming language, but it is rejected by Lean's termination checker,
202removed-- since the argument to the recursive call, `csf n`, is not "obviously
203removed-- smaller" than `n`.
204removed
205removed/--
206removederror: fail to show termination for
207removed reaches1_in
208removedwith errors
209removedfailed to infer structural recursion:
210removedCannot use parameter n:
211removed failed to eliminate recursive application
212removed reaches1_in (csf n)
213removed
214removed
215removedfailed to prove termination, possible solutions:
216removed - Use `have`-expressions to prove the remaining goals
217removed - Use `termination_by` to specify a different well-founded relation
218removed - Use `decreasing_by` to specify your own tactic for discharging this kind of goal
219removedn : Nat
220removedh✝ : ¬(n == 1) = true
221removed⊢ csf n < n
222removed-/
223removed#guard_msgs in
224removeddef reaches1_in (n : Nat) : Nat :=
225removed if n == 1 then 0
226removed else 1 + reaches1_in (csf n)
227removed
228removed-- You can write this definition in a standard programming language. This
229removed-- definition is, however, rejected by Lean's termination checker, since the
230removed-- argument to the recursive call, `csf n`, is not "obviously smaller" than
231removed-- `n`. Indeed, this isn't just a pointless limitation: functions in Lean are
232removed-- required to be total, to ensure logical consistency.
233removed
234removed-- Moreover, we can't fix it by devising a more clever termination checker:
235removed-- deciding whether this particular function is total would be equivalent to
236removed-- settling the Collatz conjecture!
237removed
238removed-- Another idea could be to express the concept "eventually reaches `1` in the
239removed-- Collatz sequence" as a *recursively defined property* of numbers
240removed-- `CollatzHoldsFor : Nat → Prop`. This is also rejected: while we could in
241removed-- principle convince Lean that `div2 n` is smaller than `n`, we certainly
242removed-- can't convince it that `(3 * n) + 1` is smaller than `n`!
243removed
244removed/--
245removederror: fail to show termination for
246removed collatz_holds_for
247removedwith errors
248removedfailed to infer structural recursion:
249removedCannot use parameter n:
250removed failed to eliminate recursive application
251removed collatz_holds_for (div2 n)
252removed
253removed
254removedfailed to prove termination, possible solutions:
255removed - Use `have`-expressions to prove the remaining goals
256removed - Use `termination_by` to specify a different well-founded relation
257removed - Use `decreasing_by` to specify your own tactic for discharging this kind of goal
258removedn x✝ : Nat
259removedh✝ : n.even = true
260removed⊢ div2 n < x✝
261removed-/
262removed#guard_msgs in
263removeddef collatz_holds_for (n : Nat) : Prop :=
264removed match n with
265removed | 0 => False
266removed | 1 => True
267removed | _ => if n.even then collatz_holds_for (div2 n)
268removed else collatz_holds_for ((3 * n) + 1)
269removed
270removed-- This recursive function is also rejected by the termination checker, since,
271removed-- while we could in principle convince Lean that `div2 n` is smaller than
272removed-- `n`, we certainly can't convince it that `(3 * n) + 1` is smaller than `n`!
273removed
274removed-- Fortunately, there is another way to do it: We can express the concept
275removed-- "reaches `1` eventually in the Collatz sequence" as an *inductively defined
276removed-- property* of numbers. Intuitively, this property is defined by a set of
277removed-- rules:
278removed
279removed-- ─────────────────── (chf_one)
280removed-- CollatzHoldsFor 1
281removed
282removed-- even n = true CollatzHoldsFor (div2 n)
283removed-- ─────────────────────────────────────────── (chf_even)
284removed-- CollatzHoldsFor n
285removed
286removed-- even n = false CollatzHoldsFor ((3 * n) + 1)
287removed-- ─────────────────────────────────────────────── (chf_odd)
288removed-- CollatzHoldsFor n
289removed
290removed-- So there are three ways to prove that a number `n` eventually reaches `1`
291removed-- in the Collatz sequence:
292removed
293removed-- - `n` is `1`;
294removed-- - `n` is even and `div2 n` eventually reaches `1`;
295removed-- - `n` is odd and `(3 * n) + 1` eventually reaches `1`.
296removed
297removed-- We can prove that a number reaches `1` by constructing a (finite)
298removed-- derivation using these rules. For instance, here is the derivation proving
299removed-- that `12` reaches `1` (where we leave out the evenness/oddness premises):
300removed
301removed-- ─────────────────────── (chf_one)
302removed-- CollatzHoldsFor 1
303removed-- ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
304removed-- CollatzHoldsFor 2
305removed-- ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
306removed-- CollatzHoldsFor 4
307removed-- ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
308removed-- CollatzHoldsFor 8
309removed-- ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
310removed-- CollatzHoldsFor 16
311removed-- ─────────────────────── (chf_odd)
312removed-- CollatzHoldsFor 5
313removed-- ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
314removed-- CollatzHoldsFor 10
315removed-- ─────────────────────── (chf_odd)
316removed-- CollatzHoldsFor 3
317removed-- ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
318removed-- CollatzHoldsFor 6
319removed-- ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
320removed-- CollatzHoldsFor 12
321removed
322removed-- Formally in Lean, the `CollatzHoldsFor` property is *inductively defined*:
323removed
324removedinductive CollatzHoldsFor : Nat → Prop where
325removed | chf_one : CollatzHoldsFor 1
326removed | chf_even (n : Nat) : n.even = true →
327removed CollatzHoldsFor (div2 n) →
328removed CollatzHoldsFor n
329removed | chf_odd (n : Nat) : n.even = false →
330removed CollatzHoldsFor ((3 * n) + 1) →
331removed CollatzHoldsFor n
332removed
333removed-- What we've done here is to use Lean's `inductive` definition mechanism to
334removed-- characterize the property "Collatz holds for..." by stating three different
335removed-- ways in which it can hold: (1) Collatz holds for `1`, (2) if Collatz holds
336removed-- for `div2 n` and `n` is even then Collatz holds for `n`, and (3) if Collatz
337removed-- holds for `(3 * n) + 1` and `n` is odd then Collatz holds for `n`. This
338removed-- Lean definition directly corresponds to the three rules we wrote informally
339removed-- above.
340removed
341removed-- For particular numbers, we can now prove that the Collatz sequence reaches
342removed-- `1` (we'll look more closely at how it works a bit later in the chapter).
343removed-- Each step applies a rule and discharges the boolean evenness premise by
344removed-- `rfl`; the recursive premise is then reduced by the kernel from
345removed-- `CollatzHoldsFor (div2 12)` to `CollatzHoldsFor 6`, etc.
346removed
347removedexample : CollatzHoldsFor 12 := by
348removed apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even; rfl
349removed apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even; rfl
350removed apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_odd; rfl
351removed apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even; rfl
352removed apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_odd; rfl
353removed apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even; rfl
354removed apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even; rfl
355removed apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even; rfl
356removed apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even; rfl
357removed exact CollatzHoldsFor.chf_one
358removed
359removed-- The Collatz conjecture then states that the sequence beginning from *any*
360removed-- positive number reaches `1`:
361removed
362removeddef collatz := ∀ n, n ≠ 0 → CollatzHoldsFor n
363removed
364removed-- If you succeed in proving this conjecture, you've got a bright future as a
365removed-- number theorist! But don't spend too long on it -- it's been open since
366removed-- 1937.
367removed
368removed-- Note to developers:
369removed-- HIDE: CH: We may want to add an exercise later proving false if one
370removed-- assumes Collatz' conjecture without the `n ≠ 0` assumption. We had that
371removed-- mistake in the script for years and no one noticed, wow!
372removed
373removed-- ### Example: Binary relation for comparing numbers
374removed
375removed-- A binary *relation* on a set `α` has Lean type `α → α → Prop`. This is a
376removed-- family of propositions parameterized by two elements of `α` -- i.e., a
377removed-- proposition about pairs of elements of `α`.
378removed
379removed-- For example, one familiar binary relation on `Nat` is
380removed-- `Le : Nat
381removed-- → Nat → Prop`, the less-than-or-equal-to relation, which can be
382removed-- inductively defined by the following two rules:
383removed
384removed-- ─────── (le_refl)
385removed-- Le n n
386removed
387removed-- Le n m
388removed-- ───────────── (le_step)
389removed-- Le n (m + 1)
390removed
391removed-- These rules say that there are two ways to show that a number is less than
392removed-- or equal to another: either observe that they are the same number, or, if
393removed-- the second has the form `m + 1`, give evidence that the first is less than
394removed-- or equal to `m`.
395removed
396removednamespace LePlayground
397removed
398removedinductive Le : Nat → Nat → Prop where
399removed | refl (n : Nat) : Le n n
400removed | step (n m : Nat) : Le n m → Le n (m + 1)
401removed
402removedscoped infix:50 (priority := high) " ≤ " => Le
403removed
404removed-- This definition is a bit simpler and more elegant than the Boolean function
405removed-- `ble` we defined in `Basics`. As usual, `Le` and `ble` are equivalent, and
406removed-- there is an exercise about that later.
407removed
408removedexample : 3 ≤ 5 := by
409removed apply Le.step; apply Le.step; exact Le.refl 3
410removed
411removedend LePlayground
412removed
413removed-- ### Example: Transitive Closure
414removed
415removed-- Another example: The *transitive closure* of a relation `R` is the smallest
416removed-- relation that contains `R` and that is transitive. This can be defined by
417removed-- the following two rules:
418removed
419removed-- R x y
420removed-- ---------------- (t_step)
421removed-- ClosTrans R x y
422removed
423removed-- ClosTrans R x y ClosTrans R y z
424removed-- ------------------------------------ (t_trans)
425removed-- ClosTrans R x z
426removed
427removed-- In Lean this looks as follows:
428removed
429removedinductive ClosTrans {α: Type} (R: α→α→Prop) : α → α → Prop where
430removed | t_step (x y : α) :
431removed R x y →
432removed ClosTrans R x y
433removed | t_trans (x y z : α) :
434removed ClosTrans R x y →
435removed ClosTrans R y z →
436removed ClosTrans R x z
437removed
438removed-- For example, suppose we define a "parent of" relation on a group of
439removed-- people...
440removed
441removedinductive Person : Type where
442removed | sage
443removed | cleo
444removed | ridley
445removed | moss
446removed
447removedinductive ParentOf : Person → Person → Prop where
448removed | po_SC : ParentOf .sage .cleo
449removed | po_SR : ParentOf .sage .ridley
450removed | po_CM : ParentOf .cleo .moss
451removed
452removed-- In this example, `sage` is a parent of both `cleo` and `ridley`; and `cleo`
453removed-- is a parent of `moss`.
454removed
455removed-- The `parent_of` relation is not transitive, but we can define an "ancestor
456removed-- of" relation as its transitive closure:
457removed
458removeddef AncestorOf : Person → Person → Prop := ClosTrans ParentOf
459removed
460removed-- Here is a derivation showing that Sage is an ancestor of Moss:
461removed
462removed-- ———————————————————(po_SC) ———————————————————(po_CM)
463removed-- ParentOf .sage .cleo ParentOf .cleo .moss
464removed-- —————————————————————(t_step) —————————————————————(t_step)
465removed-- AncestorOf .sage .cleo AncestorOf .cleo .moss
466removed-- ————————————————————————————————————————————————————(t_trans)
467removed-- AncestorOf .sage .moss
468removed
469removedexample : AncestorOf .sage .moss := by
470removed apply ClosTrans.t_trans
471removed . apply ClosTrans.t_step; apply ParentOf.po_SC
472removed . apply ClosTrans.t_step; apply ParentOf.po_CM
473removed
474removed-- Note to developers:
475removed-- HIDE: CH: A simple exercise could be nice here?
476removed
477removed-- Computing the transitive closure can be undecidable even for a relation R
478removed-- that is decidable (e.g., the `cms` relation below), so in general we can't
479removed-- expect to define transitive closure as a boolean function. Fortunately,
480removed-- Lean allows us to define transitive closure as an inductive relation.
481removed
482removed-- The transitive closure of a binary relation cannot, in general, be
483removed-- expressed in first-order logic. The logic of Lean is, however, much more
484removed-- powerful, and can easily define such inductive relations.
485removed
486removed-- ### Example: Reflexive and Transitive Closure
487removed
488removed-- As another example, the *reflexive and transitive closure* of a relation
489removed-- `R` is the smallest relation that contains `R` and that is reflexive and
490removed-- transitive. This can be defined by the following three rules (where we
491removed-- added a reflexivity rule to `ClosTrans`):
492removed
493removed-- R x y
494removed-- --------------------- (rt_step)
495removed-- ClosReflTrans R x y
496removed
497removed-- --------------------- (rt_refl)
498removed-- ClosReflTrans R x x
499removed
500removed-- ClosReflTrans R x y ClosReflTrans R y z
501removed-- ---------------------------------------------- (rt_trans)
502removed-- ClosReflTrans R x z
503removed
504removedinductive ClosReflTrans {α: Type} (R: α → α → Prop) : α → α → Prop where
505removed | rt_step (x y : α) :
506removed R x y →
507removed ClosReflTrans R x y
508removed | rt_refl (x : α) :
509removed ClosReflTrans R x x
510removed | rt_trans (x y z : α) :
511removed ClosReflTrans R x y →
512removed ClosReflTrans R y z →
513removed ClosReflTrans R x z
514removed
515removed-- For instance, this enables an equivalent definition of the Collatz
516removed-- conjecture. First we define a binary relation corresponding to the "Collatz
517removed-- step function" `csf`:
518removed
519removeddef cs (n m : Nat) : Prop := csf n = m
520removed
521removed-- This Collatz step relation can be used in conjunction with the reflexive
522removed-- and transitive closure operation to define a *Collatz multi-step* (`cms`)
523removed-- relation, expressing that a number `n` reaches another number `m` in zero
524removed-- or more Collatz steps:
525removed
526removeddef cms (n m : Nat) : Prop := ClosReflTrans cs n m
527removeddef collatz' : Prop := ∀ (n : Nat), n ≠ 0 → cms n 1
528removed
529removed-- This `cms` relation defined in terms of `ClosReflTrans` allows for more
530removed-- interesting derivations than the linear ones of the directly-defined
531removed-- `CollatzHoldsFor` relation:
532removed
533removed-- csf 16 = 8 csf 8 = 4 csf 4 = 2 csf 2 = 1
534removed-- ————————(rt_step) ———————(rt_step) ———————(rt_step) ———————(rt_step)
535removed-- cms 16 8 cms 8 4 cms 4 2 cms 2 1
536removed-- —————————————————————————(rt_trans) ————————————————————————(rt_trans)
537removed-- cms 16 4 cms 4 1
538removed-- —————————————————————————————————————————————(rt_trans)
539removed-- cms 16 1
540removed
541removed-- Note to developers:
542removed-- HIDE: CH: Would it be helpful to add an exercise later proving cms
543removed-- equivalent to CollatzHoldsFor
544removed
545removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): clos_refl_trans_sym (manually graded) ⭐
546removed
547removed-- How would you modify the `ClosReflTrans` definition above so as to define
548removed-- the reflexive, symmetric, and transitive closure?
549removed
550removed-- FILL IN HERE
551removed
552removed-- Example: Permutations
553removed
554removed-- The familiar mathematical concept of *permutation* also has an elegant
555removed-- formulation as an inductive relation. For simplicity, let's focus on
556removed-- permutations of lists with exactly three elements.
557removed
558removed-- We can define such permutations by the following rules:
559removed
560removed-- ------------------------- (perm3_swap12)
561removed-- Perm3 [a, b, c] [b, a, c]
562removed
563removed-- ------------------------- (perm3_swap23)
564removed-- Perm3 [a, b, c] [a, c, b]
565removed
566removed-- Perm3 l₁ l₂ Perm3 l₂ l₃
567removed-- ----------------------------- (perm3_trans)
568removed-- Perm3 l₁ l₃
569removed
570removed-- For instance we can derive `Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1]` as follows:
571removed
572removed-- ─────────────────────────(perm3_swap12) ─────────────────────────(perm3_swap23)
573removed-- Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [2, 1, 3] Perm3 [2, 1, 3] [2, 3, 1]
574removed-- ──────────────────────────────────────────────────(perm3_trans) ─────────────────────────(perm3_swap12)
575removed-- Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [2, 3, 1] Perm3 [2, 3, 1] [3, 2, 1]
576removed-- ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────(perm3_trans)
577removed-- Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1]
578removed
579removed-- This definition says:
580removed
581removed-- - If `l₂` can be obtained from `l₁` by swapping the first and second
582removed-- elements, then `l₂` is a permutation of `l₁`.
583removed
584removed-- - If `l₂` can be obtained from `l₁` by swapping the second and third
585removed-- elements, then `l₂` is a permutation of `l₁`.
586removed
587removed-- - If `l₂` is a permutation of `l₁` and `l₃` is a permutation of `l₂`, then
588removed-- `l₃` is a permutation of `l₁`.
589removed
590removed-- In Lean, we can define `Perm3` as follows:
591removed
592removedinductive Perm3 {α : Type} : List α → List α → Prop where
593removed | perm3_swap12 (a b c : α) :
594removed Perm3 [a, b, c] [b, a, c]
595removed | perm3_swap23 (a b c : α) :
596removed Perm3 [a, b, c] [a, c, b]
597removed | perm3_trans (l₁ l₂ l₃ : List α) :
598removed Perm3 l₁ l₂ → Perm3 l₂ l₃ → Perm3 l₁ l₃
599removed
600removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): perm (manually graded) ⭐
601removed
602removed-- According to this definition, is `\[1;2;3`] a permutation of itself?
603removed
604removed-- ### Example: Evenness (yet again)
605removed
606removed-- We've already seen two ways of stating a proposition that a number `n` is
607removed-- even: We can say
608removed
609removed-- (1) `even n = true` (using the recursive boolean function `even`), or
610removed
611removed-- (2) `∃ k, n = double k` (using an existential quantifier).
612removed
613removed-- A third possibility, which we'll use as a simple running example in this
614removed-- chapter, is to say that a number is even if we can *establish* its evenness
615removed-- from the following two rules:
616removed
617removed-- ---- (ev_0)
618removed-- Ev 0
619removed
620removed-- Ev n
621removed-- ------------ (ev_succ_succ)
622removed-- Ev (n + 2)
623removed
624removed-- Intuitively these rules say that:
625removed
626removed-- - The number `0` is even.
627removed-- - If `n` is even, then `n + 2` is even.
628removed
629removed-- (Defining evenness in this way may seem a bit confusing, since we have
630removed-- already seen two perfectly good ways of doing it. It makes a convenient
631removed-- running example because it is simple and compact, but we will soon return
632removed-- to the more compelling examples above.)
633removed
634removed-- To illustrate how this new definition of evenness works, let's imagine
635removed-- using it to show that `4` is even:
636removed
637removed-- ———— (ev_0)
638removed-- Ev 0
639removed-- ———————————— (`ev_succ_succ`)
640removed-- Ev (S (S 0))
641removed-- ———————————————————— (`ev_succ_succ`)
642removed-- Ev (S (S (S (S 0))))
643removed
644removed-- In words, to show that `4` is even, by rule `ev_succ_succ`, it suffices to
645removed-- show that `2` is even. This, in turn, is again guaranteed by rule
646removed-- `ev_succ_succ`, as long as we can show that `0` is even. But this last fact
647removed-- follows directly from the `ev_0` rule.
648removed
649removed-- We can translate the informal definition of evenness from above into a
650removed-- formal `inductive` declaration, where each "way that a number can be even"
651removed-- corresponds to a separate constructor:
652removed
653removedinductive Ev : Nat → Prop where
654removed | ev_0 : Ev 0
655removed | ev_succ_succ (n : Nat) (H : Ev n) : Ev (n + 2)
656removed
657removed-- Such definitions are interestingly different from previous uses of
658removed-- `inductive` for defining inductive datatypes like `Nat` or `List`. For one
659removed-- thing, we are defining not a `Type` (like `Nat`) or a function yielding a
660removed-- `Type` (like `List`), but rather a function from `Nat` to `Prop` -- that
661removed-- is, a property of numbers. But what is really new is that, because the
662removed-- `Nat` argument of `Ev` appears to the *right* of the colon on the first
663removed-- line, it is allowed to take *different* values in the types of different
664removed-- constructors: `0` in the type of `ev_0` and `(n + 2)` in the type of
665removed-- `ev_succ_succ`. Accordingly, the type of each constructor must be specified
666removed-- explicitly (after a colon), and each constructor's type must have the form
667removed-- `Ev n` for some natural number `n`.
668removed
669removed-- In contrast, recall the definition of `List`:
670removed
671removed-- inductive List (α:Type) : Type where
672removed-- | nil
673removed-- | cons (x : α) (l : List α)
674removed
675removed-- or (equivalently but more explicitly):
676removed
677removed-- inductive List (α:Type) : Type where
678removed-- | nil : List α
679removed-- | cons (x : α) (l : List α) : List α
680removed
681removed-- This definition introduces the `α` parameter *globally*, to the *left* of
682removed-- the colon, forcing the result of `nil` and `cons` to be the same type
683removed-- (i.e., `List α`). But if we had tried to bring `Nat` to the left of the
684removed-- colon in defining `Ev`, we would have seen an error:
685removed
686removed/--
687removederror: Mismatched inductive type parameter in
688removed WrongEv 0
689removedThe provided argument
690removed 0
691removedis not definitionally equal to the expected parameter
692removed n
693removed
694removedNote: The value of parameter `n` must be fixed throughout the inductive declaration. Consider making this parameter an index if it must vary.
695removed-/
696removed#guard_msgs in
697removedinductive WrongEv (n : Nat) : Prop where
698removed | wrong_ev_0 : WrongEv 0
699removed | wrong_ev_succ_succ (H: WrongEv n) : WrongEv (n + 2)
700removed
701removed-- In an `inductive` definition, an argument to the type constructor on the
702removed-- left of the colon is called a "parameter", whereas an argument on the right
703removed-- is called an "index" or "annotation."
704removed
705removed-- For example, in `inductive List (α : Type) := ...`, the `α` is a parameter,
706removed-- while in `inductive Ev : Nat → Prop := ...`, the unnamed `Nat` argument is
707removed-- an index.
708removed
709removed-- We can think of the inductive definition of `Ev` as defining a Lean
710removed-- property `Ev : Nat → Prop`, together with two "evidence constructors":
711removed
712removed#check (Ev.ev_0) -- Ev 0
713removed#check Ev.ev_succ_succ -- ∀ (n : Nat) (H : Ev n) : Ev (n + 2)
714removed
715removed-- Indeed, Lean also accepts the following equivalent definition of `Ev`
716removed
717removednamespace EvPlayground
718removed
719removedinductive Ev : Nat → Prop where
720removed | ev_0 : Ev 0
721removed | ev_succ_succ : ∀ (n : Nat), Ev n → Ev (n + 2)
722removed
723removedend EvPlayground
724removed
725removed-- These evidence constructors can be thought of as "primitive evidence of
726removed-- evenness", and they can be used later on just like proven theorems. In
727removed-- particular, we can use Lean's `apply` and `exact` tactics with the
728removed-- constructor names to obtain evidence for `Ev` of particular numbers...
729removed
730removedtheorem ev_4 : Ev 4 := by
731removed apply Ev.ev_succ_succ; apply Ev.ev_succ_succ; exact Ev.ev_0
732removed
733removed-- ... or we can use function application syntax to combine several
734removed-- constructors:
735removed
736removedtheorem ev_4' : Ev 4 := by
737removed exact Ev.ev_succ_succ 2 (Ev.ev_succ_succ 0 Ev.ev_0)
738removed
739removed-- ... or we can also use the `constructor` tactic we saw earlier to select
740removed-- the appropriate inductive constructor
741removed
742removedtheorem ev_4'' : Ev 4 := by
743removed constructor; constructor; constructor
744removed
745removed-- In this way, we can also prove theorems that have hypotheses involving
746removed-- `Ev`.
747removed
748removedtheorem ev_plus4 (n : Nat) (h : Ev n) : Ev (4 + n) := by
749removed rw [Nat.add_comm]
750removed exact (Ev.ev_succ_succ _ (Ev.ev_succ_succ _ h))
751removed
752removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): ev_double ⭐
753removed
754removedtheorem ev_double (n : Nat) : Ev n.double := by
755removed sorry
756removed
757removed-- ### Constructing Evidence for Permutations
758removed
759removed-- Similarly we can apply the evidence constructors to obtain evidence of
760removed-- `Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1]`:
761removed
762removedtheorem Perm3_rev : Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1] := by
763removed apply Perm3.perm3_trans (l₂:= [2, 3, 1])
764removed . apply Perm3.perm3_trans (l₂:=[2, 1, 3])
765removed . apply Perm3.perm3_swap12
766removed . apply Perm3.perm3_swap23
767removed . apply Perm3.perm3_swap12
768removed
769removed-- And again we can equivalently use function application syntax to combine
770removed-- several constructors. (Note that the Lean type checker can infer not only
771removed-- types, but also Nats and List, when they are clear from the context.)
772removed
773removedtheorem Perm3_rev' : Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1] := by
774removed exact (Perm3.perm3_trans _ [2, 3, 1] _
775removed (Perm3.perm3_trans _ [2, 1, 3] _
776removed (Perm3.perm3_swap12 _ _ _)
777removed (Perm3.perm3_swap23 _ _ _))
778removed (Perm3.perm3_swap12 _ _ _))
779removed
780removed-- So the informal derivation trees we drew above are not too far from what's
781removed-- happening formally. Formally we're using the evidence constructors to build
782removed-- *evidence trees*, similar to the finite trees we built using the
783removed-- constructors of data types such as Nat, List, binary trees, etc.
784removed
785removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): Perm3 ⭐
786removed
787removedtheorem Perm3_ex1 : Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [2, 3, 1] := by
788removed sorry
789removed
790removedtheorem Perm3_refl : ∀ (α : Type) (a b c : α ), Perm3 [a, b, c] [a, b, c] := by
791removed sorry
792removed
793removed-- ## Using Evidence in Proofs
794removed
795removed-- Besides *constructing* evidence that numbers are even, we can also
796removed-- *destruct* such evidence, reasoning about how it could have been built.
797removed
798removed-- Defining `Ev` with an `inductive` declaration tells Lean not only that the
799removed-- constructors `ev_0` and `ev_succ_succ` are valid ways to build evidence
800removed-- that some number is `Ev`, but also that these two constructors are the
801removed-- *only* ways to build evidence that numbers are `Ev`.
802removed
803removed-- In other words, if someone gives us evidence `E` for the proposition
804removed-- `Ev n`, then we know that `E` must be one of two things:
805removed
806removed-- - `E = ev_0` and `n = 0`, or
807removed
808removed-- - `E = ev_succ_succ n' E'` and `n = n' + 2`, where `E'` is evidence for
809removed-- `Ev n'`.
810removed
811removed-- This suggests that it should be possible to analyze a hypothesis of the
812removed-- form `Ev n` much as we do inductively defined data structures; in
813removed-- particular, it should be possible to argue either by *case analysis* or by
814removed-- *induction* on such evidence. Let's look at a few examples to see what this
815removed-- means in practice.
816removed
817removed-- ### Destructing and Inverting Evidence
818removed
819removed-- Suppose we are proving some fact involving a number `n`, and we are given
820removed-- `Ev n` as a hypothesis. We already know how to perform case analysis on `n`
821removed-- using `cases` or `induction`, generating separate subgoals for the case
822removed-- where `n = 0` and the case where `n = n' + 1` for some `n'`. But for some
823removed-- proofs we may instead want to analyze the evidence for `Ev n` *directly*.
824removed
825removed-- As a tool for such proofs, we can formalize the intuitive characterization
826removed-- that we gave above for evidence of `Ev n`, using `cases`.
827removed
828removedtheorem ev_inversion : ∀ (n : Nat),
829removed Ev n →
830removed (n = 0) ∨ ∃ n', n = n' + 2 ∧ Ev n' := by
831removed intro n H
832removed cases H
833removed case ev_0 =>
834removed left; rfl
835removed case ev_succ_succ n H =>
836removed right; exists n
837removed
838removed-- Facts like this are often called "inversion lemmas" because they allow us
839removed-- to "invert" some given information to reason about all the different ways
840removed-- it could have been derived.
841removed
842removed-- Here there are two ways to prove `Ev n`, and the inversion lemma makes this
843removed-- explicit.
844removed
845removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): le_inversion ⭐
846removed
847removed-- Let's prove a similar inversion lemma for `le`.
848removed
849removednamespace LePlayground
850removedtheorem le_inversion : ∀ (n m : Nat),
851removed Le n m →
852removed (n = m) ∨ (∃ m', m = m' + 1 ∧ Le n m') := by
853removed sorry
854removed
855removedend LePlayground
856removed
857removed-- We can use the inversion lemma that we proved above to help structure
858removed-- proofs:
859removed
860removedtheorem ev_succ_succ_ev : ∀ n, Ev (n + 2) → Ev n := by
861removed intro n H
862removed apply ev_inversion at H
863removed cases H
864removed case inl _ => contradiction
865removed case inr h =>
866removed let ⟨n', ⟨h₁, h₂⟩⟩ := h
867removed injections h₁ heq
868removed subst heq
869removed exact h₂
870removed
871removed-- Note how the inversion lemma produces two subgoals, which correspond to the
872removed-- two ways of proving `Ev`. The first subgoal is a contradiction that is
873removed-- discharged with `contradiction`. The second subgoal makes use of
874removed-- `injections` and `subst`.
875removed
876removed-- We've defined a handy tactic called `inversion` that factors out this
877removed-- common pattern, saving us the trouble of explicitly stating and proving an
878removed-- inversion lemma for every `inductive` definition we make.
879removed
880removed-- Here, the `inversion` tactic can detect (1) that the first case, where
881removed-- `n = 0`, does not apply and (2) that the `n'` that appears in the
882removed-- `ev_succ_succ` case must be the same as `n`.
883removed
884removed-- The details of how `inversion` is implemented are beyond the scope of this
885removed-- course, but suffice to say Lean's metaprogramming capabilities are such
886removed-- that almost any sequence of reasoning steps can be implemented as a new
887removed-- tactic.
888removed
889removedtheorem ev_succ_succ_ev' : ∀ n, Ev (n + 2) → Ev n := by
890removed intro n h
891removed inversion h; assumption
892removed
893removed-- The `inversion` tactic can apply the principle of explosion to "obviously
894removed-- contradictory" hypotheses involving inductively defined properties,
895removed-- something that takes a bit more work using our inversion lemma. Compare:
896removed
897removedtheorem one_not_even : ¬ Ev 1 := by
898removed intro H; apply ev_inversion at H; cases H
899removed /- HIDE: OL20: Someone asked here before "Why doesn't eqn:EE work
900removed here??". It has to do with the use of _ in the pattern.
901removed Anyway when destructing \/,/\, or exists, what we get from
902removed eqn:EE is only confusing for students. I think that we should
903removed remove all "eqn"s in these cases. I did it in this file. -/
904removed case inl _ => contradiction
905removed case inr h =>
906removed let ⟨n', ⟨h₁, h₂⟩⟩ := h
907removed injections
908removed
909removedtheorem one_not_even' : ¬ Ev 1 := by
910removed intro h; inversion h
911removed
912removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): inversion_practice ⭐
913removed
914removed-- Prove the following result using `inversion`. (For extra practice, you can
915removed-- also prove it using the inversion lemma.)
916removed
917removedtheorem ev_4_ev_n : ∀ n,
918removed Ev (n + 4) → Ev n := by
919removed -- ADMITTED -/
920removed intros n h
921removed inversion h
922removed case ev_succ_succ h' => apply ev_succ_succ_ev; exact h'
923removed
924removed-- - []
925removed
926removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): ev5_nonsense ⭐
927removed
928removed-- Prove the following result using `inversion`.
929removed
930removedtheorem ev5_nonsense : Ev 5 → 2 + 2 = 9 := by
931removed sorry
932removed
933removed-- - []
934removed
935removed-- We can use `inversion` to re-prove some theorems from `Tactics.lean`.
936removed
937removed-- Note that `inversion` also works on equality propositions.
938removed
939removedtheorem inversion_ex1 : ∀ (n m o : Nat),
940removed [n, m] = [o, o] → [n] = [m] := by
941removed intro n m o h
942removed inversion h; rfl
943removed
944removedtheorem inversion_ex2 : ∀ (n : Nat),
945removed n + 1 = 0 → 2 + 2 = 5 := by
946removed intro n h
947removed inversion h
948removed
949removed-- Note to developers (before next release):
950removed-- The wording there is totally awkward!
951removed
952removed-- Here's how `inversion` works in general.
953removed
954removed-- - Suppose the name `H` refers to an assumption `P` in the current context,
955removed-- where `P` has been defined by an `inductive` declaration.
956removed
957removed-- - Then, for each of the constructors of `P`, `inversion h` generates a
958removed-- subgoal in which `H` has been replaced by the specific conditions under
959removed-- which this constructor could have been used to prove `P`.
960removed
961removed-- - Some of these subgoals will be self-contradictory; `inversion` throws these
962removed-- away.
963removed
964removed-- - The ones that are left represent the cases that must be proved to establish
965removed-- the original goal. For those, `inversion` adds to the proof context all
966removed-- equations that must hold of the arguments given to `P` -- e.g., `n' = n` in
967removed-- the proof of `ev_succ_succ_ev`).
968removed
969removed-- The `ev_double` exercise above allows us to easily show that our new notion
970removed-- of evenness is implied by the two earlier ones (since, by `even_bool_prop`
971removed-- in chapter Logic, we already know that those are equivalent to each other).
972removed-- To show that all three coincide, we just need the following lemma.
973removed

976removed

1017removed-- I agree that it's all pretty chewy. Wonder if we really need any of it

1019removed-- explained it in class this time, I just observed that the destruct was

1021removed-- want, and skipped all the rest... After thinking about it for a bit,

1028removed
1029removed-- ### Induction on Evidence
1030removed
1031removed-- If this story feels familiar, it is no coincidence: We encountered similar
1032removed-- problems in the Induction chapter, when trying to use case analysis to
1033removed-- prove results that required induction. And once again the solution is...
1034removed-- induction!
1035removed
1036removed-- The behavior of `induction` on evidence is the same as its behavior on
1037removed-- data: It causes Lean to generate one subgoal for each constructor that
1038removed-- could have been used to build that evidence, while providing an induction
1039removed-- hypothesis for each recursive occurrence of the property in question.
1040removed
1041removed-- To prove that a property of `n` holds for all even numbers (i.e., those for
1042removed-- which `Ev n` holds), we can use induction on `Ev n`. This requires us to
1043removed-- prove two things, corresponding to the two ways in which `Ev n` could have
1044removed-- been constructed. If it was constructed by `ev_0`, then `n=0` and the
1045removed-- property must hold of `0`. If it was constructed by `ev_succ_succ`, then
1046removed-- the evidence of `Ev n` is of the form `ev_succ_succ n' E'`, where
1047removed-- `n = n' + 2` and `h'` is evidence for `Ev n'`. In this case, the inductive
1048removed-- hypothesis says that the property we are trying to prove holds for `n'`.
1049removed
1050removed-- Let's try proving that lemma again:
1051removed
1052removedtheorem ev_Even : ∀ n, Ev n → Even n := by
1053removed intro n h
1054removed induction h
1055removed /- h = ev_0 -/
1056removed case ev_0 => exists 0 -- (`0 = double 0` is closed by `exists`'s final `rfl`)
1057removed /- h = ev_succ_succ n' h', with ih : Even n' -/
1058removed case ev_succ_succ n' h' ih =>
1059removed let ⟨k, hk⟩ := ih
1060removed exists k + 1; rw [double_succ, hk]
1061removed
1062removed-- Here, we can see that Lean produced an `ih` that corresponds to `h`, the
1063removed-- single recursive occurrence of `Ev` in its own definition. Since `h'`
1064removed-- mentions `n'`, the induction hypothesis talks about `n'`, as opposed to `n`
1065removed-- or some other number.
1066removed
1067removed-- The equivalence between the second and third definitions of evenness now
1068removed-- follows.
1069removed
1070removedtheorem ev_Even_iff : ∀ n, Ev n ↔ Even n := by
1071removed intro n; apply Iff.intro
1072removed . intro h; exact ev_Even _ h
1073removed . intro ⟨k, hk⟩; rw [hk]; exact ev_double k
1074removed
1075removed-- As we will see in later chapters, induction on evidence is a recurring
1076removed-- technique across many areas -- in particular for formalizing the semantics
1077removed-- of programming languages.
1078removed
1079removed-- The following exercises provide simpler examples of this technique, to help
1080removed-- you familiarize yourself with it.
1081removed
1082removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): ev_sum ⭐⭐
1083removed
1084removedtheorem ev_sum : ∀ n m, Ev n → Ev m → Ev (n + m) := by
1085removed sorry
1086removed
1087removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): ev_ev__ev (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
1088removed
1089removedtheorem ev_ev__ev : ∀ n m, Ev (n + m) → Ev n → Ev m := by
1090removed /- Hint: There are two pieces of evidence you could attempt to induct upon
1091removed here. If one doesn't work, try the other. -/
1092removed sorry
1093removed
1094removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): ev_plus_plus ⭐⭐⭐
1095removed
1096removed-- This exercise can be completed without induction or case analysis. But, you
1097removed-- will need a clever `have` and some tedious rewriting. Hint: Is
1098removed-- `(n+m) + (n+p)` even?
1099removed

1104removed-- Another example of a proposition that can be characterized both recursively
1105removed-- and inductively is the `In` predicate we defined in the Logic chapter. As a
1106removed-- reminder, the recursive definition we saw looked like this:
1107removed
1108removed-- Recall the definition of `In` from last chapter:
1109removed
1110removeddef In' {α : Type} (x : α) (xs : List α) : Prop :=
1111removed match xs with
1112removed | [] => False
1113removed | x' :: xs' => x = x' ∨ In' x xs'
1114removed
1115removed-- We can also write this definition inductively like so:
1116removed
1117removedinductive In_Inductive {α : Type} (a : α) : List α → Prop
1118removed | head (as : List α) : In_Inductive a (a::as)
1119removed | tail (b : α) {as : List α} : In_Inductive a as → In_Inductive a (b::as)
1120removed
1121removed-- In fact, this is exactly how Lean defines this proposition, which it calls
1122removed-- `Mem` and which is written `x ∈ l` (the Unicode symbol is written in). A
1123removed-- good exercise to test your understanding of induction on evidence is to
1124removed-- prove the equivalence of these definitions:
1125removed
1126removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): in_mem ⭐⭐
1127removed
1128removedtheorem in_mem α (x : α) (l : List α) : In x l ↔ x ∈ l := by
1129removed sorry
1130removed
1131removed-- The characterizing lemmas for `∈` are called `List.mem_nil_iff` and
1132removed-- `List.mem_cons`
1133removed
1134removed-- ### Multiple Induction Hypotheses
1135removed
1136removed-- Recall the definition of the reflexive, transitive, closure of a relation:
1137removed
1138removednamespace ClosReflTransRemainder
1139removed
1140removedinductive ClosReflTrans {α: Type} (R: α → α → Prop) : α → α → Prop where
1141removed | rt_step (x y : α) :
1142removed R x y →
1143removed ClosReflTrans R x y
1144removed | rt_refl (x : α) :
1145removed ClosReflTrans R x x
1146removed | rt_trans (x y z : α) :
1147removed ClosReflTrans R x y →
1148removed ClosReflTrans R y z →
1149removed ClosReflTrans R x z
1150removedend ClosReflTransRemainder
1151removed
1152removed-- Let's say that a relation on a type `α` is *diagonal* if it refines the
1153removed-- identity relation -- i.e., if `R x y` implies `x = y`.
1154removed
1155removed-- Note to developers:
1156removed-- HIDE: NDS 25: I originally wanted to do this with the empty relation,
1157removed-- defined inductively, but this requires introducing the surprising
1158removed-- behavior of unhabitated types, which I don't think have been covered
1159removed-- (yet?). Maybe they should be? BCP 25: This one seems good.
1160removed
1161removeddef isDiagonal {α : Type} (R: α → α → Prop) := ∀ x y, R x y → x = y
1162removed
1163removed-- Now consider the following lemma about diagonal relations:
1164removed
1165removedtheorem closure_of_diagonal_is_diagonal : ∀ α (R: α → α → Prop),
1166removed isDiagonal R →
1167removed isDiagonal (ClosReflTrans R) := by
1168removed
1169removed intro α R hDiag x y h
1170removed induction h
1171removed /- The two first cases go as you'd expect... -/
1172removed case rt_step x' y' hr =>
1173removed rw [hDiag x' y' hr]
1174removed case rt_refl => rfl
1175removed /- ... but something interesting happens here: there are two
1176removed induction hypotheses, `ih` and `ih'`! If you think about it, it
1177removed is not that weird: we are in the case `rt_trans`, which has
1178removed two recursive components, `hxy`, relating `x` to `y` and `hyz`,
1179removed relating `y` to `z`. Hence we may want (and will actually need)
1180removed an induction hypothesis for `hxy` and one for `hyz` -- they are
1181removed called `ihxy` and `ihyz` here. In general, Lean will always
1182removed generate one induction hypothesis per recursive constructor of
1183removed the type being inducted over. -/
1184removed case rt_trans x' y' z' hxy hyz ihxy ihyz =>
1185removed rw [ihxy, ihyz]
1186removed
1187removed-- Note to developers:
1188removed-- HIDE: NDS comparing the previous proof to the pen-and-paper version
1189removed-- could be an idea to consider, as the way people tend to write it on
1190removed-- paper differs a bit from the mechanized proof. BCP 25: Yes.
1191removed

1196removed
1197removedinductive Ev' : Nat → Prop where
1198removed | ev'_0 : Ev' 0
1199removed | ev'_2 : Ev' 2
1200removed | ev'_sum n m (Hn : Ev' n) (Hm : Ev' m) : Ev' (n + m)

1205removed-- constructors of inductively defined propositions.

1207removedtheorem ev'_ev : ∀ n, Ev' n ↔ Ev n := by

1210removed-- We can do similar inductive proofs on the `Perm3` relation, which we
1211removed-- defined earlier as follows:
1212removed
1213removednamespace Perm3Reminder
1214removed
1215removedinductive Perm3 {α : Type} : List α → List α → Prop where
1216removed | perm3_swap12 (a b c : α) :
1217removed Perm3 [a, b, c] [b, a, c]
1218removed | perm3_swap23 (a b c : α) :
1219removed Perm3 [a, b, c] [a, c, b]
1220removed | perm3_trans (l₁ l₂ l₃ : List α) :
1221removed Perm3 l₁ l₂ → Perm3 l₂ l₃ → Perm3 l₁ l₃
1222removed
1223removedend Perm3Reminder
1224removed
1225removedtheorem Perm3_symm : ∀ (α : Type) (l₁ l₂ : List α),
1226removed Perm3 l₁ l₂ → Perm3 l₂ l₁ := by
1227removed
1228removed intro α l₁ l₂ h; induction h
1229removed case perm3_swap12 => constructor
1230removed case perm3_swap23 => constructor
1231removed case perm3_trans _ _ _ _ _ ih₁2 ih₂3 =>
1232removed exact Perm3.perm3_trans _ _ _ ih₂3 ih₁2

1258removed-- ## Exercising with Inductive Relations
1259removed
1260removed-- Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018, before next release):
1261removed-- Bad flow + duplication needs fixing. Could move some of this to the
1262removed-- top. In the terse version this whole section is useless, it only has a
1263removed-- (mostly) duplicated definition. For now FULLED the whole thing, but
1264removed-- better fix seems needed.
1265removed
1266removed-- Just as a single-argument proposition defines a *property*, a two-argument
1267removed-- proposition defines a *relation*.
1268removed
1269removed-- A proposition parameterized by a number (such as `Ev`) can be thought of as
1270removed-- a *property* -- i.e., it defines a subset of `Nat`, namely those numbers
1271removed-- for which the proposition is provable. In the same way, a two-argument
1272removed-- proposition can be thought of as a *relation* -- i.e., it defines a set of
1273removed-- pairs for which the proposition is provable.
1274removed
1275removednamespace Playground
1276removed
1277removed-- Just like properties, relations can be defined inductively. One useful
1278removed-- example is the "less than or equal to" relation on numbers that we briefly
1279removed-- saw above.
1280removed
1281removedinductive Le : Nat → Nat → Prop where
1282removed | refl (n : Nat) : Le n n
1283removed | succ (n m : Nat) (H : Le n m) : Le n (m + 1)
1284removed
1285removed-- (We've written the definition a bit differently this time, giving explicit
1286removed-- names to the arguments to the constructors and moving them to the left of
1287removed-- the colons.)
1288removed
1289removed-- Proofs of facts about `≤` using the constructors `Nat.le.refl` and
1290removed-- `Nat.le.step` follow the same patterns as proofs about properties, like
1291removed-- `ev` above. We can `apply` the constructors to prove `≤` goals (e.g., to
1292removed-- show that `3≤3` or `3≤6`), and we can use tactics like `inversion` to
1293removed-- extract information from `≤` hypotheses in the context (e.g., to prove that
1294removed-- `(2 ≤ 1) → 2+2=5`.)
1295removed
1296removed-- Here are some sanity checks on the definition. (Notice that, although these
1297removed-- are the same kind of simple "unit tests" as we gave for the testing
1298removed-- functions we wrote in the first few lectures, we must construct their
1299removed-- proofs explicitly -- `rw`, `dsimp` and `rfl` don't do the job, because the
1300removed-- proofs aren't just a matter of simplifying computations.)
1301removed
1302removed-- Some sanity checks...
1303removed
1304removedtheorem test_le1 : 3 ≤ 3 := by
1305removed all_goals
1306removed apply Nat.le.refl
1307removed
1308removedtheorem test_le2 : 3 ≤ 6 := by
1309removed all_goals
1310removed apply Nat.le.step; apply Nat.le.step; apply Nat.le.step; apply Nat.le.refl
1311removed
1312removedtheorem test_le3 : (2 ≤ 1) → 2 + 2 = 5 := by
1313removed all_goals
1314removed intros h
1315removed inversion h
1316removed case step h' => inversion h'
1317removed
1318removed-- The "strictly less than" relation `n < m` can now be defined in terms of
1319removed-- `Nat.le`.
1320removed
1321removeddef lt (n m : Nat) : Prop := Nat.le (n + 1) m
1322removed
1323removed-- The `≥` operation is defined in terms of `≤`. Lean provides a theorem
1324removed-- `ge_iff_le` allowing us to rewrite between them.
1325removed
1326removeddef ge (m n : Nat) : Prop := Nat.le n m
1327removed
1328removedexample : ∀ (m n : Nat), m ≥ n → n ≤ m := by
1329removed intro m n h
1330removed rw [←ge_iff_le]; assumption
1331removed
1332removedend Playground
1333removed
1334removed-- Note to developers:
1335removed-- HIDE: PR: Added the following paragraph to try to help reduce random
1336removed-- walks over the following exercises.
1337removed
1338removed-- From the definition of `le`, we can sketch the behaviors of `cases` and
1339removed-- `induction` on a hypothesis `h` providing evidence of the form `le e1 e2`.
1340removed-- Doing `cases h` will generate two cases. In the first case, `e1 = e2`, and
1341removed-- it will replace instances of `e2` with `e1` in the goal and context. In the
1342removed-- second case, `e2 = n' + 1` for some `n'` for which `le e1 n'` holds, and it
1343removed-- will replace instances of `e2` with `n' + 1`. Doing `inversion H` will
1344removed-- remove impossible cases and add generated equalities to the context for
1345removed-- further use. Doing `induction h` will, in the second case, add the
1346removed-- induction hypothesis that the goal holds when `e2` is replaced with `n'`.
1347removed

1456removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): R_provability (manually graded) ⭐⭐⭐
1457removed
1458removed-- We can define three-place relations, four-place relations, etc., in just
1459removed-- the same way as binary relations. For example, consider the following
1460removed-- three-place relation on numbers:
1461removed
1462removedinductive R : Nat → Nat → Nat → Prop where
1463removed | c1 : R 0 0 0
1464removed | c2 m n o (h : R m n o ) : R (m + 1) n (o + 1)
1465removed | c3 m n o (h : R m n o ) : R m (n + 1) (o + 1)
1466removed | c4 m n o (h : R (m + 1) (n + 1) (o + 2)) : R m n o
1467removed | c5 m n o (h : R m n o ) : R n m o
