7removedimport LF.SFLCompat
8removed
9removed-- # Logic in Lean
10removed
11removed-- Note to developers (before next release):
12removed-- Unlike earlier chapters, there are probably too many WORKINCLASSes in
13removed-- this chapter. BCP 20: But conversely some more quizzes would be great!
14removed
15removed-- Note to developers (Jonathan Chan @ionathanch):
16removed-- Classical axioms are more pervasive in Lean and the section from Rocq
17removed-- needs to be rewritten to acknowledge this and teach idiomatic style.
18removed-- `BCP: Old comment -- might be out of date?`
19removed
20removed-- Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018):
21removed-- There's several style things to mention here like `classical` vs.
22removed-- `open Classical`. `BCP: This one too?`
23removed
24removed-- IMPORTBLOCK import LF.Basics IMPORTBLOCK import LF.Induction IMPORTBLOCK
25removed-- import LF.Poly IMPORTBLOCK import LF.Tactics IMPORTBLOCK import
26removed-- LF.CustomTactics
27removed
28removedopen Nat hiding add_succ mul_succ beq beq_eq beq_refl
29removed
30removed-- (OA) : added these to use Lean's Nat.
31removed
32removedopen Nat (add add_comm add_assoc add_zero zero_add mul_zero mul_one zero_mul)
33removed
34removed-- We have now seen many examples of factual claims (i.e., *propositions*) and
35removed-- ways of presenting evidence of their truth (*proofs*). In particular, we
36removed-- have worked extensively with equality propositions (`e1 = e2`),
37removed-- implications (`P → Q`), and quantified propositions (`∀ x, P`). In this
38removed-- chapter, we will see how Lean can be used to carry out other familiar forms
39removed-- of logical reasoning.
40removed
41removed-- Before diving into details, we should talk a bit about the status of
42removed-- mathematical statements in Lean. Lean is a *typed* language, which means
43removed-- that every sensible expression has an associated type. Logical claims are
44removed-- no exception: any statement we might try to prove in Lean has a type,
45removed-- namely `Prop`, the type of *propositions*. We can see this with the
46removed-- `#check` command:
47removed
48removed-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
49removed
50removed-- ## The `Prop` Type
51removed
52removed#check (∀ n m : Nat, n + m = m + n : Prop)
53removed
54removed-- Note that *all* syntactically well-formed propositions have type `Prop` in
55removed-- Lean, regardless of whether they are true or not.
56removed
57removed-- Simply *being* a proposition is one thing; being *provable* is a different
58removed-- thing!
59removed
60removed#check (2 = 2 : Prop)
61removed#check (3 = 2 : Prop)
62removed#check (∀ n : Nat, n = 2 : Prop)
63removed
64removed-- Indeed, propositions don't just have types -- they are *first-class*
65removed-- entities that can be manipulated in all the same ways as any of the other
66removed-- things in Lean's world.
67removed
68removed-- So far, we've seen one primary place where propositions can appear: in
69removed-- `theorem` declarations.
70removed
71removedtheorem plus_2_2_is_4 : 2 + 2 = 4 := rfl
72removed
73removed-- But propositions can be used in other ways. For example, we can give a name
74removed-- to a proposition using a `def`, just as we give names to other kinds of
75removed-- expressions.
76removed
77removeddef plus_claim : Prop := 2 + 2 = 4
78removed
79removed#check (plus_claim : Prop)
80removed
81removed-- We can later use this name in any situation where a proposition is expected
82removed-- -- for example, as the claim in a `theorem` declaration.
83removed
84removedtheorem plus_claim_is_true : plus_claim := rfl
85removed
86removed-- We can also write *parameterized* propositions -- that is, functions that
87removed-- take arguments of some type and return a proposition.
88removed
89removed-- For instance, the following function takes a number and returns a
90removed-- proposition asserting that this number is equal to three:
91removed
92removeddef is_three (n : Nat) : Prop := n = 3
93removed
94removed#check (is_three : Nat → Prop)
95removed
96removed-- In Lean, functions that return propositions are said to define *properties*
97removed-- of their arguments.
98removed
99removed-- For instance, here's a (polymorphic) property defining the familiar notion
100removed-- of an *injective function*.
101removed
102removeddef injective {α β} (f : α → β) : Prop :=
103removed ∀ x y : α, f x = f y → x = y
104removed
105removedtheorem succ_inj' : injective succ := by
106removed intro x y H; injection H
107removed
108removed-- The familiar equality operator `=` is a (binary) function that returns a
109removed-- `Prop`. The expression `n = m` is notation for `Eq n m`. Because `eq` can
110removed-- be used with elements of any type, it is also polymorphic:
111removed
112removed-- Note to developers (Jonathan Chan @ionathanch):
113removed-- Actually it quantifies over `Sort`, where `Prop = Sort 0` and
114removed-- `Type u = Sort (u + 1)`. Not something that needs teaching right at
115removed-- this moment, but they'll see `Sort` when hovering.
116removed
117removed#check (Eq : ∀ {α : Type}, α → α → Prop)
118removed
119removed#check pred
120removed
121removed-- As a convenience, Lean will cast booleans by equating them to `true`, which
122removed-- is why checking them against `Prop` succeeds. It also casts boolean
123removed-- equalities to propositions by equating to `true`, and boolean inequalities
124removed-- by equating to `false`. For clarity, we will avoid relying on these
125removed-- implicit casts.
126removed
127removed#check (false : Prop)
128removed
129removed#check (true : Prop)
130removed
131removed-- _Quiz:_
132removed
133removed-- What is the type of the following expression?
134removed
135removed-- pred (succ zero) = zero
136removed
137removed-- 1. `Prop`
138removed-- 2. `Nat → Prop`
139removed-- 3. `∀ n : Nat, Prop`
140removed-- 4. `Nat → Nat`
141removed-- 5. Not typeable
142removed
143removed#check (pred (succ zero) = zero : Prop)
144removed
145removed-- _Quiz:_
146removed
147removed-- What is the type of the following expression?
148removed
149removed-- ∀ n : Nat, pred (succ n) = n
150removed
151removed-- 1. `Prop`
152removed-- 2. `Nat → Prop`
153removed-- 3. `∀ n : Nat, Prop`
154removed-- 4. `Nat → Nat`
155removed-- 5. Not typeable
156removed
157removed#check (∀ n : Nat, pred (succ n) = n : Prop)
158removed
159removed-- _Quiz:_
160removed
161removed-- What is the type of the following expression?
162removed
163removed-- ∀ n : Nat, succ (pred n)
164removed
165removed-- 1. `Prop`
166removed-- 2. `Nat → Prop`
167removed-- 3. `∀ n : Nat, Prop`
168removed-- 4. `Nat → Nat`
169removed-- 5. Not typeable
170removed
171removed#check_failure ∀ n : Nat, succ (pred n)
172removed
173removed-- _Quiz:_
174removed
175removed-- What is the type of the following expression?
176removed
177removed-- fun n : Nat => succ (pred n)
178removed
179removed-- 1. `Prop`
180removed-- 2. `Nat → Prop`
181removed-- 3. `∀ n : Nat, Prop`
182removed-- 4. `Nat → Nat`
183removed-- 5. Not typeable
184removed
185removed#check (fun n : Nat => succ (pred n) : Nat → Nat)
186removed
187removed-- _Quiz:_
188removed
189removed-- What is the type of the following expression?
190removed
191removed-- fun n : Nat => succ (pred n) = n
192removed
193removed-- 1. `Prop`
194removed-- 2. `Nat → Prop`
195removed-- 3. `∀ n : Nat, Prop`
196removed-- 4. `Nat → Nat`
197removed-- 5. Not typeable
198removed
199removed#check (fun n : Nat => succ (pred n) = n : Nat → Prop)
200removed
201removed-- _Quiz:_
202removed
203removed-- Which of the following is *not* a proposition?
204removed
205removed-- 1. `3 + 2 = 4`
206removed-- 2. `3 + 2 = 5`
207removed-- 3. `3 + 2 == 5`
208removed-- 4. `(3 + 2 == 4) = false`
209removed-- 5. `∀ n, (3 + 2 == n) = true → n = 5`
210removed-- 6. All of these are propositions
211removed
212removed#check (3 + 2 == 5 : Bool)
213removed
214removed-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
215removed
216removed-- ## Logical Connectives
217removed
218removed-- ### Conjunction
219removed
220removed-- The *conjunction*, or *logical and*, of propositions `A` and `B` is written
221removed-- `A ∧ B`; it represents the claim that both `A` and `B` are true.
222removed
223removedexample : 3 + 4 = 7 ∧ 2 * 2 = 4 := by
224removed /- A proof of a conjunction is a pair of proofs of the two components.
225removed To prove a conjunction, we build a pair using `constructor`. -/
226removed constructor
227removed case left => /- 3 + 4 = 7 -/ rfl
228removed case right => /- 2 * 2 = 4 -/ rfl
229removed
230removed-- The constructor for conjunction is `And.intro`, which concludes that
231removed-- `A ∧ B` given that `A` and `B` hold individually.
232removed
233removed#check (And.intro : ∀ {α β : Prop}, α → β → α ∧ β)
234removed
235removed-- We can also apply the constructor for the conjunction explicitly.
236removed
237removedexample : 3 + 4 = 7 ∧ 2 * 2 = 4 := by
238removed apply And.intro
239removed case left => /- 3 + 4 = 7 -/ rfl
240removed case right => /- 2 * 2 = 4 -/ rfl
241removed
242removed-- Rather than applying the constructor, we can explicitly provide the
243removed-- arguments to the constructor as an `exact` proof.
244removed
245removedexample : 3 + 4 = 7 ∧ 2 * 2 = 4 := by
246removed exact And.intro rfl rfl
247removed
248removed-- We can also use Lean's anonymous constructor notation ⟨..., ...⟩, which
249removed-- works on constructors for proofs as well.
250removed
251removedexample : 3 + 4 = 7 ∧ 2 * 2 = 4 := by
252removed exact ⟨rfl, rfl⟩
253removed
254removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): add_is_zero ⭐⭐
255removed
256removedtheorem add_is_zero (n m : Nat) : n + m = 0 → n = 0 ∧ m = 0 := by
257removed sorry
258removed
259removed-- So much for proving conjunctive statements. To go in the other direction --
260removed-- i.e., to *use* a conjunctive hypothesis to help prove something else -- we
261removed-- can use `let` to obtain the components.
262removed
263removedexample (n m : Nat) : n = 0 ∧ m = 0 → n + m = 0 := by
264removed all_goals
265removed intro h
266removed let ⟨hn, hm⟩ := h
267removed rw [hn, hm]
268removed
269removed-- As usual, we can also match on `h` right at the point where we introduce
270removed-- it, instead of introducing and then destructing it:
271removed
272removedexample (n m : Nat) : n = 0 ∧ m = 0 → n + m = 0 := by
273removed intro ⟨hn, hm⟩
274removed rw [hn, hm]
275removed
276removed-- You may wonder why we bothered packing the two hypotheses `n = 0` and
277removed-- `m = 0` into a single conjunction, since we could also have stated the
278removed-- theorem with two separate premises:
279removed
280removedexample (n m : Nat) : n = 0 → m = 0 → n + m = 0 := by
281removed intro hn hm
282removed rw [hn, hm]
283removed
284removed-- For this specific theorem, both formulations are fine. But it's important
285removed-- to understand how to work with conjunctive hypotheses because conjunctions
286removed-- often arise from intermediate steps in proofs, especially in larger
287removed-- developments. Here's a simple example:
288removed
289removedexample (n m : Nat) (h : n + m = 0) : n * m = 0 := by
290removed all_goals
291removed apply add_is_zero at h
292removed let ⟨hn, hm⟩ := h
293removed rw [hm]; rfl
294removed
295removed-- Another common situation is that we know `A /\ B` but in some context we
296removed-- need just `A` or just `B`. In such cases we can use an underscore pattern
297removed-- `_` to indicate that the unneeded conjunct should just be thrown away.
298removed
299removedtheorem proj1 (P Q : Prop) (h : P ∧ Q) : P := by
300removed let ⟨hP, _⟩ := h
301removed exact hP
302removed
303removed-- Conjunctions come with their own built-in projections, `.left` and
304removed-- `.right`, which we can use instead of pattern matching.
305removed
306removedtheorem left (P Q : Prop) (h : P ∧ Q) : P := by
307removed exact h.left
308removed
309removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): proj2 ⭐
310removed
311removedtheorem right (P Q : Prop) (h : P ∧ Q) : Q := by
312removed sorry
313removed
314removed-- Finally, we sometimes need to rearrange the order of conjunctions and/or
315removed-- the grouping of multi-way conjunctions. We can see this at work in the
316removed-- proofs of the following commutativity and associativity theorems.
317removed
318removedtheorem and_commute (P Q : Prop) (h : P ∧ Q) : Q ∧ P := by
319removed constructor
320removed case left => exact h.right
321removed case right => exact h.left
322removed
323removed-- The anonymous constructor allows us to write a much terser proof.
324removed
325removedtheorem and_commute' (P Q : Prop) (h : P ∧ Q) : Q ∧ P := by
326removed exact ⟨h.right, h.left⟩
327removed
328removed-- In the following proof of associativity, notice how projections can be
329removed-- chained in sequence to obtain components of nested conjunctions. Complete
330removed-- the proof.
331removed
332removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): and_associate ⭐
333removed
334removedtheorem and_associate (P Q R : Prop) (h : P ∧ (Q ∧ R)) : (P ∧ Q) ∧ R := by
335removed constructor
336removed case left =>
337removed sorry
338removed case right => exact h.right.right
339removed
340removed-- The infix notation `∧` is actually just syntactic sugar for `And A B`. That
341removed-- is, `And` is a Lean operator that takes two propositions as arguments and
342removed-- yields a proposition.
343removed
344removed#check (And : Prop → Prop → Prop)
345removed
346removed-- ### Disjunction
347removed
348removed-- Another important connective is the *disjunction*, or *logical or*, of two
349removed-- propositions: `A ∨ B` is true when either `A` or `B` is. This infix
350removed-- notation stands for `Or A B`, where `Or : Prop -> Prop -> Prop`.
351removed
352removed-- To use a disjunctive hypothesis in a proof, we proceed by case analysis --
353removed-- which, as with other data types like `Nat`, is done using `cases`. The two
354removed-- cases are `inl` (for "left injection", or "in the left case") and `inr`
355removed-- (for "right injection", or "in the right case").
356removed
357removedtheorem factor_is_zero (n m : Nat) (h : n = 0 ∨ m = 0) : n * m = 0 := by
358removed cases h
359removed /- `n = 0` -/
360removed case inl hn => rw [hn, zero_mul]
361removed /- `m = 0` -/
362removed case inr hm => rw [hm, mul_zero]
363removed
364removed-- We can see in this example that, when we perform case analysis on a
365removed-- disjunction `P ∨ Q`, we must separately discharge two proof obligations,
366removed-- each showing that the conclusion holds under a different assumption -- `P`
367removed-- in the first subgoal and `Q` in the second.
368removed
369removed-- Rather than performing case analysis via `cases`, we can also use `obtain`
370removed-- to match on the two possible injections, much like with `let`.
371removed
372removedtheorem and_is_false (b1 b2 : Bool) (h : (b1 = false) ∨ (b2 = false)) :
373removed (b1 && b2) = false := by
374removed obtain hb1 | hb2 := h
375removed case inl => rw [hb1, Bool.false_and]
376removed case inr => rw [hb2, Bool.and_false]
377removed
378removed-- Conversely, to show that a disjunction holds, it suffices to show that one
379removed-- of its sides holds. This can be done via the tactics `left` and `right`. As
380removed-- their names imply, the first one requires proving the left side of the
381removed-- disjunction, while the second requires proving the right side. Here is a
382removed-- trivial use...
383removed
384removedtheorem or_intro_l (P Q : Prop) (h : P) : P ∨ Q := by
385removed left; exact h
386removed
387removed-- ... and here is a slightly more interesting example requiring both `left`
388removed-- and `right`:
389removed
390removedtheorem zero_or_succ (n : Nat) : n = 0 ∨ n = pred (succ n) := by
391removed all_goals
392removed cases n
393removed case zero => left; rfl
394removed case succ n => right; rw [Nat.pred_succ]
395removed
396removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): mul_is_zero ⭐⭐
397removed
398removedtheorem mul_is_zero (n m : Nat) (h : n * m = 0) : n = 0 ∨ m = 0 := by
399removed sorry
400removed

402removed
403removedtheorem or_commute (P Q : Prop) (h : P ∨ Q) : Q ∨ P := by
404removed sorry

406removed-- ### Falsehood and Negation
407removed
408removed-- Up to this point, we have mostly been concerned with proving "positive"
409removed-- statements -- addition is commutative, appending lists is associative, etc.
410removed-- We are sometimes also interested in negative results, demonstrating that
411removed-- some proposition is *not* true. Such statements are expressed with the
412removed-- logical negation operator `¬`, which a prefix notation for `Not`.
413removed
414removed-- To see how negation works, recall the *principle of explosion* from the
415removed-- `Tactics` chapter, which asserts that, if we assume a contradiction, then
416removed-- any other proposition can be derived.
417removed
418removed-- Following this intuition, we could define `¬ P` ("not `P`") as
419removed-- `∀ Q, P → Q`. Lean makes an equivalent but slightly different choice,
420removed-- defining `~ P` as `P → False`, where `False` is a specific unprovable
421removed-- proposition defined in the standard library.
422removed
423removed#check (Not : Prop → Prop)
424removed#print Not
425removed
426removedexample : ∀ P, Not P = (P → False) := by intro; rfl
427removedexample : ∀ P, (¬ P) = (P → False) := by intro; rfl
428removed
429removed-- Since `False` is a contradictory proposition, the principle of explosion
430removed-- also applies to it. If we can get `False` into the context, we can use
431removed-- `cases` on it to complete any goal:
432removed
433removedtheorem ex_falso_quodlibet (P : Prop) (h : False) : P := by
434removed cases h
435removed
436removed-- The Latin *ex falso quodlibet* means, literally, "from falsehood follows
437removed-- whatever you like"; this is another common name for the principle of
438removed-- explosion.
439removed
440removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): not_implies_other_not ⭐⭐
441removed
442removedtheorem not_implies_other_not (P : Prop) (h : ¬ P) :
443removed (∀ Q : Prop, P → Q) := by
444removed sorry
445removed
446removed-- Inequality is a very common form of negated statement, so there is a
447removed-- special notation for it: `≠`, which is infix notation for `Ne`.
448removed
449removed#print Ne
450removed
451removedtheorem zero_not_one : 0 ≠ 1 := by
452removed /- FULL: The proposition `0 ≠ 1` is exactly the same as `¬ (0 = 1)`
453removed -- that is, `Not (0 = 1)` -- which unfolds to `(0 = 1) → False`. -/
454removed /- FULL: To prove an inequality, we may assume the opposite equality... -/
455removed intro contra
456removed /- FULL: ...and deduce a contradiction from it. Here, the equality
457removed `0 = 1` corresponds to `zero = succ zero`, which contradicts
458removed disjointness of constructors `zero` and `succ`, so `contradiction`
459removed takes care of it. -/
460removed contradiction
461removed -- JC: `cases contra` and `injection contra` both also work,
462removed -- but is probably harder to explain.
463removed
464removed-- It takes a little practice to get used to working with negation in Lean.
465removed-- Even though *you* may see perfectly well why a claim involving negation
466removed-- holds, it can be a little tricky at first to see how to make Lean
467removed-- understand it!
468removed
469removed-- Here are proofs of a few familiar facts to help get you warmed up.
470removed
471removedtheorem not_False : ¬ False := by
472removed intro h; exact h
473removed
474removedtheorem contradiction_implies_anything (P Q : Prop) (h : P ∧ ¬ P) : Q := by
475removed all_goals
476removed let ⟨hP, hnP⟩ := h
477removed apply hnP at hP; cases hP
478removed
479removedtheorem double_neg (P : Prop) (hP : P) : ¬ ¬ P := by
480removed all_goals
481removed intro h; apply h; exact hP
482removed
483removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): double_neg_informal (Advanced, manually graded) ⭐⭐
484removed

489removed

503removed-- this chapter.
504removed
505removedtheorem de_morgan_not_or (P Q : Prop) (h : ¬ (P ∨ Q)) : ¬ P ∧ ¬ Q := by

508removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): not_succ_inverse_pred ⭐
509removed
510removed-- Since we are working with natural numbers, we can disprove that `succ` and
511removed-- `pred` are inverses of each other:
512removed
513removedtheorem not_succ_pred_n : ¬ (∀ n : Nat, succ (pred n) = n) := by
514removed sorry
515removed
516removed-- Since inequality involves a negation, it also requires a little practice to
517removed-- be able to work with it fluently. Here is one useful trick.
518removed
519removed-- If you are trying to prove a goal that is nonsensical (e.g., the goal state
520removed-- is `false = true`), apply `ex_falso_quodlibet` to change the goal to
521removed-- `False`.
522removed
523removed-- This makes it easier to use assumptions of the form `¬ P` that may be
524removed-- available in the context -- in particular, assumptions of the form `x ≠ y`.
525removed
526removedtheorem not_true_is_false (b : Bool) (h : b ≠ true) : b = false := by
527removed -- FOLD
528removed cases b
529removed case false => rfl
530removed case true =>
531removed unfold Ne Not at h
532removed apply ex_falso_quodlibet
533removed apply h; rfl
534removed -- /FOLD
535removed
536removed-- Since reasoning with `ex_falso_quodlibet` is quite common, Lean provides a
537removed-- tactic, `exfalso`, for applying it.
538removed
539removedtheorem not_true_is_false' (b : Bool) (h : b ≠ true) : b = false := by
540removed cases b
541removed case false => rfl
542removed case true =>
543removed unfold Ne Not at h
544removed exfalso -- ⟵ here
545removed apply h; rfl
546removed
547removed-- Note to developers:
548removed-- HIDE: CH: I don't think this was the original intention, but some of
549removed-- these quizzes got unnecessarily tricky and pedantic. For instance, the
550removed-- first quiz below makes a big distinction between using the destruct
551removed-- tactic and destructing using an intro pattern, even if conceptually
552removed-- there is no difference. Could it be that these quizzes were devised
553removed-- when intro patterns were not taught in the course and an update would
554removed-- be helpful now? Since I don't see the gain in tricking a majority of
555removed-- students in giving the "wrong" answer, even if it's a perfectly
556removed-- sensible one.
557removed
558removed-- _Quiz:_
559removed
560removed-- To prove the following proposition, which tactics will we need besides
561removed-- `intro`, `apply`, and `exact`?
562removed
563removed-- ∀ X : Prop, ∀ a b : X, a = b ∧ a ≠ b → False
564removed
565removed-- 1. `cases`, `unfold`, `left`, and `right`
566removed-- 2. `cases` and `unfold`
567removed-- 3. only `cases`
568removed-- 4. `left` and/or `right`
569removed-- 5. only `unfold`
570removed-- 6. none of the above
571removed
572removedexample (X : Prop) (a b : X) : a = b ∧ a ≠ b → False := by
573removed intro ⟨h, hn⟩; apply hn; exact h
574removed
575removed-- _Quiz:_
576removed
577removed-- To prove the following proposition, which tactics will we need besides
578removed-- `intro`, `apply`, and `exact`?
579removed
580removed-- ∀ P Q : Prop, P ∨ Q → ¬ ¬ (P ∨ Q)
581removed
582removed-- 1. `cases`, `unfold`, `left`, and `right`
583removed-- 2. `cases` and `unfold`
584removed-- 3. only `cases`
585removed-- 4. `left` and/or `right`
586removed-- 5. only `unfold`
587removed-- 6. none of the above
588removed
589removedexample (P Q : Prop) (h : P ∨ Q) : ¬ ¬ (P ∨ Q) := by
590removed intro hn; apply hn; exact h
591removed
592removed-- _Quiz:_
593removed
594removed-- To prove the following proposition, which tactics will we need besides
595removed-- `intro`, `apply`, and `exact`?
596removed
597removed-- ∀ P Q : Prop, P → (P ∨ ¬ ¬ Q)
598removed
599removed-- 1. `cases`, `unfold`, `left`, and `right`
600removed-- 2. `cases` and `unfold`
601removed-- 3. only `cases`
602removed-- 4. `left` and/or `right`
603removed-- 5. only `unfold`
604removed-- 6. none of the above
605removed
606removedexample (P Q : Prop) (h : P) : P ∨ ¬ ¬ Q := by
607removed left; exact h
608removed
609removed-- _Quiz:_
610removed
611removed-- To prove the following proposition, which tactics will we need besides
612removed-- `intro`, `apply`, and `exact`?
613removed
614removed-- ∀ P Q : Prop, P ∨ Q → (¬ ¬ P) ∨ (¬ ¬ Q)
615removed
616removed-- 1. `cases`, `unfold`, `left`, and `right`
617removed-- 2. `cases` and `unfold`
618removed-- 3. only `cases`
619removed-- 4. `left` and/or `right`
620removed-- 5. only `unfold`
621removed-- 6. none of the above
622removed
623removedexample (P Q : Prop) (h : P ∨ Q) : (¬ ¬ P) ∨ (¬ ¬ Q) := by
624removed cases h

628removed-- _Quiz:_
629removed
630removed-- To prove the following proposition, which tactics will we need besides

636removed-- 2. `contradiction` and `unfold`
637removed-- 3. only `contradiction`
638removed-- 4. `left` and/or `right`

645removed-- ## Truth
646removed
647removed-- Besides `False`, Lean's standard library also defines `True`, a proposition
648removed-- that is trivially true. To prove it, we use the constructor `True.intro`
649removed-- explicitly, or the anonymous constructor `⟨⟩`, or the `constructor` tactic.
650removed
651removedexample : True := by exact True.intro
652removedexample : True := True.intro
653removedexample : True := by exact ⟨⟩
654removedexample : True := ⟨⟩
655removedexample : True := by constructor
656removed
657removed-- Unlike `False`, which is used extensively, `True` is used relatively
658removed-- rarely: it is trivial (and therefore uninteresting) to prove as a goal, and
659removed-- it provides no useful information when it appears as a hypothesis.
660removed
661removed-- However, `True` can be quite useful when defining complex `Prop`s using
662removed-- conditionals or as a parameter to higher-order `Prop`s. We'll come back to
663removed-- this later.
664removed
665removed-- For now, let's take a look at how we can use `True` and `False` to achieve
666removed-- an effect similar to that of the `contradiction` tactic, without literally
667removed-- using `contradiction`.
668removed
669removed-- Pattern-matching lets us do different things for different constructors. If
670removed-- the result of applying two different constructors were hypothetically
671removed-- equal, then we could use `match` to convert an unprovable statement (like
672removed-- `False`) to one that is provable (like `True`).
673removed
674removeddef discr_fun (n : Nat) : Prop :=
675removed match n with
676removed | 0 => True
677removed | _ + 1 => False
678removed
679removedtheorem discr_fun_zero : discr_fun 0 = True := rfl
680removed
681removedtheorem discr_fun_succ n : discr_fun (n + 1) = False := rfl
682removed
683removedtheorem discr_example (n : Nat) : ¬ (0 = n + 1) := by
684removed intro h
685removed have hd : discr_fun 0 := by rw [discr_fun_zero]; exact ⟨⟩
686removed rw [h, discr_fun_succ] at hd; exact hd
687removed
688removed-- To generalize this to other constructors, we simply have to provide an
689removed-- appropriate variant of `discr_fun`. To generalize it to other conclusions,
690removed-- we can use `exfalso` to replace them with `False`. The `contradiction`
691removed-- tactic takes care of all of this for us.
692removed

696removed-- `contradiction` tactic.

701removed ¬ ([] = x :: xs) := by

704removed-- ### Logical Equivalence
705removed
706removed-- The handy "if and only if" connective, which asserts that two propositions
707removed-- have the same truth value, is a structure containing the two implication
708removed-- directions. `P ↔ Q` is notation for `Iff P Q`.
709removed
710removed#print Iff
711removed
712removed#check (fun α β : Prop => α ↔ β : Prop → Prop → Prop)
713removed
714removedtheorem iff_sym (P Q : Prop) (h : P ↔ Q) : (Q ↔ P) := by
715removed all_goals
716removed constructor
717removed case mp => exact h.mpr
718removed case mpr => exact h.mp
719removed
720removedtheorem not_true_iff_false (b : Bool) : b ≠ true ↔ b = false := by
721removed constructor
722removed case mp => apply not_true_is_false
723removed case mpr => intro h; rw [h]; intro h'; contradiction

737removed constructor

739removed intro h
740removed obtain hP | (hQ | hR) := h

742removed case inr.inl => left; right; exact hQ
743removed case inr.inr => right; exact hR

748removed case inl.inr => right; left; exact hQ
749removed case inr => right; right; exact hR

758removed n * m = 0 ↔ n = 0 ∨ m = 0 := by

763removed-- ### Existential Quantification
764removed
765removed-- Another fundamental logical connective is *existential quantification*. To
766removed-- say that there is some `x` of type `T` such that some property `P` holds of
767removed-- `x`, we write `∃ x : T, P`. This is notation for the `Exists` connective,
768removed-- and is defined as `Exists (fun (x : T) => P)`. As with `∀ x : T`, the type
769removed-- annotation `: T` can be omitted if Lean is able to infer from the context
770removed-- what the type of `x` should be.
771removed
772removed-- To prove a statement of the form `∃ x, P`, we must show that `P` holds for
773removed-- some specific choice for `x`, known as the *witness* of the existential.
774removed-- This is done in two steps: First, we explicitly tell Lean which witness `t`
775removed-- we have in mind by invoking the tactic `exists t`. Then we prove that `P`
776removed-- holds after all occurrences of `x` are replaced by `t`. The `exists` tactic
777removed-- tries to close the proof with simple tactics such as `rfl` or
778removed-- `contradiction`, so we may not have to prove `P` explicitly.
779removed
780removed#check (Exists : ∀ {T : Type}, (T → Prop) → Prop)
781removed
782removedabbrev Even x := ∃ n : Nat, x = double n
783removed
784removed#check (Even : Nat → Prop)
785removed
786removedexample : Even 4 := by exists 2
787removed -- `4 = double 2` holds by `rfl`,
788removed -- but is proven automatically by `exists`
789removed
790removed-- Conversely, if we have an existential hypothesis `∃ x, P` in the context,
791removed-- can destruct it to obtain a witness `x` and a hypothesis stating that `P`
792removed-- holds of `x`.
793removed
794removedexample n : (∃ m, n = m + 4) → (∃ o, n = o + 2) := by
795removed intro ⟨m, hm⟩
796removed exists (m + 2)
797removed

826removed
827removed-- ## Recap: Logical Connectives in Lean
828removed
829removed-- Connectives introduced in this chapter:
830removed
831removed-- - `A ∧ B` (conjunction):
832removed
833removed-- - introduced with `constructor`
834removed-- - eliminated with `intro ⟨HA, HB⟩` or `let ⟨HA, HB⟩ := H`
835removed
836removed-- - `A ∨ B` (disjunction):
837removed
838removed-- - introduced with `left` and `right`
839removed-- - eliminated with `cases`
840removed
841removed-- - `False` (falsehood):
842removed
843removed-- - eliminated with `cases` or `contradiction`
844removed
845removed-- - `¬ A` (negation):
846removed
847removed-- - defined as `A → False`
848removed
849removed-- - `True` (truthhood):
850removed
851removed-- - introduced as`True.intro` or with `constructor`
852removed
853removed-- - `A ↔ B` (iff):
854removed
855removed-- - introduced with `constructor`
856removed-- - eliminated with `intro ⟨HAB, HBA⟩` or `let ⟨HAB, HBA⟩ := H`
857removed
858removed-- - `∃ x : A, P` (existential):
859removed
860removed-- - introduced with `exists t`
861removed-- - eliminated with `intro ⟨x, Hx⟩` or `let ⟨x, Hx⟩ := H`
862removed
863removed-- Fundamental connectives we've been using since the beginning:
864removed
865removed-- - equality (`e1 = e2`)
866removed-- - implication (`P → Q`)
867removed-- - universal quantification (`∀ x, P`)
868removed
869removed-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
870removed
871removed-- ## Programming with Propositions
872removed
873removed-- The logical connectives that we have seen provide a rich vocabulary for
874removed-- defining complex propositions from simpler ones. To illustrate, let's look
875removed-- at how to express teh claim that an element `x` occurs in a list `l`.
876removed-- Notice that this property has a simple recursive structure:
877removed
878removed-- We can translate this directly into a straightforward recursive function
879removed-- taken an element and a list and returning... a proposition!
880removed
881removeddef In {α : Type} (x : α) (xs : List α) : Prop :=
882removed match xs with
883removed | [] => False
884removed | x' :: xs' => x = x' ∨ In x xs'
885removed
886removedtheorem In_nil {α} (x : α) : In x [] = False := rfl
887removed
888removedtheorem In_cons {α} (x x' : α) (xs : List α) : In x (x' :: xs) = (x = x' ∨ In x xs) := rfl
889removed
890removed-- When `In` is applied to a concrete list, it exapnds into a concrete
891removed-- sequence of nested disjunctions.
892removed
893removedexample : In 4 [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] := by
894removed all_goals
895removed dsimp [In]; right; right; right; left; rfl
896removed
897removedexample (n : Nat) (h : In n [2, 4]) : ∃ n' : Nat, n = 2 * n' := by
898removed all_goals
899removed dsimp [In] at h
900removed obtain h | h | ⟨⟨⟩⟩ := h
901removed case inl => exists 1
902removed case inr.inl => exists 2
903removed /- (Notice the use of the empty pattern to discharge the last case.) -/
904removed
905removed-- We can also reason about more generic statements involving `In`.
906removed
907removedtheorem In_map (α β : Type) (f : α → β) (xs : List α) (x : α) (h : In x xs) :
908removed In (f x) (List.map f xs) := by
909removed -- TERSE: FOLD
910removed induction xs
911removed case nil => rw [In_nil] at h; contradiction
912removed case cons x' xs' ih =>
913removed rw [In_cons] at h
914removed obtain h | h := h
915removed case inl => rw [h, List.map_cons, In_cons]; left; rfl
916removed case inr => rw [List.map_cons, In_cons]; right; exact ih h
917removed -- TERSE: /FOLD
918removed
919removed-- This way of defining propositions recursively is very convenient in some
920removed-- cases, less so in others. In particular, it is subject to the usual
921removed-- restrictions regarding definitions of recursive functions, e.g., the
922removed-- requirement that they be "obviously terminating."
923removed
924removed-- In the next chapter, we will see how to define propositions *inductively*
925removed-- -- a different technique with its own strengths and limitations.
926removed
927removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): In_map_iff ⭐⭐
928removed
929removedtheorem In_map_iff (α β : Type) (f : α → β) (xs : List α) (y : β) :
930removed In y (List.map f xs) ↔ ∃ x, f x = y ∧ In x xs := by
931removed constructor
932removed case mp =>
933removed sorry
934removed case mpr =>
935removed sorry
936removed
937removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): All ⭐⭐⭐
938removed
939removed-- We noted above that functions returning propositions can be seen as
940removed-- *properties* of their arguments. For instance, if `P` has type
941removed-- `Nat -> Prop`, then `P n` says that property `P` holds of `n`.
942removed
943removed-- Drawing inspiration from `In`, write a recursive function `All` stating
944removed-- that some property `P` holds of all elements of a list `xs`. To make sure
945removed-- your definition is correct, prove the `All_In` lemma below. (Of course,
946removed-- your definition should *not* just restate the left-hand side of `All_In`.)
947removed
948removeddef All {α : Type} (P : α → Prop) (xs : List α) : Prop := sorry
949removed
950removedtheorem All_nil {α} (P : α → Prop) : All P [] = True := sorry
951removed
952removedtheorem All_cons {α} (P : α → Prop) x xs : All P (x :: xs) = (P x ∧ All P xs) := sorry
953removed
954removedtheorem All_In α (P : α → Prop) (xs : List α) :
955removed (∀ x, In x xs → P x) ↔ All P xs := by
956removed sorry

985removed-- ## Applying Theorems to Arguments
986removed
987removed-- Lean treats *proofs* as first-class objects. There is a great deal to be
988removed-- said about this, but it is not necessary to understand it all to use Lean.
989removed-- This section gives just a taste, leaving a deeper exploration for the
990removed-- optional chapters `ProofObjects` and `IndPrinciples`.
991removed
992removed-- We have seen that we can use `#check` to ask Lean whether an expression has
993removed-- a given type:
994removed
995removed#check (add : Nat → Nat → Nat)
996removed
997removed-- We can also use it to check what theorem a particular identifier refers to:
998removed
999removed#check add_comm
1000removed
1001removed#check add_assoc
1002removed
1003removed-- Lean checks the *statements* of the `add_comm` and `add_assoc` theorems in
1004removed-- the same way that it checks the *type* of any term (e.g. `add`). Leaving
1005removed-- off the colon and the type, Lean prints these types in the infoview for us.
1006removed
1007removed-- Why?
1008removed
1009removed-- The reason is that the identifier `add_comm` actually refers to a *proof
1010removed-- object* -- a logical derivation establishing the truth of the statement
1011removed-- `∀ n m, n + m = m + n`. The type of this object is the proposition that it
1012removed-- is a proof of.
1013removed
1014removed-- The type of an ordinary function tells us what we can do with it.
1015removed
1016removed-- - If we have a term of type `Nat → Nat → Nat`, we can give it two `Nat`s as
1017removed-- arguments and get a `Nat` back. Similarly, the statement of a theorem tells
1018removed-- us what we can use that theorem for.
1019removed
1020removed-- - If we have a term of type `∀ n m, n = m → n + n = m + n`, and we provide it
1021removed-- two numbers `n` and `m` and a third "arugment" of type `n = m`, we get back
1022removed-- a proof object of type `n + n = m + m`.
1023removed
1024removed-- Operationally, this analogy goes even further: by applying a theorem as if
1025removed-- it were a function, i.e., applying it to values and hypotheses with
1026removed-- matching types, we can specialize its result without having to resort to
1027removed-- intermediate assertions. For example, suppose we wanted to prove the
1028removed-- follwing result:
1029removed
1030removedexample (x y z : Nat) : x + (y + z) = (z + y) + x := by
1031removed rw [add_comm]
1032removed rw [add_comm]
1033removed sorry
1034removed
1035removed-- It appears at first sight that we ought to be able to prove this be
1036removed-- rewriting with `add_comm` twice to make the two sides match. The problem is
1037removed-- that the second rewrite undoes the effect of the first, leaving us back
1038removed-- where we started...
1039removed
1040removed-- We can fix this by applying `add_comm` to the arguments we want it to be
1041removed-- instantiated with, in much the same way as we apply a polymorphic function
1042removed-- to a type argument. Then the rewrite is forced to happen exactly where we
1043removed-- want it.
1044removed
1045removedexample (x y z : Nat) : x + (y + z) = (z + y) + x := by
1046removed rw [add_comm]
1047removed rw [add_comm z y]
1048removed
1049removed-- If we really wanted, we could in fact do it for both rewrites.
1050removed
1051removedexample (x y z : Nat) : x + (y + z) = (z + y) + x := by
1052removed rw [add_comm x (y + z)]
1053removed rw [add_comm z y]
1054removed
1055removed-- The fact that implications are functions means we can prove them by
1056removed-- explicitly providing a function.
1057removed
1058removedtheorem identity {P : Prop} : P → P := fun h => h
1059removed
1060removed-- _Quiz:_
1061removed
1062removed-- Suppose we have
1063removed
1064removed-- n m : Nat
1065removed-- H1 : n = m
1066removed-- H2 : b = 42
1067removed-- trans_eq : ∀ (α : Type) (a b c : α), a = b → b = c → a = c
1068removed
1069removed-- What is the type of this "proof object"?
1070removed
1071removed-- trans_eq Nat n m 42 H1 H2
1072removed
1073removed-- 1. `n = m`
1074removed-- 2. `42 = n`
1075removed-- 3. `n = 42`
1076removed-- 4. Does not typecheck
1077removed
1078removed-- example (n m : Nat) (h1 : n = m) (h2 : m = 42) (trans*eq : ∀ (α : Type) (a
1079removed-- b c : α), a = b → b = c → a = c) : True := by have : n = 42 := trans*eq Nat
1080removed-- n m 42 h1 h2
1081removed
1082removed-- _Quiz:_
1083removed
1084removed-- Suppose, again, we have
1085removed
1086removed-- n m : Nat
1087removed-- H1 : n = m
1088removed-- H2 : b = 42
1089removed-- trans_eq : ∀ (α : Type) (a b c : α), a = b → b = c → a = c
1090removed
1091removed-- What is the type of this proof object?
1092removed
1093removed-- trans_eq _ _ _ _ H1 H2
1094removed
1095removed-- 1. `n = m`
1096removed-- 2. `42 = n`
1097removed-- 3. `n = 42`
1098removed-- 4. Does not typecheck
1099removed
1100removed-- _Quiz:_
1101removed
1102removed-- Suppose, again, we have
1103removed
1104removed-- n m : Nat
1105removed-- H1 : n = m
1106removed-- H2 : b = 42
1107removed-- trans_eq : ∀ (α : Type) (a b c : α), a = b → b = c → a = c
1108removed
1109removed-- What is the type of this proof object?
1110removed
1111removed-- trans_eq Nat m 42 n H2
1112removed
1113removed-- 1. `m = n`
1114removed-- 2. `m = n → 42 = n`
1115removed-- 3. `42 = n → m = n`
1116removed-- 4. Does not typecheck
1117removed
1118removed-- _Quiz:_
1119removed
1120removed-- Suppose, again, we have
1121removed
1122removed-- n m : Nat
1123removed-- H1 : n = m
1124removed-- H2 : b = 42
1125removed-- trans_eq : ∀ (α : Type) (a b c : α), a = b → b = c → a = c
1126removed
1127removed-- What is the type of this proof object?
1128removed
1129removed-- trans_eq _ 42 n m
1130removed
1131removed-- 1. `n = m → m = 42 → n = 42`
1132removed-- 2. `42 = n → n = m → 42 = m`
1133removed-- 3. `n = 42 → 42 = m → n = m`
1134removed-- 4. Does not typecheck
1135removed
1136removed-- _Quiz:_
1137removed
1138removed-- Suppose, again, we have
1139removed
1140removed-- n m : Nat
1141removed-- H1 : n = m
1142removed-- H2 : b = 42
1143removed-- trans_eq : ∀ (α : Type) (a b c : α), a = b → b = c → a = c
1144removed
1145removed-- What is the type of this proof object?
1146removed
1147removed-- trans_eq _ _ _ _ H2 H1
1148removed
1149removed-- 1. `b = a`
1150removed-- 2. `42 = a`
1151removed-- 3. `a = 42`
1152removed-- 4. Does not typecheck
1153removed
1154removed-- ## Working with Decidable Properties
1155removed
1156removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
1157removed-- This will need better typesetting...
1158removed
1159removed-- We've seen two different ways of expressing logical claims in Lean: with
1160removed-- *booleans* (of type `Bool`), and with *propositions* (of type `Prop`). Here
1161removed-- are the key differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
1162removed
1163removed-- | | `Bool` | `Prop` | | ------------------- | ------ | ------ | |
1164removed-- decidable? | yes | no | | useable with match? | yes | no |
1165removed
1166removed-- FULL: The crucial difference between the two worlds is *decidability*.
1167removed-- Every (closed) expression of type `Bool` can be simplified in a finite
1168removed-- number of steps to either `true` or `false` -- i.e., there is a terminating
1169removed-- mechanical procedure for deciding whether or not it is `true`.
1170removed
1171removed-- This means that, for example, the type `Nat → Bool` is inhabited only by
1172removed-- functions that, given a `Nat`, always yield either `true` or `false` in
1173removed-- finite time; this, in turn, means (by a standard computability argument)
1174removed-- that there is *no* function in `Nat → Bool` that checks whether a given
1175removed-- number is the code of a terminating Turing machine.
1176removed
1177removed-- By contrast, the type `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1178removed-- mathematical propositions; in particular, the type `Nat → Prop` does
1179removed-- contain functions representing properties like "the nth Turing machine
1180removed-- halts."
1181removed
1182removed-- The second table row follows directly from this essential difference. To
1183removed-- evaluate a pattern match (or conditional) on a boolean, we need to know
1184removed-- whether the scrutinee evaluates to `true` or `false`; this only works for
1185removed-- `bool`, not `Prop`.
1186removed
1187removed-- Since `Prop` includes *both* decidable and undecidable properties, we have
1188removed-- two options when we want to formalize a property that happens to be
1189removed-- decidable: we can express it either as a boolean computation, or as a
1190removed-- function into `Prop`.
1191removed
1192removed-- For instance, to claim that a number `n` is even, we can say either that
1193removed-- `even n` evaluates to `true`...
1194removed
1195removedexample : even 42 = true := rfl
1196removed
1197removed-- ... or that there exists some `k` such that `n = double k`.
1198removed
1199removedexample : Even 42 := by dsimp [Even]; exists 21
1200removed
1201removed-- Of course, it would be deeply strange if these two characterizations of
1202removed-- evenness did not describe the same set of natural numbers! Fortunately,
1203removed-- they do!
1204removed
1205removed-- To prove this, we first need two helper lemmas.
1206removed
1207removedtheorem even_double (k : Nat) :
1208removed even (double k) = true := by
1209removed -- FOLD
1210removed induction k
1211removed case zero => rw [double_zero]; rfl
1212removed case succ k' ih => rw [double_succ]; exact ih
1213removed -- /FOLD
1214removed
1215removedtheorem even_double_conv (n : Nat) : ∃ k : Nat,
1216removed n = bif even n then double k else succ (double k) := by
1217removed sorry
1218removed
1219removed-- Now the main theorem:
1220removed
1221removedtheorem even_bool_prop (n : Nat) : even n = true ↔ Even n := by
1222removed -- FOLD
1223removed constructor
1224removed case mp =>
1225removed intro h
1226removed let ⟨k, hk⟩ := even_double_conv n
1227removed rw [h] at hk; dsimp at hk; dsimp [Even]; exists k
1228removed case mpr =>
1229removed intro ⟨k, hk⟩; rw [hk]; apply even_double
1230removed -- /FOLD
1231removed
1232removed-- In view of this theorem, we can say that the boolean computation `even n`
1233removed-- is *reflected* in the truth of the proposition `∃ k, n = double k`.
1234removed
1235removed-- Similarly, to state that two numbers `n` and `m` are equal, we can say
1236removed-- either
1237removed
1238removed-- 1. that `n == m` returns `true`, or
1239removed-- 2. that `n = m`.
1240removed
1241removed-- Again, these two notions are equivalent:
1242removed
1243removed-- (For the reverse direction we need the simple fact that `==` is reflexive.)
1244removed
1245removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
1246removed-- @dsainati1 wonders whether this tactic has been explained.
1247removed
1248removedtheorem beq_refl (n : Nat) : (n == n) = true := decide_eq_true rfl
1249removed
1250removedtheorem beq_eq_true (n1 n2 : Nat) :
1251removed (n1 == n2) = true ↔ n1 = n2 := by
1252removed -- FOLD
1253removed constructor
1254removed case mp => apply beq_eq
1255removed case mpr => intro H; rw [H, beq_refl]
1256removed -- /FOLD
1257removed
1258removed-- So what should we do in situations where some claim could be formalized as
1259removed-- either a proposition or a boolean computation? Which should we choose?
1260removed
1261removed-- In general, *both* can be useful. For example, booleans are more useful for
1262removed-- defining functions, since we can test whether they are true using
1263removed-- conditional expressions.
1264removed
1265removedabbrev is_even_prime (n : Nat) : Bool :=
1266removed bif n == 2 then true else false
1267removed
1268removed-- FULL: Beyond the fact that non-computable properties are possible in
1269removed-- general to phrase as boolean computations, even many *computable*
1270removed-- properties are easier to express using `Prop` than `bool`, since recursive
1271removed-- function definitions are subject to significant restrictions. For instance,
1272removed-- the next chapter shows how to define the property that a regular expression
1273removed-- matches a given string using `Prop`. Doing the same with `Bool` would
1274removed-- amount to writing a regular expression matching algorithm, which would be
1275removed-- more complicated, harder to understand, and harder to reason about than a
1276removed-- simple (non-algorithmic) definition of this property.
1277removed
1278removed-- Conversely, an important side benefit of stating facts using booleans is
1279removed-- enabling some proof automation through computation with terms, a technique
1280removed-- known as *proof by reflection*.
1281removed
1282removed-- Consider the following statement:
1283removed
1284removed-- Note to developers (Jonathan Chan @ionathanch):
1285removed-- This was originally 1000 but Lean's default recursion depth is not
1286removed-- large enough to reduce `double 50` lol
1287removed
1288removed-- The most direct way to prove this is to give the value of `k` explicitly.
1289removed
1290removedexample : Even 100 := by
1291removed exists 50
1292removed
1293removed-- The proof of the corresponding boolean statement is simpler, because we
1294removed-- don't have to invent the witness `50`: computation does it for us!
1295removed
1296removedexample : even 100 := rfl
1297removed
1298removed-- Now, the useful observation is that, since the two notions are equivalent,
1299removed-- we can use the boolean formulation to prove the other one without
1300removed-- mentioning the value 500 explicitly:
1301removed
1302removedexample : Even 100 := by
1303removed let ⟨H, _⟩ := even_bool_prop 100
1304removed apply H; rfl
1305removed
1306removed-- Although we haven't gained much in terms of proof-script simplicity in this
1307removed-- case, larger proofs can often be made considerably simpler by the use of
1308removed-- reflection.
1309removed
1310removed-- Note to developers (Jonathan Chan @ionathanch):
1311removed-- Is there a Lean version? Or maybe just mention Rocq?
1312removed
1313removed-- As an extreme example, a famous mechanized proof of the even more famous
1314removed-- *four colour theorem* uses reflection ot reduce the analysis of hundreds of
1315removed-- different cases to a boolean computation.
1316removed
1317removed-- Another advantage of booleans is that the *negation* of a claim about
1318removed-- booleans is straightforward to state and (when true) to prove: simply slip
1319removed-- the expected boolean result.
1320removed
1321removedexample : even 101 = false := rfl
1322removed
1323removed-- In contrast, propositional negation can be difficult to work with directly.
1324removed-- For example, suppose we state the nonevenness of `101` propositionally:
1325removed
1326removed-- Proving this directly -- by assuming that there is some `n` such that
1327removed-- `101 = double n` and then somehow reasoning to a contradiction -- would be
1328removed-- rather complicated.
1329removed
1330removed-- But if we convert it to a claim about the boolean `even` function, we can
1331removed-- let Lean do the work for us.
1332removed
1333removedexample : ¬ Even 101 := by
1334removed all_goals
1335removed intro h; apply (even_bool_prop 101).mpr at h
1336removed dsimp [even] at h; contradiction
1337removed
1338removed-- Conversely, there are situations where it can be easier to work with
1339removed-- propositions rather than booleans. In particular, knowing that
1340removed-- `(n == m) = true` is generally of little direct help in the middle of a
1341removed-- proof involving `n` and `m`. But if we convert the statement to the
1342removed-- equivalent form `n = m`, then we can easily rewrite with it.
1343removed
1344removedtheorem add_beq_true (n m p : Nat) (h : (n == m) = true) :
1345removed (n + p == m + p) = true := by
1346removed all_goals
1347removed apply (beq_eq_true n m).mp at h
1348removed rw [h, beq_refl]
1349removed
1350removed-- We won't discuss reflection any further for the moment, but it serves as a
1351removed-- good example showing the different strengths of booleans and general
1352removed-- propositions. Being able to cross back and forth between the boolean and
1353removed-- propositional worlds will often be convenient in later chapters.
1354removed
1355removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): logical connectives ⭐⭐
1356removed
1357removed-- The following theorems relate the propositional connectives studied in this
1358removed-- chapter to the corresponding boolean operations.
1359removed
1360removedtheorem andb_true_iff (b1 b2 : Bool) :
1361removed (b1 && b2) = true ↔ b1 = true ∧ b2 = true := by
1362removed sorry
1363removed
1364removedtheorem orb_true_iff (b1 b2 : Bool) :
1365removed (b1 || b2) = true ↔ b1 = true ∨ b2 = true := by
1366removed sorry
1367removed
1368removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): beq_list ⭐⭐⭐
1369removed
1370removed-- Given a boolean operator `beq` for testing equality of elements of some
1371removed-- type `α`, we can define a function `beq_list` for testing equality of lists
1372removed-- with elements in `α`. Complete the definition of the `beq_list` function
1373removed-- below. to make sure that your definition is correct, prove the lemma
1374removed-- `beq_list_true_iff`.
1375removed
1376removeddef beq_list {α : Type} (beq : α → α → Bool) (xs1 xs2 : List α) : Bool := sorry
1377removed
1378removedtheorem beq_list_nil_nil {α} (beq : α → α → Bool) :
1379removed beq_list beq [] [] = true := sorry
1380removed
1381removedtheorem beq_list_cons_cons {α} (beq : α → α → Bool) x1 x2 xs1 xs2 :
1382removed beq_list beq (x1 :: xs1) (x2 :: xs2) =
1383removed (beq x1 x2 && beq_list beq xs1 xs2) := sorry
1384removed
1385removedtheorem beq_list_nil_cons {α} (beq : α → α → Bool) x xs :
1386removed beq_list beq [] (x :: xs) = false := sorry
1387removed
1388removedtheorem beq_list_cons_nil {α} (beq : α → α → Bool) x xs :
1389removed beq_list beq (x :: xs) [] = false := sorry
1390removed
1391removed-- Note to developers (Jonathan Chan @ionathanch):
1392removed-- Should this also go after `propext` to use rewriting by `↔`?j
1393removed
1394removedtheorem beq_list_true_iff α (beq : α → α → Bool)
1395removed (h : ∀ x1 x2, beq x1 x2 = true ↔ x1 = x2) :
1396removed ∀ xs1 xs2, beq_list beq xs1 xs2 = true ↔ xs1 = xs2 := by
1397removed sorry
1398removed
1399removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): All_forallb ⭐⭐
1400removed
1401removed-- Prove the theorem below, which relates `forallb`, from the exercise
1402removed-- `Tactics.forall_exists_challenge`, to the `All` property defined above.
1403removed
1404removed-- Copy the definition of `forallb` from Tactics here so that this file can be
1405removed-- graded on its own.
1406removed
1407removeddef Logic.forallb {α : Type} (test : α → Bool) (xs : List α) : Bool := sorry
1408removed
1409removedtheorem forallb_nil {α} (test : α → Bool) : Logic.forallb test [] = true := sorry
1410removed
1411removedtheorem forallb_cons {α} (test : α → Bool) x xs :
1412removed Logic.forallb test (x :: xs) = (test x && Logic.forallb test xs) := sorry
1413removed
1414removedtheorem forallb_true_iff α (test : α → Bool) (xs : List α) :
1415removed Logic.forallb test xs = true ↔ All (fun x => test x = true) xs := by
1416removed sorry
1417removed
1418removed-- (Ungraded thought question) Are there any important properties often the
1419removed-- function `forallb` which are not captured by this specification?
1420removed
1421removed-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
1422removed
1423removed-- ## The Logic of Lean
1424removed
1425removed-- Lean's logical core differs in some important ways from other formal
1426removed-- systems that are used by mathematicians to write down precise and rigorous
1427removed-- definitions and proofs -- in particular from Zermelo–Fraenkel Set Theory
1428removed-- (ZFC), the most popular foundation for paper-and-pencil mathematics.
1429removed
1430removed-- We conclude this chapter with a brief discussion of some of the most
1431removed-- significant differences between these two worlds.
1432removed
1433removed-- ### Propositional Extensionality
1434removed
1435removed-- Lean's logic is quite minimalistic. This means that on occasionally
1436removed-- encounters cases where translating standard mathematical reasoning into
1437removed-- Lean is cumbersome -- or even impossible -- unless we enrich its core logic
1438removed-- with additional axioms.
1439removed
1440removed-- For example, the equality assertions that we have seen so far mostly have
1441removed-- concerned elements of inductive types (`Nat`, `Bool`, etc.). But since the
1442removed-- equality operator is polymorphic, we can use it at *any* type -- in
1443removed-- particular, we can write propositions claiming that two *propositions* are
1444removed-- equal to each other:
1445removed
1446removed#check (∀ P Q : Prop, (P ∧ Q) = (Q ∧ P) : Prop)
1447removed
1448removed-- This is an equality between two conjunctions, which itself is also a
1449removed-- proposition. It states that commuted conjunctions are equal propositions.
1450removed-- However, we cannot prove this equality by reflexivity, as the two sides
1451removed-- don't compute to the same term, and we cannot proceed by cases on `P` or
1452removed-- `Q`, as they are not inductive.
1453removed
1454removed/-- Tactic `rfl` failed -/
1455removed#guard_msgs (substring := true) in
1456removedexample (P Q : Prop) : P ∧ Q = Q ∧ P := by rfl
1457removed
1458removed/-- Tactic `cases` failed -/
1459removed#guard_msgs (substring := true) in
1460removedexample (P Q : Prop) : P ∧ Q = Q ∧ P := by cases P
1461removed
1462removed-- However, we *can* prove that P ∧ Q implies Q ∧ P, and vice versa -- this is
1463removed-- the commutativity of conjunction that we have seen earlier.
1464removed
1465removed#check (@and_comm : ∀ P Q : Prop, P ∧ Q ↔ Q ∧ P)
1466removed
1467removed-- Since it would be convenient to be able to rewrite propositions from one
1468removed-- side of `↔` to the other, Lean provides an axiom to turn `↔` into `=`,
1469removed-- which is called *propositional extensionality* (`propext`).
1470removed
1471removed#print propext
1472removed
1473removed-- (Informally, an "extensional" property is one that pertains to observable
1474removed-- behavior. Thus, propositional extensionality means that a proposition's
1475removed-- identity is completely determined by what we can observe from it -- i.e.,
1476removed-- whether the proposition holds. We can state this more explicitly:)
1477removed
1478removedtheorem prop_true (P : Prop) (h : P) : P = True := by
1479removed apply propext; exact ⟨fun _ => ⟨⟩, fun _ => h⟩
1480removed
1481removed-- Lean provides an `ext` tactic that applies `propext` for us. We can use it
1482removed-- to show that commuted conjoined propositions are equal. Similarly, we can
1483removed-- use it to show that reassociated conjoined propositions are equal as well.
1484removed
1485removedtheorem and_comm_eq (P Q : Prop) : (P ∧ Q) = (Q ∧ P) := by
1486removed ext; apply and_comm
1487removed
1488removedtheorem and_assoc_eq (P Q R : Prop) : ((P ∧ Q) ∧ R) = (P ∧ (Q ∧ R)) := by
1489removed ext; apply and_assoc
1490removed
1491removed-- Here is an example of where using `=` instead of `↔` is more convenient: we
1492removed-- show that it's possible to "flip" three conjoined propositions.
1493removed
1494removed-- This can be proven by constructing the `↔`, then destructing the `↔` in
1495removed-- `add_comm` and `add_assoc`, then applying them a few times. But this is a
1496removed-- lot of hassle, when the proof is conceptually simple: we flip `Q` and `R`,
1497removed-- then we flip that conjunction with `P`, and we finish by associativity. By
1498removed-- using `and_comm_eq`, this is easily done by rewriting equal propositions.
1499removed
1500removedtheorem and_comm_flip (P Q R : Prop) : (P ∧ Q ∧ R) ↔ (R ∧ Q ∧ P) := by
1501removed rw [and_comm_eq Q R, and_comm_eq P, and_assoc_eq]
1502removed
1503removed-- The pattern of deriving an equality of propositions out of `↔` then
1504removed-- rewriting by that equality is so common that Lean will implicitly cast `↔`
1505removed-- to `=`, allowing you to rewrite on `↔` directly. Notice that `rw` is also
1506removed-- close goals of the form `P ↔ P` by reflexivity.
1507removed
1508removedtheorem and_comm_flip' (P Q R : Prop) : (P ∧ Q ∧ R) ↔ (R ∧ Q ∧ P) := by
1509removed rw [@and_comm Q R, @and_comm P, and_assoc]
1510removed
1511removed-- Under the hood, this proof still uses `propext`, which you can check by
1512removed-- asking for all of the axioms used by a declaration.
1513removed
1514removed#print axioms and_comm_flip
1515removed
1516removed#print axioms and_comm_flip'
1517removed
1518removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): mul_eq_0_ternary ⭐
1519removed
1520removedtheorem mul_eq_0_ternary (n m p : Nat) :
1521removed n * m * p = 0 ↔ n = 0 ∨ m = 0 ∨ p = 0 := by
1522removed sorry
1523removed
1524removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): In_app_iff ⭐⭐
1525removed
1526removedtheorem In_app_iff (α : Type) (xs xs' : List α) (x : α) :
1527removed In x (xs ++ xs') ↔ In x xs ∨ In x xs' := by
1528removed sorry
1529removed
1530removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): beq_neq ⭐
1531removed
1532removed-- The following theorem is an alternative "negative" formulation of `beq_eq`
1533removed-- that is more convenient in certain situations. (We'll see examples in later
1534removed-- chapters.) Hint: `not_true_iff_false`.
1535removed
1536removedtheorem beq_neq_false (n m : Nat) : (n == m) = false ↔ n ≠ m := by
1537removed sorry
1538removed
1539removed-- ### Functional Extensionality
1540removed
1541removed-- We can also write propositions claiming that two *functions* are equal to
1542removed-- each other. In some cases, we can also prove that two functions are equal
1543removed-- by reflexivity when both reduce to the same expression:
1544removed
1545removedexample : (fun x => x + 2) = (fun x => x + (pred 3)) := rfl
1546removed
1547removed-- In general, functions can be equal for more interesting reasons. In common
1548removed-- mathematical practice, two functions `f` and `g` are considered equal if
1549removed-- they produce the same output on every input:
1550removed
1551removed-- (∀ x, f x = g x) → f = g
1552removed
1553removed-- This is known as *functional extensionality*, which Lean provides as
1554removed-- `funext`.
1555removed
1556removed#check (fun f g => funext (f := f) (g := g) :
1557removed ∀ {α β : Type} (f g : α → β), (∀ x, f x = g x) → f = g)
1558removed
1559removed-- Here, functional extensionality means that a function's identity is
1560removed-- completely determined by what we can observe from it -- i.e., the results
1561removed-- we obtain after applying it. (Its full type is actually slightly more
1562removed-- general, and is defined in terms of a more fundamental concept called
1563removed-- *quotients* rather than added directly as an axiom, but we will only
1564removed-- discuss `funext` here. This is also why, when printing axioms for theorems
1565removed-- using `funext`, it will instead display a `Quot.sound` axiom.)
1566removed
1567removed#print axioms funext
1568removed
1569removed-- Now we can prove some intuitively obvious equalities about functions that
1570removed-- would otherwise not be provable without `funext`.
1571removed
1572removedtheorem add_comm_fun : (fun (n m : Nat) => n + m) = (fun (n m : Nat) => m + n) := by
1573removed apply funext; intro n
1574removed apply funext; intro m
1575removed exact add_comm n m
1576removed
1577removed-- The `ext` tactic will also apply `funext` as many times as possible,
1578removed-- introducing all variables in one go. (The singular version of the tactic is
1579removed-- `ext1`.)
1580removed
1581removedtheorem add_comm_fun' : (fun (n m : Nat) => n + m) = (fun (n m : Nat) => m + n) := by
1582removed ext n m; exact add_comm n m
1583removed
1584removed-- ### Exercise (4 stars): tr_rev_correct ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1585removed
1586removed-- One problem with the definition of the list-reversing function `List.rev`
1587removed-- is that it performs a call to `++` on each step. Running `++` takes time
1588removed-- asymptotically linear in the size of the list, which means that `List.rev`
1589removed-- is asymptotically quadratic.
1590removed
1591removed-- We can improve this with the following two-argument definition:
1592removed
1593removeddef rev_append {α} (xs1 xs2 : List α) : List α :=
1594removed match xs1 with
1595removed | [] => xs2
1596removed | x1 :: xs1' => rev_append xs1' (x1 :: xs2)
1597removed
1598removedtheorem rev_append_nil {α} (xs : List α) : rev_append [] xs = xs := rfl
1599removed
1600removedtheorem rev_append_cons {α} (x : α) xs1 xs2 :
1601removed rev_append (x :: xs1) xs2 = rev_append xs1 (x :: xs2) := rfl
1602removed
1603removedabbrev tr_rev {α} (xs : List α) : List α := rev_append xs []
1604removed
1605removed-- This version of `rev` is said to be *tail recursive*, because the recursive
1606removed-- call to the function is the last operation that needs to be performed
1607removed-- (i.e., we don't have to execute `++` after the recursive call); a decent
1608removed-- compiler will generate very efficient code in this case.
1609removed
1610removed-- Prove that the two definitions are indeed equivalent.
1611removed
1612removed-- FILL IN HERE
1613removed
1614removedtheorem tr_rev_correct {α} : @tr_rev α = @List.rev α := by
1615removed sorry
1616removed
1617removed-- ### Classical vs. Constructive Logic
1618removed
1619removed-- We have seen that it is not possible to test whether or not a proposition
1620removed-- `P` holds while defining a Lean function. You may be surprised to learn
1621removed-- that a similar restriction applies in *proofs*! In other words, the
1622removed-- following intuitive reasoning principle is not derivable in Lean:
1623removed
1624removedabbrev excluded_middle := ∀ P : Prop, P ∨ ¬ P
1625removed
1626removed-- To understand operationally why this is the case, recall that, to prove a
1627removed-- statement of the form `P ∨ Q`, we use the `left` and `right` tactics, which
1628removed-- effectively require knowing which side of the disjunction holds. But the
1629removed-- universally quantified `P` in `excluded_middle` is an *arbitrary*
1630removed-- proposition, which we know nothing about. We don't have enough information
1631removed-- to choose which of `left` or `right` to apply.
1632removed
1633removed-- However, in the special case where we happen to know that `P` is reflected
1634removed-- in some boolean term `b`, knowing whether it holds or not is trivial: we
1635removed-- just have to check the value of `b`.
1636removed
1637removedtheorem restricted_excluded_middle (P : Prop) (b : Bool) (h : P ↔ b = true) :
1638removed P ∨ ¬ P := by
1639removed cases b
1640removed case false => right; rw [h]; intro; contradiction
1641removed case true => left; rw [h]
1642removed
1643removed-- In partiuclar, the excluded middle is valid for equations `n = m` between
1644removed-- natural numbers `n` and `m`.
1645removed
1646removedtheorem excluded_middle_nat_eq (n m : Nat) : n = m ∨ n ≠ m := by
1647removed apply restricted_excluded_middle (n = m) (n == m)
1648removed symm; apply beq_eq_true
1649removed
1650removed-- Sadly, this trick only works for decidable propositions.
1651removed
1652removed-- Logical systems in which excluded middle does not hold are referred to as
1653removed-- *constructive logics*. They are so called because to prove a proposition,
1654removed-- we must give a construction for it; for instance, a proof of `∃ x, P x` is
1655removed-- proven by providing a particular value of `x`.
1656removed
1657removed-- Logical systems in which excluded middle does hold, such as ZFC set theory,
1658removed-- are referred to as *classical*. Lean provides classical reasoning
1659removed-- principles in the `Classical` library, including excluded middle.
1660removed
1661removed#check (Classical.em : ∀ P, P ∨ ¬ P)
1662removed
1663removed-- All classical reasoning principles in `Classical` are derived from one
1664removed-- axiom, the axiom of choice. This is the C in ZFC.
1665removed
1666removed#print Classical.choice
1667removed
1668removed/-- Classical.choice -/
1669removed#guard_msgs (substring := true) in
1670removed#print axioms Classical.em
1671removed
1672removed-- Lean also provides a `by_cases` tactic that applies `Classical.em` on a
1673removed-- given proposition. Theorems proven using this tactic implicitly use
1674removed-- classical axioms.
1675removed
1676removedtheorem em : ∀ P, P ∨ ¬ P := by
1677removed intro P; by_cases h : P
1678removed /- h : P -/
1679removed case pos => left; exact h
1680removed /- h : ¬ P -/
1681removed case neg => right; exact h
1682removed
1683removed/-- Classical.choice -/
1684removed#guard_msgs (substring := true) in
1685removed#print axioms em
1686removed
1687removed-- The following example illustrates why assuming the excluded middle may lead
1688removed-- to nonconstructive proofs:
1689removed
1690removed-- *Claim*: There exist irrational numbers `a` and `b` such that `a ^ b` (`a`
1691removed-- to the power `b`) is rational.
1692removed
1693removed-- *Proof*: It is not difficult to show that `sqrt 2` is irrational. So if
1694removed-- `sqrt 2 ^ sqrt 2` is rational, it suffices to take `a = b = sqrt 2` and we
1695removed-- are done. Otherwise, `sqrt 2 ^ sqrt 2` is irrational. In this case, we can
1696removed-- take `a = sqrt 2 ^ sqrt 2` and `b = sqrt 2`, since
1697removed-- `a ^ b = sqrt 2 ^ (sqrt 2 * sqrt 2) = sqrt 2 ^ 2 = 2`. QED.
1698removed
1699removed-- Do you see what happened here? We used the excluded middle to consider
1700removed-- separately the cases where `sqrt 2 ^ sqrt 2` is rational and where it is
1701removed-- not, without knowing which one actually holds! Because of this, we finish
1702removed-- the proof knowing that such `a` and `b` exist, but not being sure of their
1703removed-- actual values.
1704removed
1705removed-- As useful as constructive logic is, it does have its limitations: There are
1706removed-- many statements that can easily be proven in classical logic but that have
1707removed-- only much more complicated constructive proofs, and there are some that are
1708removed-- known to have no constructive proof at all! Fortunately, like functional
1709removed-- extensionality, the excluded middle is known to be compatible with Lean's
1710removed-- logic, allowing it to be added safely as an axiom. However, the results
1711removed-- that we cover in Logical Foundations can be developed entirely within
1712removed-- constructive logic.
1713removed
1714removed-- It takes some practice to understand which proof techniques must be avoided
1715removed-- in constructive reasoning, but arguments by contradiction, in particular,
1716removed-- are infamous for leading to nonconstructive proofs. Here's a typical
1717removed-- example: suppose that we want to show that there exists `x` with some
1718removed-- property `P`, i.e., such that `P x`. We start by assuming that our
1719removed-- conclusion is false; that is, `¬ ∃ x, P x`. From this premise, it is not
1720removed-- hard to derive `∀ x, ¬ P x`. If we manage to show that this results in a
1721removed-- contradiction, we arrive at an existence proof without ever exhibiting a
1722removed-- value of `x` for which `P x` holds!
1723removed
1724removed-- The technical flaw here, from a constructive standpoint, is that we claimed
1725removed-- to prove `∃ x, P x` using a proof of `¬ ¬ ∃ x, P x`. Allowing ourselves to
1726removed-- remove double negations from arbitrary statements is equivalent to assuming
1727removed-- the excluded middle law, as shown in one of the exercises below.
1728removed
1729removed-- Once again, Lean's `Classical` library provides double negation
1730removed-- elimination, which relies on the `Classical.choice` axiom.
1731removed
1732removed#check Classical.not_not
1733removed
1734removed/-- Classical.choice -/
1735removed#guard_msgs (substring := true) in
1736removed#print axioms Classical.not_not
1737removed
1738removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): excluded_middle_irrefutable ⭐⭐⭐
1739removed
1740removed-- The following theorem implies that it is always save to assume a
1741removed-- decidability axiom (i.e., an instance of excluded middle) for any
1742removed-- *particular* proposition `P`. Why? Because the negation of such an axiom
1743removed-- leands to a contradiction. If `¬ (P ∨ ¬ P)` were provable, then by
1744removed-- `de_morgan_not_or` as proven above, `P ∧ ¬ P` would be provable, which
1745removed-- would be a contradiction. So, it is safe to add `P ∨ ¬ P` as an axiom for
1746removed-- any particular `P`.
1747removed
1748removedtheorem excluded_middle_irrefutable (P : Prop) : ¬ ¬ (P ∨ ¬ P) := by
1749removed sorry
1750removed
1751removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): not_exists_dist (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
1752removed
1753removed-- It is a theorem of classical logic that the following two assertions are
1754removed-- equivalent:
1755removed
1756removed-- ¬ ∃ x, ¬ P x
1757removed-- ∀ x, P x
1758removed
1759removed-- The `dist_not_exists` theorem proves one side of this equivalence.
1760removed-- Interestingly, the other direction cannot be proven in constructive logic,
1761removed-- but we can prove it here using `by_cases`.
1762removed
1763removedtheorem not_exists_dist (α : Type) (P : α → Prop) :
1764removed (¬ ∃ x, ¬ P x) → (∀ x, P x) := by
1765removed sorry
1766removed
1767removed-- ### Exercise (5 stars): classical_axioms ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
1768removed
1769removed-- For those who like a challenge, here is an exercise adapted from the
1770removed-- Coq'Art book by Bertot and Casteran (p. 123). Each of the following five
1771removed-- statements, together with `excluded_middle`, can be considered as
1772removed-- characterizing classical logic. We can't prove any one of them in Lean
1773removed-- without `Classical`, but adding any *one* of them as an axiom allows us to
1774removed-- work classically.
1775removed
1776removed-- To see this, prove that all six propositions (these five plus
1777removed-- `excluded_middle`) are equivalent.
1778removed
1779removed-- Hint: Rather than considering all pairs of statements pairwise, prove a
1780removed-- single circular chain of implications that connects them all. You should
1781removed-- not use `by_cases`, as this implicitly introduces a dependency on
1782removed-- `excluded_middle`.
1783removed
1784removedabbrev peirce := ∀ P Q : Prop, ((P → Q) → P) → P
1785removed
1786removedabbrev not_not := ∀ P : Prop, ¬ ¬ P → P
1787removed
1788removedabbrev de_morgan_not_and_not := ∀ P Q : Prop, ¬ (¬ P ∧ ¬ Q) → P ∨ Q
1789removed
1790removedabbrev imp_or := ∀ P Q : Prop, (P → Q) → (¬ P ∨ Q)
1791removed
1792removedabbrev consequentia_mirabilis := ∀ P : Prop, (¬ P → P) → P
1793removed

1removedimport LF.Induction
