5removed
6removed-- # Poly: Polymorphism and Higher-Order Functions
7removed
8removed-- ## Polymorphism
9removed
10removed-- In this chapter we continue our development of basic concepts of functional
11removed-- programming. The critical new ideas are *polymorphism* (abstracting
12removed-- functions over the types of the data they manipulate) and *higher-order
13removed-- functions* (treating functions as data). We begin with polymorphism.
14removed
15removed-- ### Polymorphic Lists
16removed
17removed-- In the last chapter, we worked with lists containing just numbers.
18removed-- Obviously, interesting programs also need to be able to manipulate lists
19removed-- with elements from other types — lists of booleans, lists of lists, etc. We
20removed-- *could* just define a new inductive datatype for each of these, for
21removed-- example...
22removed
23removedinductive BoolList : Type where
24removed | nil
25removed | cons (b : Bool) (l : BoolList)
26removed
27removed-- ... but this would quickly become tedious: not only would we have to make
28removed-- up different constructor names for each datatype, but — even worse — we
29removed-- would also need to define new versions of all the list manipulating
30removed-- functions (`length`, `++`, `reverse`, etc.) and all their properties
31removed-- (`rev_length`, `app_assoc`, etc.) for each new definition.
32removed
33removed-- To avoid this repetition, we can make the element type itself an *argument*
34removed-- to the definition. Lean calls such definitions *polymorphic*. Here is a
35removed-- polymorphic list type:
36removed
37removedinductive MyList (α : Type) : Type where
38removed | nil : MyList α
39removed | cons (x : α) (l : MyList α) : MyList α
40removed
41removed-- This is exactly like the definition of `Natlist` from the previous chapter,
42removed-- except that the `Nat` argument to the `cons` constructor has been replaced
43removed-- by an arbitrary type `α`, a type parameter `α` has been added to the header
44removed-- on the first line, and the occurrences of `Natlist` in the types of the
45removed-- constructors have been replaced by `MyList α`. We can now write
46removed-- `MyList Nat` instead of a dedicated nat-list type.
47removed
48removed-- What sort of thing is `MyList` itself? A good way to think about it is as a
49removed-- *type constructor* — that is, a function from `Type`s to `Type`s. For any
50removed-- particular type `α`, the type `MyList α` is the inductively defined type of
51removed-- lists whose elements are of type `α`.
52removed
53removed-- Note to developers (Yipeng Liu @berberman):
54removed-- A trick used below: parenthesizing the declaration makes it a term —
55removed-- Lean elaborates it and prints its inferred function type, instead of
56removed-- the declaration signature: `MyList (α : Type) : Type`.
57removed
58removed#check (MyList)
59removed
60removed-- MyList : Type → Type
61removed
62removed-- The `α` in the definition of `MyList` automatically becomes a parameter to
63removed-- the constructors `nil` and `cons` — that is, `nil` and `cons` are now
64removed-- polymorphic constructors. In Lean, the type parameter is *implicit* by
65removed-- default: Lean will infer it from context. For example, `MyList.nil` is the
66removed-- empty list, and Lean figures out the element type from how it is used.
67removed
68removed#check MyList.nil
69removed
70removed-- MyList.nil {α : Type} : MyList α
71removed
72removed-- Similarly, `MyList.cons` adds an element of type `Nat` to a list of type
73removed-- `MyList Nat`. Here is an example of forming a list containing just the
74removed-- natural number 3.
75removed
76removed#check MyList.cons 3 MyList.nil
77removed
78removed-- MyList.cons 3 MyList.nil : MyList Nat
79removed
80removed-- What is the full type of `MyList.nil`? We can read off the result type
81removed-- `MyList α` from the definition, but to state the full type we must also
82removed-- bind `α`. Since the type argument to the constructor is implicit, Lean
83removed-- writes its type as `{α : Type} → MyList α`.
84removed
85removed#check MyList.nil
86removed
87removed-- MyList.nil {α : Type} : MyList α
88removed
89removed-- Similarly, the type of `MyList.cons` includes the implicit type parameter:
90removed
91removed#check MyList.cons
92removed
93removed-- MyList.cons {α : Type} (x : α) (l : MyList α) : MyList α
94removed
95removed-- Having to supply a type argument for every single use of a list constructor
96removed-- would be rather burdensome. Fortunately, the type argument is implicit, so
97removed-- Lean will normally infer it from context.
98removed
99removed-- We can now go back and make polymorphic versions of all the list-processing
100removed-- functions that we wrote before. Here is `myRepeat`, for example:
101removed
102removeddef myRepeat (α : Type) (x : α) (count : Nat) : MyList α :=
103removed match count with
104removed | 0 => .nil
105removed | count' + 1 => .cons x (myRepeat α x count')
106removed
107removed-- Some simple facts about `myRepeat`:
108removed
109removedtheorem myRepeat_zero (α : Type) (v : α) : myRepeat α v 0 = MyList.nil := rfl
110removed
111removedtheorem myRepeat_succ (α : Type) (v : α) (count : Nat) :
112removed myRepeat α v (count + 1) = MyList.cons v (myRepeat α v count) := rfl
113removed
114removed-- We can use `myRepeat` by applying it first to a type and then to an element
115removed-- of this type (and a number):
116removed
117removedexample : myRepeat Nat 4 2 = .cons 4 (.cons 4 .nil) := by rfl
118removed
119removed-- To use `myRepeat` to build other kinds of lists, we simply pass a different
120removed-- type and an element of that type:
121removed
122removedexample : myRepeat Bool false 1 = .cons false .nil := by rfl
123removed
124removed-- _Quiz:_
125removed
126removed-- What is the type of `MyList.cons true (MyList.cons 3 MyList.nil)`?
127removed
128removed-- (A) `MyList Nat`
129removed
130removed-- (B) `{α : Type} → α → MyList α → MyList α`
131removed
132removed-- (C) `MyList Bool`
133removed
134removed-- (D) `MyList (Nat × Bool)`
135removed
136removed-- (E) Ill-typed
137removed
138removed-- _Quiz:_
139removed
140removed-- What is the type of `myRepeat`?
141removed
142removed-- (A) `Nat → Nat → MyList Nat`
143removed
144removed-- (B) `(α : Type) → α → Nat → MyList α`
145removed
146removed-- (C) `(α : Type) → {β : Type} → α → Nat → MyList β`
147removed
148removed-- (D) Ill-typed
149removed
150removed-- _Quiz:_
151removed
152removed-- What is the type of `myRepeat 1 2`?
153removed
154removed-- (A) `MyList Nat`
155removed
156removed-- (B) `(α : Type) → α → Nat → MyList α`
157removed
158removed-- (C) `MyList Bool`
159removed
160removed-- (D) Ill-typed
161removed
162removed-- From now on, we'll use Lean's built-in `List` type and its associated
163removed-- notation. The built-in `List` is defined just like our `MyList` above, but
164removed-- with notation `[]` for `List.nil`, `::` for `List.cons`, and `[1, 2, 3]`
165removed-- for list literals. The `++` operator is list append. The type arguments to
166removed-- the list constructors are implicit.
167removed
168removed-- Using Lean's built-in list notations, we can now write lists in the natural
169removed-- way:
170removed
171removeddef list123 : List Nat := [1, 2, 3]
172removed
173removed-- #### Type Annotation Inference
174removed
175removed-- Let's write the definition of `myRepeat` again, but this time we won't
176removed-- specify the type of the parameter `α`. Will Lean still accept it?
177removed
178removeddef myRepeat' α (x : α) (count : Nat) : List α :=
179removed match count with
180removed | 0 => .nil
181removed | count' + 1 => .cons x (myRepeat' α x count')
182removed
183removed-- Indeed it will. Lean infers that `α` is a type. The generated `u_1` is part
184removed-- of Lean's bookkeeping for treating types more generally. We will not need
185removed-- to interpret names like this for now — you can ignore them when they appear
186removed-- in Lean's output unless we explicitly call attention to them.
187removed
188removed#check myRepeat'
189removed
190removed-- myRepeat'.{u_1} (α : Type u_1) (x : α) (count : Nat) : List α
191removed
192removed-- Lean was able to use *type inference* to deduce what the type of `α` must
193removed-- be, based on how it is used. Since `α` is an argument to `List`, it must be
194removed-- a `Type`, since `List` expects a `Type` as its argument.
195removed
196removed-- This facility means we don't always have to write explicit type annotations
197removed-- everywhere, although explicit type annotations can still be quite useful as
198removed-- documentation, so we will continue to use them much of the time.
199removed
200removed-- #### Type Argument Synthesis
201removed
202removed-- To use a polymorphic function, we need to pass it one or more types in
203removed-- addition to its other arguments. For example, the recursive call in the
204removed-- body of the `myRepeat` function above must pass along the type `α`. But
205removed-- since the second argument to `myRepeat` is an element of `α`, it seems
206removed-- entirely obvious that the first argument can only be `α` — why should we
207removed-- have to write it explicitly?
208removed
209removed-- Fortunately, Lean permits us to avoid this kind of redundancy. In place of
210removed-- any type argument we can write a "hole" `_`, which can be read as "Please
211removed-- try to figure out for yourself what belongs here." More precisely, when
212removed-- Lean encounters a `_`, it will attempt to *unify* all locally available
213removed-- information — the type of the function being applied, the types of the
214removed-- other arguments, and the type expected by the context in which the
215removed-- application appears — to determine what concrete type should replace the
216removed-- `_`.
217removed
218removed-- Using holes, the `myRepeat'` function can be written like this:
219removed
220removeddef myRepeat'' (α : Type) (x : α) (count : Nat) : List α :=
221removed match count with
222removed | 0 => []
223removed | count' + 1 => x :: myRepeat'' _ x count'
224removed
225removed-- Alternatively, we can declare an argument to be implicit when defining the
226removed-- function itself, by surrounding it in curly braces instead of parentheses.
227removed-- For example:
228removed
229removeddef myRepeat''' {α : Type} (x : α) (count : Nat) : List α :=
230removed match count with
231removed | 0 => []
232removed | count' + 1 => x :: myRepeat''' x count'
233removed
234removed-- (Note that we didn't even have to provide a type argument to the recursive
235removed-- call to `myRepeat'''`. Indeed, it would be invalid to provide one, because
236removed-- Lean is not expecting it.)
237removed
238removed-- #### Supplying Type Arguments Explicitly
239removed
240removed-- One small problem with implicit arguments is that, once in a while, Lean
241removed-- does not have enough local information to determine a type argument; in
242removed-- such cases, we need to tell Lean the type explicitly. For example:
243removed
244removed-- This fails because Lean can't figure out the type of the empty list:
245removed-- `def mynil := []` — error: type not known We can fix this with an explicit
246removed-- type annotation:
247removed
248removed-- We can use the `@` prefix to supply the type argument explicitly. The `@`
249removed-- makes all implicit arguments of a function explicit:
250removed
251removed#check @List.nil
252removed
253removeddef myNil' := @List.nil Nat
254removed
255removed-- @List.nil : {α : Type u_1} → List α
256removed
257removed-- _Quiz:_
258removed
259removed-- Which type does Lean assign to the following expression? (The square
260removed-- brackets in this quiz and the following ones are list brackets.)
261removed
262removed-- [1, 2, 3]
263removed
264removed-- (A) `List Nat`
265removed
266removed-- (B) `List Bool`
267removed
268removed-- (C) `Bool`
269removed
270removed-- (D) No type can be assigned
271removed
272removed-- _Quiz:_
273removed
274removed-- What about this one?
275removed
276removed-- [3 + 4] ++ []
277removed
278removed-- (A) `List Nat`
279removed
280removed-- (B) `List Bool`
281removed
282removed-- (C) `Bool`
283removed
284removed-- (D) No type can be assigned
285removed
286removed-- _Quiz:_
287removed
288removed-- What about this one?
289removed
290removed-- (true && false) :: []
291removed
292removed-- (A) `List Nat`
293removed
294removed-- (B) `List Bool`
295removed
296removed-- (C) `Bool`
297removed
298removed-- (D) No type can be assigned
299removed
300removed-- _Quiz:_
301removed
302removed-- What about this one?
303removed
304removed-- [1, []]
305removed
306removed-- (A) `List Nat`
307removed
308removed-- (B) `List (List Nat)`
309removed
310removed-- (C) `List Bool`
311removed
312removed-- (D) No type can be assigned
313removed
314removed-- _Quiz:_
315removed
316removed-- What about this one?
317removed
318removed-- [[1], []]
319removed
320removed-- (A) `List Nat`
321removed
322removed-- (B) `List (List Nat)`
323removed
324removed-- (C) `List Bool`
325removed
326removed-- (D) No type can be assigned
327removed
328removed-- _Quiz:_
329removed
330removed-- And what about this one?
331removed
332removed-- [1] :: [[]]
333removed
334removed-- (A) `List Nat`
335removed
336removed-- (B) `List (List Nat)`
337removed
338removed-- (C) `List Bool`
339removed
340removed-- (D) No type can be assigned
341removed
342removed-- _Quiz:_
343removed
344removed-- This one?
345removed
346removed-- @List.nil Bool
347removed
348removed-- (A) `List Nat`
349removed
350removed-- (B) `List (List Nat)`
351removed
352removed-- (C) `List Bool`
353removed
354removed-- (D) No type can be assigned

356removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): mumble_grumble (manually graded) ⭐⭐
357removed
358removed-- Consider the following two inductively defined types.
359removed
360removedinductive Mumble : Type where
361removed | a : Mumble
362removed | b (x : Mumble) (y : Nat) : Mumble
363removed | c : Mumble
364removed
365removedinductive Grumble (X: Type) : Type where
366removed | d (m : Mumble) : Grumble X
367removed | e (x : X) : Grumble X
368removed
369removed-- Which of the following are well-typed elements of `Grumble X` for some type
370removed-- `X`? (Add YES or NO to each line.)
371removed
372removed-- - `Grumble.d (Mumble.b Mumble.a 5)`
373removed-- - `@Grumble.d Mumble (Mumble.b Mumble.a 5)`
374removed-- - `@Grumble.d Bool (Mumble.b Mumble.a 5)`
375removed-- - `@Grumble.e Bool true`
376removed-- - `@Grumble.e Mumble (Mumble.b Mumble.c 0)`
377removed-- - `@Grumble.e Bool (Mumble.b Mumble.c 0)`
378removed-- - `Mumble.c`
379removed
380removed-- #### Exercises
381removed
382removeddef List.rev {α : Type} (l : List α) : List α :=
383removed match l with
384removed | .nil => .nil
385removed | .cons h t => rev t ++ (.cons h .nil)
386removed
387removedtheorem rev_nil {α : Type} : ([] : List α).rev = [] := by rfl
388removed
389removedtheorem rev_cons {α : Type} (head : α) (tail : List α) :
390removed (head :: tail).rev = tail.rev ++ [head] := by rfl
391removed
392removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): poly_exercises ⭐⭐
393removed
394removed-- Here are a few simple exercises, just like ones in the `Lists` chapter, for
395removed-- practice with polymorphism. Complete the proofs below. You will likely find
396removed-- useful the following characterizing lemmas for `List.append` in Lean
397removed-- standard library:
398removed
399removed#check List.nil_append
400removed#check List.cons_append
401removed
402removed-- List.cons_append.{u} {α : Type u} {a : α} {as bs : List α} : a :: as ++ bs = a :: (as ++ bs)
403removed
404removed-- List.nil_append.{u} {α : Type u} (as : List α) : [] ++ as = as
405removed
406removedtheorem app_nil_r {α : Type} (l : List α) :
407removed l ++ [] = l := by
408removed sorry
409removed
410removedtheorem app_assoc {α : Type} (l m n : List α) :
411removed l ++ m ++ n = l ++ (m ++ n) := by
412removed sorry
413removed
414removedtheorem app_length {α : Type} {l₁ l₂ : List α} :
415removed (l₁ ++ l₂).length = l₁.length + l₂.length := by
416removed sorry
417removed
418removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): more_poly_exercises ⭐⭐
419removed
420removed-- Here are some slightly more interesting ones...
421removed
422removedtheorem rev_app_distr {α : Type} {l₁ l₂ : List α} :
423removed (l₁ ++ l₂).rev = l₂.rev ++ l₁.rev := by
424removed sorry
425removed
426removedtheorem rev_involutive {α : Type} (l : List α) :
427removed l.rev.rev = l := by
428removed sorry
429removed
430removed-- ### Polymorphic Pairs
431removed
432removed-- Like `inductive`s, `structure`s can also be made polymorphic. If we
433removed-- generalize the definition `NatProd` of pairs of natural numbers from last
434removed-- chapter, we get polymorphic pairs, often called *products*:
435removed
436removedstructure MyProd (α β : Type) where
437removed fst : α
438removed snd : β
439removed
440removed-- Lean's built-in product type `Prod` provides a `Prod.mk` constructor, and
441removed-- `fst` and `snd` functions for accessing the first and second components of
442removed-- the pair. It also has special syntax for creating products:
443removed
444removed#check (1, true)
445removed#eval (1, true).fst
446removed#eval (1, true).snd
447removed
448removed-- (1, true) : Nat × Bool
449removed
450removed-- 1
451removed
452removed-- true
453removed
454removed-- You can also use `.1` instead of `.fst` and `.2` instead of `.snd`
455removed
456removedexample : (3, 5).1 = 3 := by rfl
457removedexample : (3, 5).2 = 5 := by rfl
458removed
459removed-- Lean writes the product type `Prod α β` as `α × β`. In VS Code you can type
460removed-- `\times` or `\x` to enter the `×` symbol.
461removed
462removed-- It is easy at first to get `(x, y)` and `α × β` confused. Remember that
463removed-- `(x, y)` is a *value* built from two other values, while `α × β` is a
464removed-- *type* built from two other types. If `x` has type `α` and `y` has type
465removed-- `β`, then `(x, y)` has type `α × β`.
466removed
467removed-- The following function takes two lists and combines them into a list of
468removed-- pairs.
469removed
470removeddef zip {α β : Type} (lx : List α) (ly : List β) : List (α × β) :=
471removed match lx, ly with
472removed | [], _ => []
473removed | _, [] => []
474removed | x :: tx, y :: ty => (x, y) :: zip tx ty
475removed
476removedtheorem zip_nil_r {α β : Type} (ly : List β) : zip [] ly = ([] : List (α × β)) := by rfl
477removed
478removedtheorem zip_nil_l {α β : Type} (lx : List α) : zip lx [] = ([] : List (α × β)) := by
479removed cases lx <;> rfl
480removed
481removedtheorem zip_cons {α β : Type} {lx : List α} {ly : List β} {x : α} {y : β} :
482removed zip (x :: lx) (y :: ly) = (x, y) :: zip lx ly := by rfl
483removed
484removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): zip_checks ⭐
485removed
486removed-- Try answering the following questions on paper and checking your answers in
487removed-- Lean:
488removed
489removed-- - What is the type of `zip` (i.e., what does `#check @zip` print?)
490removed-- - What does
491removed
492removed-- #eval zip [1, 2] [false, false, true, true]
493removed
494removed-- print?
495removed
496removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): split ⭐⭐
497removed
498removed-- The function `unzip` goes in the other direction from `zip`: it takes a
499removed-- list of pairs and returns a pair of lists.
500removed
501removed-- Fill in the definition of `unzip` below. Make sure it passes the given unit
502removed-- test, and you can prove the simplification lemmas about it
503removed
504removeddef unzip {α : Type} {β : Type} (l : List (α × β)) : List α × List β := sorry
505removed
506removedtheorem unzip_nil {α β : Type} : unzip [] = (([], []) : List α × List β) := sorry
507removed
508removedtheorem unzip_cons_fst {α β : Type} {l : List (α × β)} {x : α} {y : β} :
509removed (unzip ((x, y) :: l)).fst = x :: (unzip l).fst := sorry
510removed
511removedtheorem unzip_cons_snd {α β : Type} {l : List (α × β)} {x : α} {y : β} :
512removed (unzip ((x, y) :: l)).snd = y :: (unzip l).snd := sorry
513removed
514removedexample : unzip [(1, false), (2, false)] = ([1, 2], [false, false]) := sorry
515removed
516removed-- ### Polymorphic Options
517removed
518removed-- Our last polymorphic type for now is *polymorphic options*. Lean's standard
519removed-- library provides `Option α`, with constructors `none` and `some`. (We
520removed-- already saw `NatOption` in the `Lists` chapter.) Let's briefly look at the
521removed-- definition:
522removed
523removednamespace OptionPlayground
524removed
525removedinductive Option (α : Type) : Type where
526removed | none : Option α
527removed | some (x : α) : Option α
528removed
529removedend OptionPlayground
530removed
531removed-- We can now rewrite the `nthError` function so that it works with any type
532removed-- of list.
533removed
534removeddef nthError {α : Type} (l : List α) (n : Nat) : Option α :=
535removed match l with
536removed | [] => none
537removed | a :: l' => match n with
538removed | 0 => some a
539removed | n' + 1 => nthError l' n'
540removed
541removedexample : nthError [4, 5, 6, 7] 0 = some 4 := by rfl
542removedexample : nthError [[1], [2]] 1 = some [2] := by rfl
543removedexample : nthError [true] 2 = none := by rfl
544removed
545removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): hd_error_poly ⭐
546removed
547removed-- Complete the definition of a polymorphic version of the `hdError` function
548removed-- from the last chapter. Be sure that it passes the unit tests below.
549removed
550removeddef hdError {α : Type} (l : List α) : Option α := sorry
551removed
552removedtheorem hdError_nil {α : Type} : hdError ([] : List α) = none := sorry
553removed
554removedtheorem hdError_cons {α : Type} {head : α} {tail : List α} : hdError (head :: tail) = some head :=
555removed sorry
556removed
557removedexample : hdError [1, 2] = some 1 := sorry
558removed
559removedexample : hdError [[1], [2]] = some [1] := sorry
560removed
561removed-- ## Functions as Data
562removed
563removed-- Like most modern programming languages — especially other "functional"
564removed-- languages, including OCaml, Haskell, Racket, Scala, Clojure, etc. — Lean
565removed-- treats functions as first-class citizens, allowing them to be passed as
566removed-- arguments to other functions, returned as results, stored in data
567removed-- structures, etc.
568removed
569removed-- ### Higher-Order Functions
570removed
571removed-- Functions that manipulate other functions are often called *higher-order*
572removed-- functions. Here's a simple one:
573removed
574removedabbrev doIt3Times {α : Type} (f : α → α) (n : α) : α :=
575removed f (f (f n))
576removed
577removed-- The argument `f` here is itself a function (from `α` to `α`); the body of
578removed-- `doIt3Times` applies `f` three times to some value `n`.
579removed
580removed#check doIt3Times
581removed
582removedexample : doIt3Times Nat.minustwo 9 = 3 := by rfl
583removed
584removedexample : doIt3Times not true = false := by rfl
585removed
586removed-- doIt3Times {α : Type} (f : α → α) (n : α) : α
587removed
588removed-- ### Filter
589removed
590removed-- Here is a more useful higher-order function, taking a list of `α`s and a
591removed-- *predicate* on `α` (a function from `α` to `Bool`) and "filtering" the list
592removed-- to yield a new list containing just those elements for which the predicate
593removed-- returns `true`.
594removed
595removeddef filter {α : Type} (test : α → Bool) (l : List α) : List α :=
596removed match l with
597removed | [] => []
598removed | head :: tail =>
599removed bif test head then head :: filter test tail
600removed else filter test tail
601removed
602removed-- For example, if we apply `filter` to the predicate `Nat.even` and a list of
603removed-- numbers, it returns a list containing just the even members.
604removed
605removedexample : filter Nat.even [1, 2, 3, 4] = [2, 4] := by rfl
606removed
607removedabbrev lengthIs1 {α : Type} (l : List α) : Bool :=
608removed l.length == 1
609removed
610removedexample : filter lengthIs1
611removed [[1, 2], [3], [4], [5, 6, 7], [], [8]]
612removed = [[3], [4], [8]] := by rfl
613removed
614removedtheorem filter_nil {α : Type} {test : α → Bool} : filter test [] = [] := by rfl
615removed
616removedtheorem filter_cons_success {α : Type} {test : α → Bool} {head : α}
617removed {tail : List α} (h : test head) :
618removed filter test (head :: tail) = head :: filter test tail := by
619removed dsimp [filter]
620removed rw [h]
621removed dsimp
622removed
623removedtheorem filter_cons_fail {α : Type} {test : α → Bool} {head : α}
624removed {tail : List α} (h : test head = false) :
625removed filter test (head :: tail) = filter test tail := by
626removed dsimp [filter]
627removed rw [h]
628removed dsimp
629removed
630removed-- We can use `filter` to give a concise version of the `countOddMembers`
631removed-- function from the `Lists` chapter.
632removed
633removedabbrev countOddMembers' (l : List Nat) : Nat :=
634removed (filter Nat.odd l).length
635removed
636removedexample : countOddMembers' [1, 0, 3, 1, 4, 5] = 4 := by rfl
637removedexample : countOddMembers' [0, 2, 4] = 0 := by rfl
638removedexample : countOddMembers' [] = 0 := by rfl
639removed
640removed-- ### Anonymous Functions
641removed
642removed-- It is arguably a little sad, in the example just above, to be forced to
643removed-- define the function `lengthIs1` and give it a name just to be able to pass
644removed-- it as an argument to `filter`, since we will probably never use it again.
645removed-- Indeed, when using higher-order functions, we *often* want to pass as
646removed-- arguments "one-off" functions that we will never use again; having to give
647removed-- each of these functions a name would be tedious.
648removed
649removed-- Fortunately, there is a better way. We can construct a function "on the
650removed-- fly" without declaring it at the top level or giving it a name. Lean
651removed-- provides two syntaxes for anonymous functions:
652removed
653removed-- - `fun n => n * n` — traditional lambda syntax
654removed-- - `(· * ·)` — "term with holes" syntax, where `·` marks arguments
655removed
656removedexample : doIt3Times (fun n => n * n) 2 = 256 := by rfl
657removed
658removed-- The expression `fun n => n * n` can be read as "the function that, given a
659removed-- number `n`, yields `n * n`."
660removed
661removed-- Lean also supports a shorter notation using `·` as a placeholder for the
662removed-- argument:
663removed
664removedexample : doIt3Times (· + 1) 0 = 3 := by rfl
665removed
666removed-- Here is the `filter` example, rewritten to use an anonymous function.
667removed
668removedexample : filter (fun l => l.length == 1)
669removed [[1, 2], [3], [4], [5, 6, 7], [], [8]]
670removed = [[3], [4], [8]] := by rfl
671removed
672removedexample : filter (·.length == 1)
673removed [[1, 2], [3], [4], [5, 6, 7], [], [8]]
674removed = [[3], [4], [8]] := by rfl
675removed
676removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): filter_even_gt7 ⭐⭐
677removed

679removed-- `filterEvenGt7` that takes a list of natural numbers as input and returns a
680removed-- list of just those that are even and greater than 7.
681removed
682removedabbrev filterEvenGt7 (l : List Nat) : List Nat := sorry
683removed
684removedexample : filterEvenGt7 [1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 3, 12, 8] = [10, 12, 8] := sorry
685removed
686removedexample : filterEvenGt7 [5, 2, 6, 19, 129] = [] := sorry

688removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): partition ⭐⭐⭐
689removed
690removed-- Use `filter` to write a Lean function `partition` that, given a type `α`, a
691removed-- predicate of type `α → Bool` and a `List α`, should return a pair of lists.
692removed-- The first member of the pair is the sublist of the original list containing
693removed-- the elements that satisfy the test, and the second is the sublist
694removed-- containing those that fail the test. The order of elements in the two
695removed-- sublists should be the same as their order in the original list.
696removed
697removedabbrev partition {α : Type} (test : α → Bool) (l : List α) : List α × List α := sorry
698removed
699removedexample : partition (· % 2 != 0) [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] = ([1, 3, 5], [2, 4]) := sorry
700removedexample : partition (fun _ => false) [5, 9, 0] = ([], [5, 9, 0]) := sorry
701removed
702removed-- ### Map
703removed
704removed-- Another handy higher-order function is called `map`.
705removed
706removeddef map {α : Type} {β : Type} (f : α → β) (l : List α) : List β :=
707removed match l with
708removed | [] => []
709removed | head :: tail => f head :: map f tail
710removed
711removed-- It takes a function `f` and a list `l = [n1, n2, n3, ...]` and returns the
712removed-- list `[f n1, f n2, f n3, ...]`, where `f` has been applied to each element
713removed-- of `l` in turn. For example:
714removed
715removedexample : map (· + 3) [2, 0, 2] = [5, 3, 5] := by rfl
716removed
717removed-- The element types of the input and output lists need not be the same, since
718removed-- `map` takes *two* type arguments, `α` and `β`; it can thus be applied to a
719removed-- list of numbers and a function from numbers to booleans to yield a list of
720removed-- booleans:
721removed
722removedexample : map Nat.odd [2, 1, 2, 5] = [false, true, false, true] := by rfl
723removed
724removed-- It can even be applied to a list of numbers and a function from numbers to
725removed-- *lists* of booleans to yield a *list of lists* of booleans:
726removed
727removedexample : map (fun n => [n.even, n.odd]) [2, 1, 2, 5]
728removed = [[true, false], [false, true], [true, false], [false, true]] := by rfl
729removed
730removed-- _Quiz:_
731removed
732removed-- Recall the definition of `map`:
733removed
734removed-- def map (f : α → β) (l : List α) : List β :=
735removed-- match l with
736removed-- | [] => []
737removed-- | head :: tail => f head :: map f tail
738removed
739removed-- What is the type of `@map`?
740removed
741removed-- (A) `{α β : Type} → α → β → List α → List β`
742removed
743removed-- (B) `α → β → List α → List β`
744removed
745removed-- (C) `{α β : Type} → (α → β) → List α → List β`
746removed
747removed-- (D) `{α : Type} → (α → α) → List α → List α`
748removed
749removed-- Exercises
750removed
751removedtheorem map_nil {α : Type} {β : Type} {f : α → β} : map f [] = [] := by rfl
752removed
753removedtheorem map_cons {α : Type} {β : Type} {f : α → β} {head : α} {tail : List α} :
754removed map f (head :: tail) = f head :: map f tail := by rfl
755removed
756removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): map_rev ⭐⭐⭐
757removed
758removed-- Show that `map` and `rev` commute. (Hint: You may need to define an
759removed-- auxiliary lemma.)
760removed
761removed-- FILL IN HERE
762removed
763removedtheorem map_rev {α : Type} {β : Type} : ∀ (f : α → β) (l : List α),
764removed map f l.rev = (map f l).rev := by
765removed sorry
766removed
767removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): flat_map ⭐⭐
768removed
769removed-- The function `map` maps a `List α` to a `List β` using a function of type
770removed-- `α → β`. We can define a similar function, `flatMap`, which maps a `List α`
771removed-- to a `List β` using a function `f` of type `α → List β`. Your definition
772removed-- should work by 'flattening' the results of `f`, like so:
773removed
774removed-- flatMap (fun n => [n, n + 1, n + 2]) [1, 5, 10]
775removed-- = [1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12]
776removed
777removeddef flatMap {α : Type} {β : Type} (f : α → List β) (l : List α) : List β := sorry
778removed
779removedexample : flatMap (fun n => [n, n, n]) [1, 5, 4]
780removed = [1, 1, 1, 5, 5, 5, 4, 4, 4] := sorry
781removed
782removedtheorem flatMap_nil {α : Type} {β : Type} (f : α → List β) : flatMap f [] = [] :=
783removed sorry
784removed
785removedtheorem flatMap_cons {α : Type} {β : Type} (f : α → List β) h t :
786removed flatMap f (h :: t) = f h ++ flatMap f t := sorry
787removed
788removed-- Lists are not the only inductive type for which `map` makes sense. Here is
789removed-- a `map` for the `Option` type:
790removed
791removeddef optionMap {α : Type} {β : Type} (f : α → β) (x? : Option α) : Option β :=
792removed match x? with
793removed | none => none
794removed | some x => some (f x)
795removed
796removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): implicit_args ⭐⭐
797removed
798removed-- The definitions and uses of `filter` and `map` use implicit arguments in
799removed-- many places. Replace the curly braces around the implicit arguments with
800removed-- explicit parentheses, and then fill in explicit type parameters where
801removed-- necessary and use Lean to check that you've done so correctly. (This

805removed-- ### Fold
806removed
807removed-- An even more powerful higher-order function is `fold`. It is the
808removed-- inspiration for the "reduce" operation that lies at the heart of Google's
809removed-- map/reduce distributed programming framework.
810removed
811removeddef fold {α : Type} {β : Type} (f : α → β → β) (l : List α) (b : β) : β :=
812removed match l with
813removed | [] => b
814removed | head :: tail => f head (fold f tail b)
815removed
816removed-- Intuitively, the behavior of the `fold` operation is to insert a given
817removed-- binary operator `f` between every pair of elements in a given list. For
818removed-- example, `fold (· + ·) [1, 2, 3, 4]` intuitively means `1 + 2 + 3 + 4`. To
819removed-- make this precise, we also need a "starting element" that serves as the
820removed-- initial second input to `f`. So, for example,
821removed
822removed-- fold (· + ·) [1, 2, 3, 4] 0
823removed
824removed-- yields
825removed
826removed-- 1 + (2 + (3 + (4 + 0))).
827removed
828removedexample : fold (· && ·) [true, true, false, true] true = false := by rfl
829removed
830removedexample : fold (· * ·) [1, 2, 3, 4] 1 = 24 := by rfl
831removed
832removedexample : fold (· ++ ·) [[1], [], [2, 3], [4]] [] = [1, 2, 3, 4] := by rfl
833removed
834removedexample : fold (fun l n => l.length + n) [[1], [], [2, 3, 2], [4]] 0 = 5 := by rfl
835removed
836removedtheorem fold_nil {α : Type} {β : Type} {f : α → β → β} {b : β} : fold f [] b = b := by rfl
837removed
838removedtheorem fold_cons {α : Type} {β : Type} {f : α → β → β} {head : α} {tail : List α} {b : β} :
839removed fold f (head :: tail) b = f head (fold f tail b) := by rfl
840removed
841removed-- _Quiz:_
842removed
843removed-- Here is the definition of `fold` again:
844removed
845removed-- def fold {α : Type} {β : Type} (f : α → β → β) (l : List α) (b : β) : β :=
846removed-- match l with
847removed-- | [] => b
848removed-- | head :: tail => f head (fold f tail b)
849removed
850removed-- What is the type of `@fold`?
851removed
852removed-- (A) `{α β : Type} → (α → β → β) → List α → β → β`
853removed
854removed-- (B) `α → β → (α → β → β) → List α → β → β`
855removed
856removed-- (C) `{α β : Type} → α → β → β → List α → β → β`
857removed
858removed-- (D) `α → β → α → β → β → List α → β → β`
859removed
860removed-- _Quiz:_
861removed
862removed-- What does `fold (· + ·) [1, 2, 3, 4] 0` simplify to?
863removed
864removed-- (A) `[1, 2, 3, 4]`
865removed
866removed-- (B) `0`
867removed
868removed-- (C) `10`
869removed
870removed-- (D) `[3, 7, 0]`
871removed
872removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): fold_types_different (manually graded) ⭐
873removed
874removed-- Observe that the type of `fold` is parameterized by *two* type variables,
875removed-- `α` and `β`, and the parameter `f` is a binary operator that takes an `α`
876removed-- and a `β` and returns a `β`. The examples above show one instance where it
877removed-- is useful for `α` and `β` to be different. Can you think of any others?
878removed
879removed-- ### Functions That Construct Functions
880removed
881removed-- Most of the higher-order functions we have talked about so far take
882removed-- functions as arguments. Let's look at some examples that involve
883removed-- *returning* functions as the results of other functions. To begin, here is
884removed-- a function that takes a value `x` (drawn from some type `α`) and returns a
885removed-- function from `Nat` to `α` that yields `x` whenever it is called, ignoring
886removed-- its `Nat` argument.
887removed
888removedabbrev constFun {α : Type} (x : α) : Nat → α :=
889removed fun _ => x
890removed
891removedabbrev fTrue := constFun true
892removed
893removedexample : fTrue 0 = true := by rfl
894removed
895removedexample : constFun 5 99 = 5 := by rfl
896removed
897removed-- In fact, the multiple-argument functions we have already seen are also
898removed-- examples of passing functions as data. To see why, recall the type of
899removed-- addition:
900removed
901removed#check Nat.add
902removed
903removed-- Nat.add : Nat → Nat → Nat
904removed
905removedabbrev plus3 := Nat.add 3
906removed#check plus3
907removed
908removedexample : plus3 4 = 7 := by rfl
909removedexample : doIt3Times plus3 0 = 9 := by rfl
910removedexample : doIt3Times (Nat.add 3) 0 = 9 := by rfl
911removed
912removed-- plus3 : Nat → Nat
913removed
914removed-- Similarly, we can write:
915removed
916removedabbrev fold_plus : List Nat → Nat → Nat :=
917removed fold (· + ·)
918removed
919removed#check fold_plus
920removed
921removed-- fold_plus : List Nat → Nat → Nat
922removed
923removed-- What's happening here is called *partial application*. In Lean, the type
924removed-- constructor `→` is right-associative, meaning a function type like
925removed-- `α → β → γ` is parsed like `α → (β → γ)`, or "a function from `α` to a
926removed-- function from `β` to `γ`."
927removed
928removed-- We can think of `fold` not as a three-argument function, but as a
929removed-- one-argument function that:
930removed
931removed-- 1. Takes an argument `f` of type `α → β → β`
932removed-- 2. Returns a function of type `List α → β → β` that "remembers" `f`
933removed
934removed-- When we write `fold (· + ·)`, we're giving `fold` its first argument,
935removed-- `(· + ·)`, and getting back a specialized function that can sum up the
936removed-- elements of any list of numbers. This new function still expects two more
937removed-- arguments: a list and a starting value.
938removed
939removed-- ## Additional Exercises
940removed
941removednamespace Exercises
942removed
943removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): fold_length ⭐⭐
944removed
945removed-- Many common functions on lists can be implemented in terms of `fold`. For
946removed-- example, here is an alternative definition of `length`:
947removed
948removedabbrev foldLength {α : Type} (l : List α) : Nat :=
949removed fold (fun _ n => n + 1) l 0
950removed
951removedexample : foldLength [4, 7, 0] = 3 := by rfl
952removed
953removed-- Prove the correctness of `foldLength`.
954removed
955removed-- Hint: It may help to use `dsimp [foldLength, fold]` to unfold the
956removed-- definition.
957removed
958removedtheorem fold_length_correct {α : Type} (l : List α) :
959removed foldLength l = l.length := by
960removed sorry
961removed
962removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): fold_map (manually graded) ⭐⭐⭐
963removed
964removed-- We can also define `map` in terms of `fold`. Finish `foldMap` below.
965removed
966removedabbrev foldMap {α : Type} {β : Type} (f : α → β) (l : List α) : List β := sorry
967removed
968removed-- Write down a theorem `fold_map_correct` stating that `foldMap` is correct,
969removed-- and prove it in Lean.
970removed
971removed-- FILL IN HERE
972removed
973removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): currying (Advanced) ⭐⭐
974removed
975removed-- The type `α → β → γ` can be read as describing functions that take two
976removed-- arguments, one of type `α` and another of type `β`, and return an output of
977removed-- type `γ`. Recall from our discussion of partial application that this type
978removed-- is written `α → (β → γ)` when fully parenthesized. That is, if we have
979removed-- `f : α → β → γ`, and we give `f` an input of type `α`, it will give us as
980removed-- output a function of type `β → γ`. If we then give that function an input
981removed-- of type `β`, it will return an output of type `γ`. That is, every function
982removed-- in Lean takes only one input, but some functions return a function as
983removed-- output. This is precisely what enables partial application, as we saw above
984removed-- with `plus3`.
985removed
986removed-- By contrast, functions of type `α × β → γ` — which when fully parenthesized
987removed-- is written `(α × β) → γ` — require their single input to be a pair. Both
988removed-- arguments must be given at once; there is no possibility of partial
989removed-- application.
990removed
991removed-- It is possible to convert a function between these two types. Converting
992removed-- from `α × β → γ` to `α → β → γ` is called *currying*, in honor of the
993removed-- logician Haskell Curry. Converting from `α → β → γ` to `α × β → γ` is
994removed-- called *uncurrying*.
995removed
996removed-- We can define currying as follows:
997removed
998removedabbrev prodCurry {α β γ : Type} (f : α × β → γ) (x : α) (y : β) : γ := f (x, y)
999removed
1000removed-- As an exercise, define its inverse, `prodUncurry`. Then prove the theorems
1001removed-- below to show that the two are really inverses.
1002removed
1003removedabbrev prodUncurry {α β γ : Type} (f : α → β → γ) (p : α × β) : γ := sorry
1004removed
1005removed-- As a (trivial) example of the usefulness of currying, we can use it to
1006removed-- shorten one of the examples that we saw above:
1007removed
1008removedexample : map (Nat.add 3) [2, 0, 2] = [5, 3, 5] := by rfl
1009removed
1010removed-- Thought exercise: before running the following commands, can you calculate
1011removed-- the types of `prodCurry` and `prodUncurry`?
1012removed
1013removed#check @prodCurry
1014removed#check @prodUncurry
1015removed
1016removed-- @prodCurry : {α β γ : Type} → (α × β → γ) → α → β → γ
1017removed
1018removed-- @prodUncurry : {α β γ : Type} → (α → β → γ) → α × β → γ
1019removed
1020removedtheorem uncurry_curry {α β γ : Type} (f : α → β → γ) (x : α) (y : β) :
1021removed prodCurry (prodUncurry f) x y = f x y := by
1022removed sorry
1023removed
1024removedtheorem curry_uncurry {α β γ : Type} (f : α × β → γ) {p : α × β} :
1025removed prodUncurry (prodCurry f) p = f p := by
1026removed sorry
1027removed
1028removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): nth_error_informal (Advanced, manually graded) ⭐⭐
1029removed
1030removed-- Recall the definition of the `nthError` function:
1031removed
1032removed-- def nthError (l : List α) (n : Nat) : Option α :=
1033removed-- match l with
1034removed-- | [] => none
1035removed-- | a :: l' => match n with
1036removed-- | 0 => some a
1037removed-- | n' + 1 => nthError l' n'
1038removed
1039removed-- Write a careful informal proof of the following theorem:
1040removed
1041removed-- ∀ (l : List α) (n : Nat), l.length = n → nthError l n = none
1042removed
1043removed-- Make sure to state the induction hypothesis *explicitly*.
1044removed
1045removed-- SOLUTION Theorem: For all types `α`, lists `l`, and natural numbers `n`, if
1046removed-- `l.length = n` then `nthError l n = none`.
1047removed
1048removed-- Proof: By induction on `l`. There are two cases to consider:
1049removed
1050removed-- - If `l = []`, we must show `nthError [] n = none`. This follows immediately
1051removed-- from the definition of `nthError`.
1052removed
1053removed-- - Otherwise, `l = x :: l'` for some `x` and `l'`, and the induction
1054removed-- hypothesis tells us that `l'.length = n' → nthError l' n' = none`, for any
1055removed-- `n'`.
1056removed
1057removed-- Let `n` be the length of `l`. We must show that
1058removed-- `nthError (x :: l') n = none`.
1059removed
1060removed-- But we know that `n = l.length = (x :: l').length = l'.length + 1`. So it's
1061removed-- enough to show `nthError l' l'.length = none`, which follows directly from
1062removed-- the induction hypothesis, picking `l'.length` for `n'`. /SOLUTION
1063removed
1064removed-- ### Church Numerals (Advanced)
1065removed
1066removed-- The following exercises explore an alternative way of defining natural
1067removed-- numbers using the *Church numerals*, which are named after their inventor,
1068removed-- the mathematician Alonzo Church. We can represent a natural number `n` as a
1069removed-- function that takes a function `f` as a parameter and returns `f` iterated
1070removed-- `n` times.
1071removed
1072removednamespace Church
1073removed
1074removeddef CNat := (α : Type) → (α → α) → α → α
1075removed
1076removed-- Let's see how to write some numbers with this notation. Iterating a
1077removed-- function once should be the same as just applying it. Thus:
1078removed
1079removeddef one : CNat :=
1080removed fun (X : Type) (f : X → X) (x : X) => f x
1081removed
1082removed-- Similarly, `two` should apply `f` twice to its argument:
1083removed
1084removeddef two : CNat :=
1085removed fun (X : Type) (f : X → X) (x : X) => f (f x)
1086removed
1087removed-- Defining `zero` is somewhat trickier: how can we "apply a function zero
1088removed-- times"? The answer is actually simple: just return the argument untouched.
1089removed
1090removeddef zero : CNat :=
1091removed fun (X : Type) (_ : X → X) (x : X) => x
1092removed
1093removed-- More generally, a number `n` can be written as
1094removed-- `fun X f x => f (f ... (f x) ...)`, with `n` occurrences of `f`. Let's
1095removed-- informally notate that as `fun X f x => f^n x`, with the convention that
1096removed-- `f^0 x` is just `x`. Note how the `doit3times` function we've defined
1097removed-- previously is actually just the Church representation of 3.
1098removed
1099removeddef three : CNat := @doIt3Times
1100removed
1101removed-- So `n X f x` represents "do it `n` times", where `n` is a Church numeral
1102removed-- and "it" means applying `f` starting with `x`.
1103removed
1104removed-- Another way to think about the Church representation is that function `f`
1105removed-- represents the successor operation on `α`, and value `x` represents the
1106removed-- zero element of `α`. We could even rewrite with those names to make it
1107removed-- clearer:
1108removed
1109removeddef zero' : CNat :=
1110removed fun (X : Type) (_ : X → X) (zero : X) => zero
1111removeddef one' : CNat :=
1112removed fun (X : Type) (succ : X → X) (zero : X) => succ zero
1113removeddef two' : CNat :=
1114removed fun (X : Type) (succ : X → X) (zero : X) => succ (succ zero)
1115removed
1116removed-- If we passed in `Nat.succ` as `succ` and `0` as `zero`, we'd even get the
1117removed-- Peano naturals as a result:
1118removed
1119removedexample : zero Nat Nat.succ 0 = 0 := by rfl
1120removedexample : one Nat Nat.succ 0 = 1 := by rfl
1121removedexample : two Nat Nat.succ 0 = 2 := by rfl
1122removed
1123removed-- One very interesting implication of the Church numerals is that we don't
1124removed-- strictly need the natural numbers to be built-in to a functional
1125removed-- programming language, or even to be definable with an inductive data type.
1126removed-- It's possible to represent them purely (if not efficiently) with functions.
1127removed
1128removed-- Of course, it's not enough just to "represent" numerals; we need to be able
1129removed-- to do arithmetic with the representation. Show that we can by completing
1130removed-- the definitions of the following functions. Make sure that the
1131removed-- corresponding unit tests pass by proving them with `rfl`.
1132removed
1133removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): church_scc (Advanced) ⭐⭐
1134removed
1135removed-- Define a function that computes the successor of a Church numeral. Given a
1136removed-- Church numeral `n`, its successor `scc n` should iterate its function
1137removed-- argument once more than `n`. That is, given `fun X f x => f^n x` as input,
1138removed-- `scc` should produce `fun X f x => f^(n+1) x` as output. In other words, do
1139removed-- it `n` times, then do it once more.
1140removed
1141removeddef scc (n : CNat) : CNat := sorry
1142removed
1143removedexample : scc zero = one := sorry
1144removedexample : scc one = two := sorry
1145removedexample : scc two = three := sorry
1146removed
1147removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): church_plus (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
1148removed
1149removed-- Define a function that computes the addition of two Church numerals. Given
1150removed-- `fun X f x => f^n x` and `fun X f x => f^m x` as input, `plus` should
1151removed-- produce `fun X f x => f^(n + m) x` as output. In other words, do it `n`
1152removed-- times, then do it `m` more times.
1153removed
1154removed-- Hint: the "zero" argument to a Church numeral need not be just `x`.
1155removed
1156removeddef plus (n m : CNat) : CNat := sorry
1157removed
1158removedexample : plus zero one = one := sorry
1159removedexample : plus two three = plus three two := sorry
1160removedexample : plus (plus two two) three = plus one (plus three three) := sorry
1161removed
1162removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): church_mult (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
1163removed
1164removed-- Define a function that computes the multiplication of two Church numerals.
1165removed
1166removed-- Hint: the "successor" argument to a Church numeral need not be just `f`.
1167removed
1168removed-- Warning: Lean will not let you pass `CNat` itself as the type `X` argument
1169removed-- to a Church numeral; you will get a "sort mismatch" error between `Type 1`
1170removed-- and `Type 2`. Don't worry too much about what this means right now, but
1171removed-- know that this is Lean's way of preventing a paradox in which a type
1172removed-- contains itself. So leave the type argument unchanged.
1173removed
1174removeddef mult (n m : CNat) : CNat := sorry
1175removed
1176removedexample : mult one one = one := sorry
1177removedexample : mult zero (plus three three) = zero := sorry
1178removedexample : mult two three = plus three three := sorry
1179removed
1180removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): church_exp (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
1181removed
1182removed-- Exponentiation:
1183removed
1184removed-- Define a function that computes the exponentiation of two Church numerals.
1185removed
1186removed-- Hint: the type argument to a Church numeral need not just be `α`. Finding
1187removed-- the right type can be tricky.
1188removed
1189removeddef exp (n m : CNat) : CNat := sorry
1190removed
1191removedexample : exp two two = plus two two := sorry
1192removedexample : exp three zero = one := sorry
1193removedexample : exp three two = plus (mult two (mult two two)) one := sorry
1194removed

11removed-- Copied from `SubVerso.Compat` to avoid making generated projects depend on verso.
12removed-- We want to have info state and messages available right after the elaboration,
13removed-- so we need to disable `Elab.async` which would let diagnostics produced asynchronously
14removed-- through spanshot tasks.
15removedprivate def commandWithoutAsync (act : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
16removed match (← get).scopes with
17removed | [] => act
18removed | h :: t =>
19removed let mut orig : Option Bool := none
20removed try
21removed orig := h.opts.get? `Elab.async
22removed modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := h.opts.setBool `Elab.async false } :: t }
23removed act
24removed finally
25removed if let h :: t := (← get).scopes then
26removed let opts := orig.map (h.opts.setBool `Elab.async) |>.getD (h.opts.erase `Elab.async)
27removed modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := opts } :: t }
28removed
29removedprivate def withRestoringState (keepMsgs : Bool) (m : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
30removed let savedState ← get
31removed try
32removed m
33removed finally
34removed let state ← get
35removed set { savedState with
36removed -- Preserve the info tree
37removed infoState := state.infoState
38removed messages := if keepMsgs then state.messages else savedState.messages }

40removednamespace IndentedCommands
41removed
42removed/-! # Block Commands Parser
43removed Parse an indented command block. Commands are separated by new lines.
44removed Since we want to capture parsing errors in `sf_expect_failure`,
45removed we can't use Lean command parser directly in our command's syntax,
46removed because any parsing error occurred would fail `sf_expect_failure` itself.
47removed One possible solution is to first parse the whole indented body as raw syntax,
48removed and then run Lean's command parser followed by command elaboration.
49removed-/
50removed
51removedopen Parser
52removed
53removedprivate def rawLineEndFn : ParserFn :=
54removed eoiFn <|> satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break"
55removed
56removed/-- Consumes everything until the next newline and then consumes the newline itself. -/
57removedprivate def rawLineFn : ParserFn :=
58removed takeUntilFn (· == '\n') >> rawLineEndFn
59removed
60removed/- For each line after the first body line, consumes leading whitespaces.
61removed If it's blank, consumes the newline; otherwise consumes the line
62removed requiring the indentation.
63removed-/
64removedprivate def rawIndentedLineFn : ParserFn := atomicFn <|
65removed takeWhileFn (· == ' ') >>
66removed (satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break" <|>
67removed (checkColGeFn "indented command sequence" >> rawLineFn))
68removed
69removedprivate def rawCommandBlockFn : ParserFn :=
70removed rawFn (rawLineFn >> manyFn rawIndentedLineFn) (trailingWs := true)
71removed
72removedprivate def rawCommandBlock : Parser := { fn := rawCommandBlockFn }
73removed
74removed@[combinator_parenthesizer rawCommandBlock]
75removedprivate def rawCommandBlock.parenthesizer := PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer.visitToken
76removed
77removed@[combinator_formatter rawCommandBlock]
78removedprivate def rawCommandBlock.formatter := PrettyPrinter.Formatter.visitAtom Name.anonymous
79removed
80removedprivate partial def runRawCmdsAux
81removed (ictx : InputContext) (pstate : ModuleParserState) : CommandElabM Unit := do
82removed let state ← get
83removed let scope := state.scopes.head!
84removed let pctx := {
85removed env := state.env
86removed options := scope.opts
87removed currNamespace := scope.currNamespace
88removed openDecls := scope.openDecls : ParserModuleContext
89removed }
90removed let (cmd, pstate, messages) := parseCommand ictx pctx pstate state.messages
91removed modify fun state => { state with messages }
92removed unless cmd.isOfKind ``Command.eoi do
93removed elabCommand cmd
94removed runLinters cmd
95removed unless isTerminalCommand cmd do
96removed runRawCmdsAux ictx pstate
97removed
98removed/- Recovers the source info and elaborates the commands -/
99removedprivate def runRawCmds (body : Syntax) : CommandElabM Unit := do
100removed let some source := body.getSubstring? (withLeading := false) (withTrailing := false)
101removed | throwErrorAt body "command sequence has no source range"
102removed let fileName ← getFileName
103removed let fileMap ← getFileMap
104removed -- Recall that `rawIndentedLineFn` may consume whitespaces after the newline.
105removed -- Here we move the ending back to the last non-whitespace character to produce
106removed -- correctly positioned diagnostics.
107removed let stopPos := source.trimRight.stopPos
108removed if h : stopPos ≤ fileMap.source.rawEndPos then
109removed let ictx := InputContext.mk fileMap.source fileName
110removed (fileMap := fileMap) (endPos := stopPos) (endPos_valid := h)
111removed runRawCmdsAux ictx { pos := source.startPos, recovering := false, hasLeading := false }
112removed else
113removed throwErrorAt body "invalid command-sequence source range"
114removed
115removedend IndentedCommands
116removed
117removedend

5removed
6removed-- # Tactics: More Basic Tactics
7removed
8removed-- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1):
9removed-- [BCP: Old comment -- might be out of date?] There is a section here on
10removed-- unfolding definitions that should probably move earlier, to `Basics` or
11removed-- `Induction`, once those chapters are rewritten to not use arithmetic.
12removed-- This will also require changing the examples.
13removed
14removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
15removed-- (Old and possibly out of date -- check!) Many exercises in this chapter
16removed-- are based on defining and proving properties about Nat.ble and BEq.eq,
17removed-- which are not idiomatic in Lean. We should consider replacing these
18removed-- with a different set of exercises.
19removed
20removed-- Note to developers (before next release):
21removed-- This chapter could maybe use one or two more WORKINCLASS tags...
22removed
23removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, before next release, 2025):
24removed-- General comment: All the previous chapters have felt pretty smooth.
25removed-- This one suddenly feels like we're throwing a huge amount of
26removed-- information at them, with little scaffolding -- just a bunch of
27removed-- miscellaneous tactics and examples. Wish it flowed better, somehow.
28removed
29removed-- This chapter introduces several additional proof strategies and tactics
30removed-- that allow us to begin proving more interesting properties of functional
31removed-- programs.
32removed
33removed-- We will see:
34removed
35removed-- - how to use auxiliary lemmas in both "forward-" and "backward-style" proofs;
36removed
37removed-- - how to reason about data constructors -- in particular, how to use the fact
38removed-- that they are injective and disjoint;
39removed
40removed-- - how to strengthen an induction hypothesis, and when such strengthening is
41removed-- required; and
42removed
43removed-- - more details on how to reason by case analysis.
44removed
45removed-- OA: added these to use Lean's Nat.
46removed
47removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
48removed-- Deserves a comment. (In general, the reader should be given enough
49removed-- information to understand every line in the files we give them. This
50removed-- will not always be possible, but when it is not we should mark it
51removed-- explicitly.)
52removed
53removedopen Nat (add_comm add_assoc add_zero add_succ mul_one succ_sub_succ)
54removed
55removed-- ## The `apply` Tactic
56removed
57removed-- We often encounter situations where the goal to be proved is *exactly* the
58removed-- same as some hypothesis in the context or some previously proved lemma.
59removed
60removedtheorem silly1 (n m : Nat) : n = m → n = m := by
61removed intro eq
62removed /- Here, we could finish with `rw [eq]` as we
63removed have done several times before. Or we can finish
64removed by using `apply`: -/
65removed apply eq
66removed
67removed-- The `apply` tactic also works with *conditional* hypotheses and lemmas: if
68removed-- the statement being applied is an implication, then the premises of this
69removed-- implication will be added to the list of subgoals needing to be proved.
70removed
71removedtheorem silly2 (n m o p : Nat) :
72removed n = m →
73removed (n = m → [n, o] = [m, p]) →
74removed [n, o] = [m, p] := by
75removed intro eq1 eq2
76removed apply eq2
77removed apply eq1
78removed
79removed-- Typically, when we use `apply h`, the statement `h` will begin with a
80removed-- `forall` that introduces some *universally quantified variables*.
81removed
82removed-- When Lean matches the current goal against the conclusion of `h`, it will
83removed-- try to find appropriate values for these variables. For example, when we do
84removed-- `apply eq2` in the following proof, the universal variable `q` in `eq2`
85removed-- gets instantiated with `n`, and `r` gets instantiated with `m`.
86removed
87removedtheorem silly2a (n m : Nat) :
88removed (n, n) = (m, m) →
89removed (∀ (q r : Nat), (q, q) = (r, r) → [q] = [r]) →
90removed [n] = [m] := by
91removed intro eq1 eq2
92removed apply eq2
93removed apply eq1
94removed
95removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): silly_ex ⭐⭐
96removed
97removed-- Complete the following proof using only `intros` and `apply`.
98removed
99removedtheorem silly_ex p :
100removed (∀ (n : Nat), n.even = true → (n + 1).even = false) →
101removed (∀ (n : Nat), n.even = false → n.odd = true) →
102removed p.even = true →
103removed (p + 1).odd = true := by
104removed sorry
105removed
106removed-- To use the `apply` tactic, the (conclusion of the) fact being applied must
107removed-- match the goal exactly (perhaps after simplification) -- for example,
108removed-- `apply` will not work if the left and right sides of the equality are
109removed-- swapped.
110removed
111removedtheorem silly3 (n m : Nat) :
112removed n = m →
113removed m = n := by
114removed intro H
115removed -- Here we cannot use `apply` directly...
116removed /- ...but we can use the `symm` tactic, which switches the left
117removed and right sides of an equality in the goal. -/
118removed symm; apply H
119removed
120removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): apply_exercise1 ⭐⭐
121removed
122removed-- You can use `apply` with previously defined theorems, not just hypotheses
123removed-- in the context. Use a previously-defined theorem about `rev` from Poly. Use
124removed-- that theorem as part of your (relatively short) solution to this exercise.
125removed-- You do not need `induction`.
126removed
127removedtheorem rev_exercise1 {α} (l l' : List α) :
128removed l = l'.rev →
129removed l' = l.rev := by
130removed intro eq
131removed rw [eq]; symm
132removed apply rev_involutive
133removed -- /ADMITTED
134removed
135removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): apply_rewrite (manually graded) ⭐
136removed
137removed-- Briefly explain the difference between the tactics `apply` and `rw`. What
138removed-- are the situations where both can usefully be applied?
139removed
140removed-- ### Supplying arguments to `apply`
141removed
142removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
143removed-- This note is probably dead...
144removed--
145removed-- AAA dislikes the `...with...` variants of tactics, which he feels don't
146removed-- work very well. But we (Arthur and BCP) decided to leave things alone
147removed-- for now, since removing `...with...` would require changing MANY
148removed-- proofs.
149removed
150removed-- The following silly example uses two rewrites in a row to get from `\[a;b`]
151removed-- to `\[e;f`].
152removed
153removedtheorem trans_eq_example (a b c d e f : Nat) :
154removed [a, b] = [c, d] →
155removed [c, d] = [e, f] →
156removed [a, b] = [e, f] := by
157removed intro eq1 eq2
158removed rw [eq1, eq2]
159removed
160removed-- Since this is a common pattern, we might like to pull it out as a lemma
161removed-- that records, once and for all, the fact that equality is transitive.
162removed
163removed-- Note to developers:
164removed-- `HIDE: Robert Rand: I found using m, n and o throughout this discussion
165removed-- super confusing -- m doesn't come between n and o! Rocq's eq_trans uses
166removed-- x, y and z, which is what I wanted to change this too anyhow.`
167removed
168removedtheorem trans_eq {α : Type} (x y z : α) :
169removed x = y → y = z → x = z := by
170removed intro eq1 eq2
171removed rw [eq1, eq2]
172removed
173removed-- Nowwe **should** be able to use `trans_eq` to prove the above example.
174removed
175removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
176removed-- `Is this still true?
177removed--
178removed-- Robert Rand: This one makes a nice workinclass. You can show
179removed-- the various ways around the problem, including named "with",
180removed-- unnamed "with", and (if you desire), explicitly providing the
181removed-- arguments to trans_eq.`
182removed
183removed-- But it doesn't *quite* work. If we simply tell Lean `apply
184removed-- trans_eq` after
185removed-- the `intro`, it can tell (by matching the goal against the conclusion of
186removed-- the lemma) that it should instantiate `α` with `List Nat`, `x` with
187removed-- `[a, b]`, and `z` with `[e,f]`. However, the matching process doesn't
188removed-- determine an instantiation for `y`, nor does it know which hypothese to use
189removed-- for the premises to `trans_eq`.
190removed
191removedtheorem trans_eq_example' (a b c d e f : Nat) :
192removed [a, b] = [c, d] →
193removed [c, d] = [e, f] →
194removed [a, b] = [e, f] := by
195removed intro eq1 eq2
196removed apply trans_eq
197removed sorry
198removed sorry
199removed sorry
200removed
201removed-- As we saw earlier, `apply` would generate new goals for these premises, and
202removed-- we could finish the proof by explicitly applying these hypotheses to those
203removed-- new goals. But we can also be more direct by supplying those hypotheses
204removed-- directly to `apply`.
205removed
206removedtheorem trans_eq_example'' (a b c d e f : Nat) :
207removed [a, b] = [c, d] →
208removed [c, d] = [e, f] →
209removed [a, b] = [e, f] := by
210removed intro eq1 eq2
211removed apply trans_eq [a, b] [c, d] [e, f] eq1 eq2
212removed
213removed-- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1, NOW):
214removed-- This and below are new (my addition), thoughts?
215removed
216removed-- In the previous example, we had to specify the `x` and `z` arguments to
217removed-- `trans_eq` before we could supply `[c, d]` for `y` or `eq1` and `eq2` for
218removed-- the premises. However, we just said that Lean was able to infer these
219removed-- arguments, so it's a bit redundant (and wordy) for us to do it. Thankfully,
220removed-- Lean allows us to use `_`s for positional arguments that it can infer.
221removed
222removedtheorem trans_eq_example''' (a b c d e f : Nat) :
223removed [a, b] = [c, d] →
224removed [c, d] = [e, f] →
225removed [a, b] = [e, f] := by
226removed intro eq1 eq2
227removed apply trans_eq _ _ _ eq1 eq2
228removed
229removed-- Aside: if we know the name of the argument we are supplying (in this case
230removed-- `y`), we can just name it directly and avoid typing any `_`s.
231removed
232removedtheorem trans_eq_example'''' (a b c d e f : Nat) :
233removed [a, b] = [c, d] →
234removed [c, d] = [e, f] →
235removed [a, b] = [e, f] := by
236removed intro eq1 eq2
237removed apply trans_eq (y := [c, d])
238removed apply eq1
239removed apply eq2
240removed
241removed-- Like any other kind of software, there are conventions and best practices
242removed-- associated with writing proofs in Lean. One of these conventions concerns
243removed-- the use of the `exact` tactic. When fully applying another theorem like in
244removed-- the previous examples, it is considered good practice to use the `exact`
245removed-- tactic instead of `apply`. This signals to a reader of the proof that the
246removed-- proof is "exactly" an instance of another lemma, and that nothing of
247removed-- particular interest is happening here. This achieves a similar goal as when
248removed-- a mathematician says that one result is "just" an instance of another.
249removed
250removedtheorem trans_eq_example_exact (a b c d e f : Nat) :
251removed [a, b] = [c, d] →
252removed [c, d] = [e, f] →
253removed [a, b] = [e, f] := by
254removed intro eq1 eq2
255removed exact trans_eq _ _ _ eq1 eq2
256removed
257removed-- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1, NOW):
258removed-- if we decide we want to introduce `calc` earlier, we can remove this
259removed-- explanation or tweak it. BCP: I think we did introduce it earlier...
260removed
261removed-- Lean also has a built-in tactic `calc` that accomplishes the same purpose
262removed-- as applying `trans_eq`. The tactic allows us to specify the in-between
263removed-- states of any transitive relation. The notation is reminiscent of the
264removed-- proofs you might see in a mathematics textbook.
265removed
266removedtheorem trans_eq_example''''' (a b c d e f : Nat) :
267removed [a, b] = [c, d] →
268removed [c, d] = [e, f] →
269removed [a, b] = [e, f] := by
270removed intro eq1 eq2
271removed calc
272removed [a, b] = [c, d] := by rw [eq1]
273removed [c, d] = [e, f] := by rw [eq2]
274removed
275removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): trans_eq_exercise ⭐⭐⭐
276removed
277removedtheorem trans_eq_exercise (n m o p : Nat) :
278removed m = o.minustwo →
279removed (n + p) = m →
280removed (n + p) = o.minustwo := by
281removed sorry
282removed
283removed-- ## The `injection` and `contradiction` Tactics
284removed
285removed-- Recall the definition of natural numbers:
286removed
287removed-- inductive Nat : Type :=
288removed-- | zero
289removed-- | succ (n : Nat).
290removed
291removed-- It is obvious from this definition that every number has one of two forms:
292removed-- either it is the constructor `0` or it is built by applying the constructor
293removed-- `.succ` to another number. But there is more here than meets the eye:
294removed-- implicit in the definition are two additional facts:
295removed
296removed-- - The constructor `.succ` is *injective* (or *one-to-one*). That is, if
297removed-- `n + 1 = m + 1`, it must also be that `n = m`.
298removed
299removed-- - The constructors `0` and `.succ` are *disjoint*. That is, `0` is not equal
300removed-- to `n + 1` for any `n`.
301removed
302removed-- Similar principles apply to every inductively defined type: all
303removed-- constructors are injective, and the values built from distinct constructors
304removed-- are never equal. For lists, the `cons` constructor is injective and the
305removed-- empty list `nil` is different from every non-empty list. For booleans,
306removed-- `true` and `false` are different. (Since `true` and `false` take no
307removed-- arguments, their injectivity is neither here nor there.) And so on.
308removed
309removed-- SOON: FSR'25 - I wrote an explanation for `have` here, though I feel its
310removed-- inclusion here breaks the flow.
311removed
312removed-- Lean's `have` tactic, used above, adds the given hypothesis to the context,
313removed-- but it first requires you to prove the hypothesis as a new goal.
314removed
315removed-- This technique for injectivity can be generalized to any constructor by
316removed-- writing the equivalent of `pred` -- i.e., writing a function that "undoes"
317removed-- one application of the constructor.
318removed
319removed-- As a convenient alternative, Lean provides a tactic called `injection` that
320removed-- allows us to exploit the injectivity of any constructor. Here is an
321removed-- alternate proof of the above theorem using `injection`:
322removed
323removedtheorem succ_injective' (n m : Nat) :
324removed n + 1 = m + 1 →
325removed n = m := by
326removed intro h
327removed injection h with hmn
328removed
329removed-- By writing `injection h with hmn` at this point, we are asking Lean to
330removed-- generate all equations that it can infer from `h` using the injectivity of
331removed-- constructors (in the present example, the equation `n = m`). This equation
332removed-- is added as a hypothesis (called `hmn` in this case) into the context.
333removed-- Because this equation is exactly our goal, in this case the `injection`
334removed-- tactic is able to automatically close the goal.
335removed
336removed-- Here's a more interesting example that shows how `injection` can derive
337removed-- multiple equations at once.
338removed
339removedtheorem injection_ex1 (n m o : Nat) :
340removed [n, m] = [o, o] →
341removed n = m := by
342removed intro h
343removed all_goals
344removed injection h with h1 h2
345removed injection h2 with h3
346removed rw [h1, h3]
347removed
348removed-- There is also a related tactic, `injections`, that applies the `injection`
349removed-- tactic to all your hypotheses at once, as many times in a row as it can.
350removed-- Using this tactic can avoid needing to repeatedly use `injection` on lists,
351removed-- for example.
352removed
353removedtheorem injection_ex2 (n m o : Nat) :
354removed [n, m] = [o, o] →
355removed n = m := by
356removed intro h
357removed all_goals
358removed injections h1 _ h3
359removed rw [h1, h3]
360removed
361removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): injection_ex3 ⭐⭐⭐
362removed
363removedtheorem injection_ex3 {α : Type} (x y z : α) (l j : List α) :
364removed x :: y :: l = z :: j →
365removed j = z :: l →
366removed x = y := by
367removed intro eq1 eq2
368removed injections hxz hyl_j
369removed have hyl_zl : y :: l = z :: l := by rw [hyl_j, eq2]
370removed injections hyz
371removed rw [hxz, hyz]
372removed
373removed-- So much for injectivity of constructors. What about disjointness?
374removed
375removed-- The principle of disjointness says that two terms beginning with different
376removed-- constructors (like `0` and `succ`, or `true` and `false`) can never be
377removed-- equal. This means that, any time we find ourselves in a context where we've
378removed-- *assumed* that two such terms are equal, we are justified in concluding
379removed-- anything we want, since the assumption is nonsensical.
380removed
381removed-- The `contradiction` tactic, which we've already seen for handling cases
382removed-- where we have assumed `False`, also embodies this principle: if we have a a
383removed-- hypothesis involving an equality between different constructors (e.g.,
384removed-- `false = true`), `contradiction` solves the current goal immediately. Some
385removed-- examples:
386removed
387removedtheorem disjoint_ex1 (n m : Nat) :
388removed false = true →
389removed n = m := by
390removed intro contra
391removed contradiction
392removed
393removedtheorem disjoint_ex2 (n : Nat) :
394removed n + 1 = 0 →
395removed 2 + 2 = 5 := by
396removed intro contra
397removed contradiction
398removed
399removed-- These examples are instances of a logical principle known as the *principle
400removed-- of explosion*, which asserts that a contradictory hypothesis entails
401removed-- anything (even manifestly false things!).
402removed
403removed-- If you find the principle of explosion confusing, remember that these
404removed-- proofs are *not* simply showing that the conclusion of the statement holds.
405removed-- Rather, they are showing that, *if* the nonsensical situation described by
406removed-- the premise did somehow hold, *then* the nonsensical conclusion would hold
407removed-- too (because we'd be living in an inconsistent universe where every
408removed-- statement is true).
409removed
410removed-- We'll explore the principle of explosion in more detail in the next
411removed-- chapter.
412removed
413removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): disjoint_ex3 ⭐
414removed
415removedtheorem disjoint_ex3 {α : Type} (x y z : α) (l : List α) :
416removed x :: y :: l = [] →
417removed x = z := by
418removed sorry
419removed
420removed-- For a more useful example, we can use `contradiction` to make a connection
421removed-- between the two different notions of equality (`=` and `==`) that we have
422removed-- seen for natural numbers.
423removed
424removedtheorem beq_0_l (n : Nat) :
425removed (0 == n) = true →
426removed n = 0 := by
427removed intro h
428removed -- We can proceed by case analysis on `n`. The first case is trivial.
429removed cases n
430removed case zero => rfl
431removed -- However, the second one doesn't look so simple: assuming
432removed -- `(0 == n' + 1) = true`, we must show `n' + 1 = 0`! The way forward
433removed -- is to observe that the assumption itself is nonsensical:
434removed case succ n' =>
435removed -- If we use `contradiction` here, Lean confirms that the subgoal
436removed -- we are working on is impossible and removes it from further
437removed -- consideration.
438removed contradiction
439removed
