14removed-- ## More powerful Natural Numbers
15removed
16removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
17removed-- Is Basics needed explicitly? And why are these here instead of at the
18removed-- top of the file?
19removed
20removed-- Until now, we have been working with our own custom natural numbers, using
21removed-- the `Nat` type that we defined in `Basics.lean`.
22removed
23removed-- However, Lean has a built-in type of natural numbers, which is more
24removed-- powerful and comes with many useful features. They are very slightly
25removed-- different from our custom `Nat`, but these differences are mostly
26removed-- superficial. The built-in natural numbers are defined in the `Init` module,
27removed-- which is automatically imported by Lean. We will refer to them as `Nat` as
28removed-- well, but they are not the same as the `Nat` we defined in `Basics.lean`.
29removed
30removed-- In Lean, programmers and mathematicians don't re-prove the basic properties
31removed-- of natural numbers from scratch, nor do they tend to write out `rewrite`
32removed-- steps for basic properties of natural numbers by hand.
33removed
34removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
35removed-- Just making a note that we need to explain the `zero.succ.succ`
36removed-- notation someplace well before this file!
37removed--
38removed-- Have we already explained sections, and how they differ from
39removed-- namespaces? Will it be clear to readers why we need one here? Can we
40removed-- choose a better name than `long_example`?
41removed
42removed-- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1):
43removed-- We turn off the postfix notation for our new definition of succ in
44removed-- `Basics`, should we also turn it off here for Nats? I really find it to
45removed-- be less readable, but maybe that's just me.
46removed
47removedsection long_example
48removedopen NatPlayground.Nat
49removed
50removed-- Previously, we did computation like this...
51removed
52removedtheorem test_mult1' : (two * two : NatPlayground.Nat) = four := by
53removed rewrite [two_eq_succ_one, one_eq_succ_zero]
54removed rewrite [mul_succ, mul_succ, mul_zero]
55removed rewrite [add_succ, add_succ, add_zero]
56removed rewrite [add_succ, add_succ, add_zero]
57removed rfl
58removedend long_example
59removed
60removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, NOW):
61removed-- The info viewed in the InfoView during this proof is kind of mysterious
62removed-- (to me) here. Have we already given people enough help to understand it
63removed-- here?
64removed
65removed-- This approach is useful in a textbook for understanding the structure of
66removed-- natural numbers and for providing early practice with writing proofs. But
67removed-- it is also tedious in the long term.
68removed
69removed-- Instead of doing this, programmers and mathematicians use the built-in
70removed-- `Nat` and the powerful features of Lean to *automatically* prove properties
71removed-- about natural numbers and to compute with them.
72removed
73removedtheorem test_mult1_nat : (3 * 3 : Nat) = 9 := by
74removed rfl
75removed
76removed-- The annotation `: Nat` tells Lean that we are using its built-in `Nat`
77removed-- type.
78removed
79removed-- In this chapter we will learn how to use the built-in `Nat` and some
80removed-- powerful features for computing with and proving properties about natural
81removed-- numbers. Specifically, we will learn about `dsimp`, `calc`, and `simp`
82removed-- annotations, which enable more powerful and concise proofs.
83removed
84removed-- In fact, from now on, we will use the built-in `Nat` type and its powerful
85removed-- features, writing `Nat.<theorem>` to reference Lean's version of
86removed-- `<theorem>`.
87removed
88removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
89removed-- Why can't we just write <theorem>?
90removed
91removed-- ### `rfl` and computation with `Nat`
92removed
93removed-- With Lean's `Nat`, much of the computation happens automatically, and `rfl`
94removed-- suffices to close any equality of computation on literals.
95removed
96removedtheorem complicated_computation : (2 * 3 + 4 * 5 : Nat) * 6 = 156 := by
97removed rfl
98removed
99removed-- This quickly becomes necessary, as natural numbers quickly get large!
100removed
101removed-- Of course, `rfl` can't close more complicated goals where the values of the
102removed-- terms are unknown.
103removed
104removedtheorem rfl_not_enough (n m : Nat) (h : n = m) : n = m := by
105removed -- rfl will not work here!
106removed /- First rewrite the goal with `h`; then the two sides are identical. -/
107removed rewrite [h]
108removed rfl
109removed
110removed-- The same proof can be written more compactly with `rw`. In this example,
111removed-- `rw [h]` rewrites with `h` and then closes the resulting reflexive goal.
112removed
113removedtheorem rfl_not_enough' (n m : Nat) (h : n = m) : n = m := by
114removed rw [h]
115removed
116removed-- We will continue to show more powerful tools for manipulating the context
117removed-- and goal of a proof to bring them closer to what can be solved with `rfl`.
118removed
119removed-- ## Using the Standard Library
120removed
121removed-- As part of using Lean's standard `Nat` type, we will also begin using
122removed-- theorems about `Nat`s from the standard library. Because we did not write
123removed-- or prove these theorems ourselves, however, we may not know all the
124removed-- available theorems off the top of our heads.
125removed
126removed-- Lean provides a few ways to search through the standard library to find
127removed-- theorems that may be useful during a particular proof. The first such way
128removed-- is the `exact?` tactic. This tactic searches the standard library for a
129removed-- theorem that can be applied, along with the hypotheses in the context, to
130removed-- exactly close the current goal.
131removed
132removedexample (a b : Nat) : a + b = b + a := by
133removed /- this will suggest that we use `exact Nat.add_comm a b` to close this goal -/
134removed exact?
135removed
136removed-- If you are using the Lean 4 extension in VSCode, the InfoView will have a
137removed-- blue `[apply]` button that shows the suggested theorem to close the goal.
138removed-- Alternatively, VSCode may show an inline suggestion (light bulb) button
139removed-- above the `exact?`. You can click either of these buttons to replace the
140removed-- occurrence of `exact?` with the tactic it found to complete the proof;
141removed-- idiomatic Lean does not leave `exact?` tactics (or any other `?` tactics,
142removed-- as we will see shortly) in the finished versions of proofs and instead
143removed-- replaces them with the tactics they found during search.
144removed
145removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
146removed-- Why do we say "Lean 4" in some places, instead of just "Lean"
147removed
148removed-- The `exact?` tactic is useful when we just need a single library theorem to
149removed-- get us over the finish line of a proof, but it is not so helpful when we
150removed-- are deep in the middle of a proof or are wondering how to get started on
151removed-- one. Luckily, there are other tactics that will help us with this.
152removed
153removed-- The `rw?` tactic works like `exact?`, except that it searches for any
154removed-- theorems that you could use to rewrite the current goal.
155removed
156removedexample (a b : Nat) : a + b = b + a := by
157removed /- this will suggest that we use `rw [Nat.add_comm]` to close this goal -/
158removed rw?
159removed
160removed-- However, unlike `exact?`, just because `rw?` suggests a theorem to you does
161removed-- not automatically imply that it will be useful. In the example below, many
162removed-- of the theorems `rw?` suggests will not progress towards completing the
163removed-- proof; you will need to carefully look through its suggestions to see which
164removed-- ones seem useful. We strongly recommend against blindly using `rw?` and
165removed-- accepting its suggestions without due consideration! You will find this a
166removed-- very slow and frustrating way to write proofs. Instead, we suggest figuring
167removed-- out what you would like your next step to be, conceptually, and then using
168removed-- `rw?` to search for a theorem that implements it. If no such theorem
169removed-- exists, that may be a sign that you need to prove it yourself.
170removed
171removedexample (n m q : Nat) :
172removed (n + m) + q = m + (n + q) := by
173removed -- lots of suggestions to look through here!
174removed rw?
175removed sorry
176removed
177removed-- Prove the following theorems about `Nat`s. You should not need induction
178removed-- for any of these; you can find the theorems you need using `rw?` and
179removed-- `exact?`.
180removed
181removedtheorem mul_three (p : Nat) :
182removed 3 * p = p + p + p := by
183removed sorry
184removed
185removedtheorem mul_three_beq (p : Nat) :
186removed (3 * p == p + p + p) = true := by
187removed sorry
188removed
189removed-- ## Structuring proofs with `calc`
190removed
191removed-- In Lean proofs, long `rw` chains are useful, but they are sometimes hard to
192removed-- read because the intermediate goals are invisible. Furthermore, sometimes
193removed-- we *know* exactly how we want to manipulate the terms of a proof, but don't
194removed-- want to have the tactics like `add_comm` and `add_assoc` "guess" which
195removed-- subterms to rewrite.
196removed
197removed-- The `calc` tactic writes down the intermediate goals of a proof, and allows
198removed-- us to specify exactly which rewrite rules to apply at each step. It is a
199removed-- powerful tool for structuring proofs, and is often more readable than long
200removed-- `rw` chains.
201removed
202removed-- `calc` is designed to mimic the style of proofs in mathematics textbooks,
203removed-- which will often look something like this:
204removed
205removed-- a + (b + c)
206removed-- = (a + b) + c ... [by associativity of addition]
207removed-- = (b + a) + c ... [by commutativity of addition]
208removed-- = b + (a + c) ... [by associativity of addition]
209removed
210removed-- Note how we can see each intermediate step of this proof when we look at it
211removed-- this way. Let's look at how we might prove this theorem (i.e., that
212removed-- `a + (b + c) = b + (a + c)`) in Lean.
213removed
214removed-- First, a proof in the style we already know.
215removed
216removedtheorem add_swap (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := by
217removed rw [← Nat.add_assoc, Nat.add_comm a b, Nat.add_assoc]
218removed
219removed-- Here we present the same theorem, written with `calc`. Note how each
220removed-- intermediate goal is visible in the source.
221removed
222removedtheorem add_swap' (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := by
223removed calc a + (b + c) /- one side of the goal is the argument to `calc`... -/
224removed /- ... and each subsequent line is a transformation, with a tactic. -/
225removed a + (b + c) = (a + b) + c := by rw [Nat.add_assoc]
226removed (a + b) + c = (b + a) + c := by rw [Nat.add_comm a b]
227removed /- once a line matches the other side of the equality in the main goal
228removed (in this case `(b + (a + c)`), the calc tactic succeeds. -/
229removed (b + a) + c = b + (a + c) := by rw [Nat.add_assoc]
230removed
231removed-- We can also write the proof like this to be a bit more concise:
232removed
233removedtheorem add_swap'' (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := by
234removed calc a + (b + c)
235removed _ = (a + b) + c := by rw [Nat.add_assoc]
236removed _ = (b + a) + c := by rw [Nat.add_comm a b]
237removed _ = b + (a + c) := by rw [Nat.add_assoc]
238removed
239removed-- Whereas before, the left-hand side of each equality in the `calc` tactic
240removed-- was repeated from the right-hand side of the previous one, we can replace
241removed-- the left-hand side entirely with an `_`. Now our Lean proof looks quite a
242removed-- bit like the textbook one we saw earlier!
243removed
244removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): succ_mul_succ ⭐
245removed
246removedtheorem succ_mul_succ (n m : Nat) :
247removed (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 := by
248removed rw [Nat.add_mul, Nat.one_mul, Nat.mul_add, Nat.mul_one, ← Nat.add_assoc]
249removed
250removed-- Given this proof with `rw`, rewrite it with `calc`. Reminder that you can
251removed-- use `rw?` to find appropriate rules to rewrite by.
252removed
253removedtheorem succ_mul_succ' (n m : Nat) :
254removed (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 := by
255removed sorry
256removed
257removed-- If you prefer `rw` to `calc`, that's fine! Each has particular uses, and
258removed-- both will be tools in your ever-growing toolbox of tactics.
259removed
260removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
261removed-- Needs some exercises!!
262removed
263removed-- ## Definitional simplification: `dsimp`
264removed
265removed-- Often, rather than rewriting by a known equation like
266removed
267removed-- `n + succ m = succ (n + m)` using `rw [add_succ]`,
268removed
269removed-- we just want to simplify the function (here `add`) automatically when we
270removed-- can.
271removed
272removed-- The `dsimp` tactic ("definitionally simplify") unfolds definitions and
273removed-- performs definitional simplifications. You can give it hints in square
274removed-- brackets: `dsimp [f]` tells it to unfold the definition of `f`. You can
275removed-- also simplify a hypothesis `h` in the context by writing
276removed-- `dsimp [...] at h`. `dsimp` will also close goals by `rfl` when possible.
277removed
278removeddef square (n : Nat) : Nat := n * n
279removed
280removeddef triple (n : Nat) : Nat := n + n + n
281removed
282removed-- When the goal depends on a fact about an unknown value, `rfl` fails. Here,
283removed-- `dsimp` makes progress, exposing a goal the fact can close.
284removed
285removedexample (n m : Nat) (h : n + n = m) : triple n = m + n := by
286removed -- rfl will not work here!
287removed dsimp [triple]
288removed /- The goal can now be rewritten by `h`. -/
289removed rw [h]
290removed
291removed-- As we have seen, `rw` can also unfold definitions. In this example, either
292removed-- style is fine: use `dsimp [triple]` when you want to emphasize definitional
293removed-- simplification, or `rw [triple, h]` when the proof is just a sequence of
294removed-- rewrites.
295removed
296removedexample (n m : Nat) (h : n + n = m) : triple n = m + n := by
297removed /- `rw [triple]` unfolds `triple n`. -/
298removed rw [triple, h]
299removed
300removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): dsimp1 ⭐⭐
301removed
302removed-- Complete this proof, using `dsimp` or `rw` as appropriate.
303removed
304removedexample (n m : Nat) (h : m = n) : triple m = n + (n + n) := by
305removed sorry
306removed
307removed-- `dsimp at h` also works on hypotheses, which rfl can't touch.
308removed
309removedexample (n : Nat) (h : square n = 16) : n * n = 16 := by
310removed dsimp [square] at h
311removed exact h
312removed
313removed-- Aside: `rw [...] at h` also works on hypotheses too, as does `rw? at h`
314removed
315removedexample (n m : Nat) (h : 2 * n = m * 2) : n + n = m + m := by
316removed rw [Nat.mul_comm, Nat.mul_two, Nat.mul_two] at h
317removed exact h
318removed
319removed-- `dsimp` also takes definitional steps such as `+ 0`, so it can finish goals
320removed-- that rfl would close.
321removed
322removedexample (n : Nat) : square n + 0 = n * n := by
323removed dsimp [square]
324removed
325removed-- Like `rw` and `exact`, `dsimp` also has a `?` version that searches for
326removed-- functions to simplify by. Many Lean tactics have `?` versions; try it out
327removed-- if you are unsure.
328removed
329removed-- Note to developers (Roger Burtonpatel @rogerburtonpatel, NOW):
330removed-- Hard pointer needed to this section once we versify. Also, we may want
331removed-- a pointer to where we introduce `simp` (and *maybe* `grind` in the next
332removed-- volume).
333removed
334removed-- ### A New Step Towards Automation
335removed
336removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
337removed-- This section reference should be a live pointer, at least in the HTML.
338removed
339removed-- In the section on `Irreducibility, Rewriting, and Proof
340removed-- Engineering` of
341removed-- `Basics.lean`, we hinted at introducing more automated tactics than
342removed-- `rewrite` for writing proofs. The first of these is `dsimp`: by using
343removed-- `dsimp`, we allow Lean to introduce a small amount of its own automatic
344removed-- reasoning using other basic tactics like `rfl`. If you're ever confused by
345removed-- what `dsimp` is doing, don't be afraid to switch back to `rewrite` to
346removed-- examine what's going on.
347removed
348removed-- Later in this volume, we will introduce the more powerful automated tactic
349removed-- `simp`, which can sometimes solve complex goals by itself and is
350removed-- accordingly extremely common in real-world Lean developments.
351removed
352removed-- But, using this tactic now does not help (in fact, it hurts!) the process
353removed-- of learning logical reasoning, formal theorem proving, and Lean.
354removed-- Additionally, real Lean programmers are careful when using automation: it
355removed-- can hurt the readability of a proof, and real-world Lean is often used to
356removed-- *communicate* a result as much as to prove it. We will continue to use only
357removed-- simple tactics, like `dsimp` and `rw`, for most of this volume so that you
358removed-- have a firm grasp of both the logic behind the proofs you are writing and
359removed-- the ways to structure those proofs to make your logic clear.
360removed
361removed-- ## Redefining Functions and Lemmas over Nats
362removed
363removed-- Now that we've switched over to using Lean's standard library, we can
364removed-- redefine some of the functions from the last few chapters on `Nat`s. Note
365removed-- that, for the built-in `Nat` type, the patterns `0` and `n + 1` correspond
366removed-- to `zero` and `succ n`. Likewise, the pattern `n + 2` is equivalent to
367removed-- `n + 1 + 1`.
368removed
369removed-- Prove some of these theorems using the techniques we've discussed this
370removed-- chapter.
371removed
372removeddef Nat.even (n : Nat) :=
373removed match n with
374removed | 0 => true
375removed | 1 => false
376removed | n + 2 => even n
377removed
378removeddef Nat.odd (n : Nat) := !(even n)
379removed
380removedtheorem Nat.odd_def (n : Nat) : n.odd = !(n.even) := rfl
381removed
382removeddef Nat.minustwo (n : Nat) : Nat :=
383removed match n with
384removed | 0 => 0
385removed | 1 => 0
386removed | n' + 2 => n'
387removed
388removeddef Nat.double (n : Nat) : Nat :=
389removed match n with
390removed | 0 => 0
391removed | n' + 1 => double n' + 2
392removed
393removed-- Note that we defined these functions in the `Nat` namespace; Lean's naming
394removed-- conventions advise that functions on a type should be defined in that
395removed-- type's namepsace in almost all circumstnaces.
396removed
397removed-- When we define functions this way, something interesting happens to the way
398removed-- Lean's InfoView prints them. Take a look at the info view inside the proof
399removed-- of this thoerem (i.e., before the `rfl` tactic):
400removed
401removedtheorem even_add_three (n : Nat) : Nat.even (n + 3) = Nat.even (n + 1) := by
402removed rfl
403removed
404removed-- Instead of printing the goal the way we wrote it in the theorem statement,
405removed-- Lean prints `(n + 3).even = (n + 1).even`! This is an example of Lean's
406removed-- *field notation*, whereby Lean prints functions inside the namespace of a
407removed-- type *after* their first argument, separated by a `.`. At first glance,
408removed-- this may appear similar to how object-oriented methods work, but it's
409removed-- really just a syntactic variation on the normal fu8nction-application style
410removed-- we've seen so far. That is, `Nat.even n` and `n.even` are just different
411removed-- ways to write the exact same term.
412removed
413removed-- In previous chapters we disabled this notation by putting
414removed-- `set_option pp.fieldNotation false` at the top of each file, but from now
415removed-- on we will leave it enabled, since field notation is recommended in
416removed-- idiomatic Lean developments.
417removed
418removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
419removed-- Cut this: "It can also be disabled just for a specific function or
420removed-- constructor by writing `attribute [pp_nodot] <Name>`." Do they need to
421removed-- know it in SFL?
422removed
423removed-- As an example, observe the difference in how Lean prints the goal in the
424removed-- following two examples:
425removed
426removedexample (n : Nat) : Nat.double (n + 0) = Nat.double n := by
427removed rfl
428removed
429removedattribute [pp_nodot] Nat.double
430removed
431removedexample (n : Nat) : Nat.double (n + 0) = Nat.double n := by
432removed rfl
433removed
434removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): even_succ ⭐⭐
435removed
436removedtheorem even_succ (n : Nat) :
437removed (n + 1).even = !(n.even) := by
438removed sorry
439removed
440removed-- Note to developers (NOW):
441removed-- talk about using `Nat.add_zero` and friends from now on.
442removed
443removed-- (OA) : added lemmas proved for our Nat for Lean's Nat to prevent later
444removed-- files from breaking.
445removed
446removedtheorem even_zero : Nat.even 0 = true := by rfl
447removed
448removedtheorem double_zero : Nat.double 0 = 0 := by rfl
449removed
450removedtheorem double_succ (n : Nat) : (n + 1).double = n.double + 2 := by rfl
451removed
452removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): double_add ⭐⭐
453removed
454removedtheorem double_add (n : Nat) : n.double = n + n := by
455removed sorry
456removed
457removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): double_mul ⭐⭐
458removed
459removedtheorem double_mul (n : Nat) : n.double = 2 * n := by
460removed sorry
461removed
462removed-- ## Using Code Actions to Generate Match Skeletons
463removed
464removed-- Lean's language server can suggest *code actions*, which are small editor
465removed-- commands that modify the source code. In VSCode, a light-bulb icon appears
466removed-- on the left when a code action is available at your cursor. You can click
467removed-- the icon or open the code action menu with `Ctrl + .` on Windows/Linux or
468removed-- `Command + .` on macOS.
469removed
470removed-- For more information, see [Lean 4 VS Code extension
471removed-- manual](https://github.com/leanprover/vscode-lean4/blob/master/vscode-lean4/manual/manual.md#code-actions).
472removed
473removed-- Some code actions can generate the explicit branches needed for pattern
474removed-- matching. This is especially useful when working with `match` expressions,
475removed-- or with tactics such as `cases` and `induction`, which we saw in previous
476removed-- chapters.
477removed
478removed-- Let's look at an example using `induction`.
479removed
480removed-- For example, suppose we start with the following incomplete proof:
481removed
482removedsf_expect_failure
483removed theorem foo (n : Nat) : Nat.beq n n := by
484removed induction n
485removed
486removed-- Put your cursor on `induction n` and open the code action menu. You should
487removed-- see "Generate an explicit pattern match for 'induction'." in the list. If
488removed-- you choose this action, Lean adds an explicit branch for each constructor:
489removed
490removedexample (n : Nat) : Nat.beq n n := by
491removed induction n with
492removed | zero => sorry
493removed | succ n _ => sorry
494removed
495removed-- This gives us basic structure of the proof without requiring us to write
496removed-- each branch by hand. We can then focus on proving each case.
497removed
498removed-- One possible proof is:
499removed
500removedexample (n : Nat) : Nat.beq n n := by
501removed induction n with
502removed | zero => rfl
503removed | succ n ih => rw [Nat.beq, ih]
504removed
505removed-- Note that Lean used `_` for the induction hypothesis in the generated
506removed-- `.succ` branch. At that point, Lean didn't know the unfinished proof would
507removed-- need to refer to the hypothesis. Since we use it in `rw`, we replace `_`
508removed-- with the name `ih`.
509removed
510removed-- In later chapters, we will see some tactics that can make such inaccessible
511removed-- names available again.
512removed
513removed-- The same trick also works for `match` expressions. For example, suppose we
514removed-- start with
515removed
516removedsf_expect_failure
517removed def isZero (n : Nat) : Bool :=
518removed match n
519removed
520removed-- Lean can generate the missing branches:
521removed
522removedsf_expect_failure
523removed def isZero (n : Nat) : Bool :=
524removed match n with
525removed | 0 => _
526removed | n + 1 => _
527removed
